I do not see how Canada
differs from the United States in that respect. We have internal trade. We have the "freedom" without the trade. There is no argument about that. The real prosperity in the United States is due to the fact that capital feels safe in its investment there; every man Who invests his money in business knows exactly the competitive conditions with which he is faced. He knows that he is not going to have unfair competition. He knows that Japanese and Chinese goods, made by labour that is paid ten cents a day, are not going to be dumped into the United States in competition with him, because he has the protection. So there is stability in that country; trade is regulated; there Is an ability to export in large quantities and to capture markets where people have not the good sense or the strength of mind to put up barriers similar to those erected by the United States.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend recognize that as between Canada, and its geographical conditions, its population, and so on, and the United States, the differences are tremendous?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My contention is that people have gone to the United States because they can better themselves, and they can better themselves because they can find jobs that pay. That is why they have gone there. As

to geographical conditions, they are not so dissimilar. If they have cotton in the United States, we have timber in Canada. But the difference is this:	they manufacture very
largely their cotton in their own country, or have done of late years, while we send our pulpwood and other natural resources to them to be manufactured and to give employment to their people; whereupon they send the manufactured article to Canada for consumption.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Suppose that an intending settler in Canada or in the United States were to listen to my hon. friend's speech, which country would he settle in?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Well, he would probably have a desire to contribute his good judgment to oust the Liberal government in this country and thus bring nearer the possibility of his remaining within its borders.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if my arguments are sound at all, why is there this tendency towards low tariffs? My submission is that it is entirely because of the Progressive party, and very largely their views from a purely economic point of view are sound. They say: We produce wheat in our country; we sell in the markets of the world and we buy in a protected market; therefore if we can eliminate the protective duties we may get our goods cheaper and have a bigger margin of profit or be able to sell more wheat in the markets of the world. That is a hard argument to answer from the economic point of view. If the country is to remain entirely agricultural in its character, the argument is a good one. But let us consider for a moment what element in value exercises this dominating influence upon Canada's fiscal policy. I have made a calculation from information furnished by the Bureau of Statistics, and I find that in 1924 the gross agricultural production of Canada was valued at $1,453,000,000. We are dealing, you will note, only with the one activity of agriculture. The value of wheat and wheat flour exported was $327,000,000, or 22 per cent of the total agricultural production. So that this 22 per cent, representing the views of the prairie provinces through the Progressive party in this parliament, are dominating the government and' the fiscal policy of this country. There is our trouble.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
You will have to remove
the Progressives; that is the only thing to do.

The Budget-Mr. Ladner

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, they are too good
fellows to remove. But my contention is that-

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
May I ask a question
right there?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
disagree with me on this point?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
put a duty on wheat in order to 'benefit the farmers of Canada?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, I would not. Personally I do not know much about duties, nor,
I think, do other hon. members know very much about them. These are things that should first be decided by people who do know, by a scientific board that will adjust our fiscal policy for the development of this country, and not for the development of any other country.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The hon. member has
stated that wheat and wheat products exported amount to $300,000,000, or 22 per cent. Will he tell us what the total agricultural exportation was, including animal and animal products?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I have not the total agricultural exportation, as I did not think it of importance for this reason: the markets of the United States for our major products have been largely cut off, and our products are now going to the Old Country and other countries where they have low tariffs and do not send back to us similar goods. This has relationship more with the United States.
In Canada we have manufacturing business to a very large extent. We have our minerals, and the business and industries incidental to them. We have our great forest products, lumber, pulp and paper. We have our Shipping interests, and our fisheries, to which there is also a manufacturing end. We have our trade by exporters and importers. We have financial houses, and we have other activities of a diversified character in which our people are engaged. Now my point is this: I do not think it is sound or in the interests of this country that 22 per cent of one industry should control the fiscal policy of the entire country affecting all these other industries.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
take the pains to look into the question of the total exports of Canada? If he does, he will find that agriculture is responsible for more than half the total exports of this country. Will he then say that agriculture dominates, though representing only 22 per cent?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I did not look into those
figures.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Why don't you?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I did not have the benefit of the advice of the hon. member at the time. If I had had the benefit of his wisdom before, I might have got those figures.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I will get them for you.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
But it does not make a
particle of difference. As a matter of fact, I believe there is some confusion as to just what is included in the figures of agricultural exports; I am only speaking from memory. But even if half our exports were agricultural products, he would stilt have to consider that we have a large number of other industries, mines and manufacturing establishments in this country which desire protection, and my point is that those who uphold this idea of low tariffs should not dominate the fiscal policy of this country where we are trying to develop a self-sustaining nation.
Mr. MILLAR,: In 1923, of the 400,000,000
bushels of wheat produced, what percentage was exported?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I have the figures here
from the Bureau of Statistics. I thought I had them handy. I have a letter from the chief statistician giving that data, but cannot lay my hands on it at the moment.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
We could only consume six
bushels per head; that would be 54,000,000 bushels. So we -must have exported all the rest.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My data comes from the
Bureau of Statistics and is checked with the trade reports. I am certain my data is accurate because I have taken particular care with it, and I worked out the same data last year, and have compared this year with last, and I am certain the figures are correct. I want to repeat, for the benefit of hon. gentlemen to my left, with whom I have the most agreeable personal relationships, but with whom I disagree in the most decided manner on the fiscal policy that is best for this country, that the fiscal policy of Canada is to-day being determined by a small proportion of the agricultural interests, in total disregard of the manufacturing interest and all the other economic activities throughout the country. I say that is not sound, and although political expediency may justify and maintain that policy in force to-day, time and experience and the force of public opinion will! eliminate it because, if persisted in, it will ruin the country.
The Budget-Mr. Ladner

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The hon. member has stated that a very small proportion of the country is endeavouring to dominate, and is dominating, the fiscal policy of the country to the detriment of the majority. Might I ask what proportion of the people of the country voted in 1921 for a much lower tariff than we have at the present time?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Sometimes the public are not informed of all the facts. Sometimes they hear so many stories, even from the lips of the Prime Minister of Canada, and if he were here he would ask me to show line and page, that they really do not know where they are at, and it depends largely upon the individuality of the man when they make their election. But the fact is that to-day they are feeling in their pockets, and in their business and in their affaire the effect of the policy which is prevailing in this country, and they are going to change it sooner or later just as they changed it in 1878.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Is the hon. member really serious in stating that it is his belief that the west is dominating the economic policy of the country?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Absolutely. I do not
think there is much question about that, and I do not think the hon. gentleman thinks there is much question about it. If it had not been for the Progressive party and their influence upon the government, the government wouid have had a higher tariff than we have now, but in that case the Progressive party would not have voted for the budget last year, just as they are voting against the budget this year because the tariff is not coming down. The government is between the devil and the deep sea. They promised one thing in 1919, and several members promised many things, and the Progressives say that they have practically the same platform as the Liberals, and the inevitable result is that the government are losing the confidence of the people.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Which is the devil?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I do not like to be personal.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I asked this question of the speaker yesterday, and I notice they have not got it in Hansard as I meant it, but whether that is my mistake or somebody else's, I am not going to say. The hon. member is trying to argue that by the government yielding to the Progressives we are in a much worse shape, particularly our industries, than we were in 1921 when the Conservative government was in power. If that is the case, how is it that the report of the Compensation

Board for the province of Ontario shows that the industries of the province of Ontario paid out in wages in 1924, $9,000,000 more than they paid out in 1921? In the face of that report, does the hon. member argue that we are in worse shape now than we were then?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I cannot vouch for the
accuracy of the report. I prefer to judge by studies I have made of statistical data, and by what I have learned through coming in contact with people doing business in the country. It is fallacious to say that because you have paid out more wages in one year than another, therefore all these things follow; they do not necessarily follow at all. There are a hundred and one factors to be taken into account. The actual fact is, and the hon. member knows it, that we are overburdened with taxation in Canada to-day, and business is not good. Even the Minister of Labour will admit that.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The working men have the proof in their pockets, a/t all events, that they have $9,000,000 more to-day than they had in 1921.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Nobody is more pleased to hear that than I am, but does the hon. gentleman seriously suggest that business in Canada is good?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
It is better than it
was.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: That is always the government's answer. Year after year they always say, it is better than it was. It is like a frog climbing up a well one foot at a time and slipping back two.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
indicate some country or countries in the world that are comparatively speaking better off than Canada?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Yes, France.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Capital levy.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I had occasion to make
careful inquiries in order to get accurate information. The industrial conditions and the condition of the farmers in France are better than in Canada. It may be temporary, but the conditions in France and in the United States are better than the conditions in Canada. People go from Canada to the States.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend not speaking only >of the employment situation in France?

The Budget-Mr. Ladner

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: No, I am speaking of business conditions, exports, employment and wages. You can hardly hire people there, the demand for labour is so great.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: It is being done on borrowed money.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Lots of people run their
businesses in that way. Some of our Progressive friends have said that they were running farms on borrowed money but they were still happy.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Is the value of the French franc and our dollar to be taken into consideration?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
[DOT] The determining factor in the situation is the workman. He is working all day, comes home at night, has his food and clothing and something to put in the bank and it does not matter how you work out the value of the franc.
Hon. members were asking about duties a moment ago and I have a word to say about that question. I had an inquiry made in the Bureau of Statistics as to the ad valorem rates of customs duty on dutiable goods imported into Canada as compared with the United States respectively for the fiscal years 1870, 1880, 1890, 1901, 1911, 1923 and 1924. Now I think we can learn from the experience of others. The figures are as follows:

imports-	Per cent Per cent

So that during the last fifty-five years the customs duties on dutiable goods entering the United States as compared with Canada have been from 50 per cent to 235 per cent higher than those in Canada. Yet when you go there to live, pay taxes, and buy your food and 'clothing, you pay less taxes, pay less for your food and clothing, you have more employment and are better able to save and put a little money in the bank. What further proof does any reasonable man want than that of the soundness of the policy?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean when he says that he pays more taxes here than in the United States?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had
been here ia few moments ago he would have heard the figures I gave at that time.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My hon. friend had
reference simply to the tariff taxes.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, I have reference to
all taxes, the burden on the people. If the hon. gentleman wishes to take the income tax, I tell him it is from two to six times as much in Canada as in the United States.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
permit me to make a statement?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
If it is not too long, go
ahead.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I have lived over there
and I know personally that my taxes were a good deal higher than they were when I came to Canada. At the present time they are higher all the way through in the United States than they are here. I know that because I have lived in both places, and I am acquainted over there now just as well as the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Perhaps it is some years
since my hon. friend lived there. I have my information on good authority, not guess-work. It is vouched for by people who know the facts from accurate data.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Before my hon. friend proceeds, would he not think it much fairer to make the comparison with rates on total imports, rather than on dutiable imports?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, I would not, because
in figuring out the customs duty, the thing which concerns us-that is if the incidence of taxation falls upon the consumer in the country to which it is consigned-is the amount you pay on the dutiable goods.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: In the case of a nation which admitted 95 per cent of the goods free and levied a duty of 100 per cent on the balance of 5 per cent importation, would it be fair to compare that with a nation which has a flat rate of 10 per cent on all imports? Does the hon. gentleman not see that in one case they paid a tax of 100 per cent duty and in the other case they paid only 10 per cent? Does the hon. gentleman not see the point?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Yes, but you can work
these things out in different ways. I have worked it out according to the manner in which the authorities work it out when they want to get at the true facts of the case. I have been told the proper way to figure it out is the method I have adopted, and I do not think there can be much argument about it.
The Budget-Mr. Ladner

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Is there a higher duty collected per capita in the United States than in Canada?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I have not the information on that point.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My hon. friend lacks
a lot of information he should have.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The hon. gentleman lacks a good deal of information too, or he would not be advocating the idea he is now propounding. It is very easy to ask about an isolated case which particularly appeals to the questioner, but I do not pretend to be a walking encyclopaedia,

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Can the hon. gentleman tell
us how much higher the duties were under the Conservative government than under the Liberal government?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I am not talking about
party politics. I say the Conservative party never did impose a protective tariff in this country, and they would have been better off if they had done so.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Why did they not do so?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I suppose they were trying to be friends with the Progressives, and this government will come to the same disastrous end if they maintain that unholy alliance.
In submitting the proposals which I have presented and the ideas which I have advanced, I have done so not merely because it is in the interests of Canada, but. because in British Columbia it is of very special and great importance. British Columbia is the third largest manufacturing province in Canada. We have 2,407 industries, employing 23,700 employees, in which there is invested $210,000,000, producing last year $163,000,000. That is the business of manufacturing. Then we have the business of mining, the total results of which last year amounted to $49,000,000. Our greatest industry is lumbering and pulp. We have invested $190,000,000 in sawmills, pulp, paper and logging. The export trade after eight years has increased from 43,000,000 feet to 500,000,000 feet. There are 40,000 people employed in the lumbering business and allied interests, with a total payroll of $50,000,000 a year. We are not lacking in agricultural activities. We produce $61,000,000 in agriculture and in shipping $23,000,000. Our shipping business is developing. We have forty-two regular steamship lines running out of the city of Vancouver.
These facts : disclose diversified interests. British Columbia is a miniature Canada, and the people who live and who are engaged in

business in British Columbia know full well if the province is to develop just as Canada is to develop, we must as far as possible manufacture the raw products in this country instead of exporting them to other countries to build up their cities and towns and to provide work for their workmen. We are confronted daily with that situation. A large quantity of our raw material goes across to the state of Washington where our minerals are put into smelters and our logs into the lumber industry. But the provincial government, realizing the advantages to be derived from stopping undue export of our raw materials, have imposed restrictions upon the export of logs, so that the American investor has seen fit to bring his manufacturing business into British Columbia and to do his business there. In British Columbia, as I have said, we have a miniature Canada; we have diversified interests. We want to provide business or employment for different people, for the farmer, the miner, the fishermen and people of that kind.
Let me say a word about the Australian treaty. It is difficult to know why the government has not taken a more decided and active interest in the Australian treaty. We are especially interested in British Columbia because we expect to benefit by it, chiefly as regards the salmon industry. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, canned salmon section, sent this telegram to myself and no doubt to other members from British Columbia. It is in these words and they are significant: Failure of government to ratify Australian treaty owing to opposition on part certain members parliament to proposed increased duty on dried fruits-
It seems to me I know where that comes from.
-from other than Australian sources will have effect on British Columbia salmon canners of depriving them of very substantial market for their product in Australia. That market heretofore supplied principally by American canners and opposition to proposed treaty if successful will react exactly in manner hoped for by American interests in enabling them continue dominate Australian market as they did in New Zealand prior to our securing preference there. Trust you will use best efforts with opponents' treaty in House in interest securing largely increased market for Canadian salmon which would inevitably follow treaty adoption.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Is it not a fact
that my hon. friend's leader (Mr. Meighen) publicly opposed the treaty with Australia in a campaign in British Columbia last fall?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I have never heard of
such a thing. The probability is that he questioned the delay of the government to act. The government have failed in initiative. If they do not want the treaty, they should say: No, we do not want the treaty, and then men carrying on business with Australia would know

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
what to do and make their contracts accordingly. It is the old question of vacillation, lack of action. They are in the balance. They know who their masters are and they stand there in fearful delay that is prejudicial to the interests of this country.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
favour the treaty?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Yes. I favour any trade treaty that is reasonably worked out as good for the country.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Does the hon. member really think it fair that the people of Canada should be asked to pay more for raisins just to benefit the saknon canners of British Columbia?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
That is the same old fallacy and delusion as regards free trade. It all comes down to this:	If you put a tariff on,
you pay extra money. The incidence of taxation does not always follow that. The amount of money the hon. member would pay for the currants 'he would eat would be disproportionate entirely to the benefit we would receive through increased production in canned salmon. Of course, it is a difference of opinion.
I wanted to say a few words on the oriental question, but my time is limited. We have had advocated in the country and here with the government certain measures with respect to restricting the activities of Chinese and Japanese in British Columbia. I realize, in speaking on a matter of this kind, it is a delicate question and requires mature judgment to work out the best method of safeguarding the interests of Canada. In my judgment we should not allow orientals to come into British Columbia. We do not want them in British Columbia. They cannot be assimilated into the economic activities nor into the social life of our country. They are not inferior, but they are incompatible in temperament. As regards those Chinese and Japanese who are in British Columbia now, my judgment is that it is difficult to control by legislation their economic activities. If you restrict the number who are allowed to have fishing licenses for salt herring or some other fish, you eliminate four or five hundred Japanese out of that industry. They must live and they have the right to freedom in this country to engage in something. They will exercise that by going into some other industry. They have gone into the business of growing berries, and now the Berry Growers' communicate with us-and I have some communications from them-saying that it is not right that Japanese and Chinese
should work in competition with the berry growers, and they think they should be taken out of this industry by legislation. So if the government pursues a policy of legislating the kind of business in which these people shall not engage, they will go into some other kind of business. They will go into farming. If they are legislated out of farming,, they will work at something else. In other words, acts of parliament to control economic activities of that kind are futile as aigainst the economic laws. When people are in our country with limitations of reason and judgment and after certain exemptions are given to special oases, it is consistent with the dignity of Canada and the interests of our relationship as a nation with the other great nations with which we expect to establish trade and commerce, that we should be careful in passing legislation of that kind. It is not effective. It assists, let us say, fishermen by taking a certain number of orientals from that industry, but it hurts another group of men engaged in another business. I have not quite finished and I would rather conclude my remarks after eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

Mr. Chairman, I quite

It should be borne in mind that there are no shareholders in this company, only policyholders. The annual meeting is called, at which the general business of the company is transacted. One of the most important functions at that annual meeting is the election of directors. Let us get the background clearly before us. I think we are all agreed that we want legislation passed that is uniform and, as far as possible, free from beclouding clauses that might be capable of various interpretations. Consequently parliament in its wisdom passed what we know as the general Insurance Act of 1917. That act is supposed to be in the very best possible form. Like the Bank Act, it is revised periodically, and, as many hon. members will recall, it was revised very carefully a year or two ago.
I want to draw this to the attention of the committee. This company, which in years gone by was not under the general Insurance Act, is by this bill brought under it; that is, the company willingly places itself under the act, so that all the regular provisions of that act apply to it. In this case the original charter provided for the appointment of a certain number of directors, the maximum being twelve. Now it is desired to fix the minimum at twelve and the maximum at twenty-one, bringing it into harmony with the general Insurance Act. And it does something further. This company-and I say this not for the purpose of advertising the company because I happen to be a policyholder- this company is one of Canada's most outstanding insurance companies, and it is one of the best managed. It wants to come into harmony with the general Insurance Act and, furthermore, it wants to make its directorate more representative. I understand that the policyholders of my own province have expressed a desire to have a director on the board, and I think a similar desire has been expressed by policjdiolders in the province of Quebec, where it is desired to have two directors, one English speaking and the other French speaking. This is desired in order

to make the board completely representative of the whole Dominion. The clause under discussion provides particularly for the fixing of the number cf directors at a special general meeting. The general Insurance Act, and nearly all if not all the provincial companies acts, provide that special general meetings shall be called for special purposes. Let us consider the section for a moment; and I shall confine myself to the section under consideration. It says:
The property, business and affairs of the company shall be managed by a board of twelve, fifteen, eighteen or twenty-one directors. The company may, by the said by-law, provide that the directors or any of them, shall be elected for one,

maintopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext:
When the House took recess at six o'clock I had been discussing some questions of protection and had not concluded my remarks, when my friends askied some questions, being interested in the subject, or rather perhaps I should say they were not interested in it. I had intended to give as an example of the unreasonableness of the relative protective tariffs or the relative tariffs in Canada and in the United States in regard to the commodity of eggs. Our American friends in the state of Washington informed us that their chief market for eggs was the city of New York and the city of Vancouver. With their cooperative system they were able to send their

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
eggs into Vancouver against a duty of three cents a dozen, but when my friends in British Columbia desired to return the compliment by sending eggs to the state of Washington they were met with a duty of eight cents a dozen. We have a large quantity of eggs coming in from China. The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is supposed to have a Marking Act, or something by which he can restrict or limit that importation, but we find that he does not do so. Either his regulations are at fault or his free trade theories prevail. Nevertheless Chinese eggs are coming in and are a source of considerable comment and objection, on account of the unfair treatment of the people of our province.
I think perhaps the best example of the government's efforts to make fruitless the effectiveness of the law is disclosed in the Duncan report. The anti-dumping law was applied, and legitimately so, at the request of the producers of fruit. The duty was paid, and when everything had died down, so far as public disclosure was concerned, at the request of the combine the government calmly paid back, consistent with its free trade ideas, the anti-dumping duty, and the suppliers of fruit kept on sending it in, knowing perfectly well that they were dealing with the department in a manner that would enable them to escape payment of duty all the time by this questionable method. The facts are disclosed in the Duncan report. There has been no action. I have noticed that one of these very provinces decided that they would not take action so far as the Duncan report was concerned and stated that it was the responsibility of the federal government. No doubt the government will make their decision shortly.

I am afraid the government will dilly-dally along, no action will be taken, and the trusts, combines and mergers will prevail, notwithstanding the good commencement in their restrictions. It seems to me that the practices as disclosed in the Duncan report are so reprehensible, so much in defiance of the law and against the will of parliament, that the government should and ought to act expeditiously in this matter 156i
and if the province does not intend to take action, the federal government should do so.
I wanted to say a few words on an important question affecting ' our province, namely the question of freight rates. Not seeing the Prime Minister in his seat at this moment, I believe that our friend, Mr. John Oliver is rapping at his door to gain entrance for consideration of this question, and as the Premier of British Columbia does not smoke and the right hon. leader of the government will not be able to give him a cigar, I am wondering what he will give him on this occasion. The freight rates question has been standing a long time. The government was going to bring down1 a great announcement, embodying the principle of some kind of Magna Charta, for the benefit of downtrodden Canada. But it has not come. They were going to remedy this freight rates question. The Supreme Court of Canada followed the law and made a decision which has caused confusion and distress in many places throughout Canada, so that business concerns are unable to make their plans and injustices are being practised from one end of the country to the other. I take it that freight rates have four main purposes, and I am quoting from a pamphlet of a Mr. Payne which seems to summarize the matter effectively: First, in the aggregate results, to provide for operating expenses; second, to earn fixed charges on outstanding liabilities; third, to yield a fair and reasonable return on capital investment, and fourth, to leave a credit balance for the purpose of needed additions and betterments. I think that will appeal to the reasonable good judgment of every hon. member; but we are not going to obtain those purposes by political freight rates or by cases of political expediency or political alliances by building up such an instrument of turmoil as the Crowsnest pass agreement, so far as it is applicable to-day. Every day we read in communications from the west and also from Ontario objections by boards of trade and other public bodies of all kinds. Yet we find no action on the part of the government. The House has been sitting for several months and very little has been done on this most important question. In fact, so far as I can see, very little has been accomplished in regard to any other question. We are just drifting along; we shall soon be in the hot weather and be running home, not knowing what we have done or why we have done it. It is interesting to note that, compared with other countries, freight rates in Canada, calculated on a basis of earnings per ton-mile
The Budget-Mr. Ladner

of railways, are lower than in any other country. They are as follows:

I give these in detail because I want the record on Hansard. Therefore, if we are going to accomplish the four-fold purposes that I mentioned a moment ago and maintain rates which are already low and retain our system in a position that it will not only meet the fixed charges but warrant onfidence on the part of the investing public, something must be done at the present time to grapple with the situation. We from British Columbia, believe; in fact, we know that for many years there has been an unfairness in the treatment of that province in respect to freight rates on many of our important articles. We have had a partial remedy. We have had the mountain scale of rates reduced by one-half, and this clearly indicates that the principle of the mountain scale of rates is wrong. We say that the balance should be eliminated. There are other injustices, inequalities, which should be remedied, and for my part I would not like to see parliament make political freight rates for either British Columbia or any other part of Canada. You can make freight rates only by the advice and judgment of people competent to determine the question, and those people are the institution created by the late Laurier government, the Board of Railway Commissioners. I think it would be a great mistake if parliament attempted to deal with this question and to have brought to bear upon members of parliament as well as the government political influence which will be calculated only to bring about results suited to the interests of some particular section because it has political control. It will be a disaster for the country if we are faced with a situation of that kind.
