If there is not a good chairman on the board, the government is here to rectify the situation. That is the 9 p.m. duty of no one else. I suggest to the hon. member that I doubt very much whether he or any of his friends, faced with the responsibility, would place upon parliament the determination of the freight rates question in this country. I think they would prefer some tribunal qualified by experience in the matter to determine such a complicated question. I hope the government will at some time speak, because there is a patient and long-waiting public in British Columbia seeking to find out exactly the policy of the government on this freight rates question. The government is no doubt in a difficulty. They are no doubt face to face with their masters, and the Crowsnest pass agreement is one of the big things which my friends to the left would like to hold and carry back to the prairies and, without doubt, seek to get some political advantage out of in a contest. I speak quite sincerely when I say I hope and believe individual members looking to the interest of Canada as a whole will have the breadth of mind and altruism of spirit that they will be disposed to leave a question of that kind outside of the realm of politics and entirely within the realm of a body capable of dealing with it. Certainly parliament is not such a body.
Before sitting down, I should like to draw to the attention of the government the fact that the amendments to the Pension Act are still not brought down. I should like to remind the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), if he were here, of that challenging and defiant speech which he made on the

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
last day of parliament, when parliament was about to prorogue and nobody could answer him, as regards what he was going to do with the Senate as they had done such grievous injury to the soldiers of Canada, when in fact, by the deliberate intention of the government, I believe, the government deferred bringing that measure down in the House and placing it before the Senate so that the latter could have no time to discuss and pass it. This session of parliament is passing on. We assembled on the 5th February; two months and a half have gone by, and the measure is still within the confidence of the Minister of 'Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mb Beland). Communications have come to me and, no doubt, similar ones have come to other hon. members from soldier bodies throughout Canada asking what is going to happen and saying: Do you calculate the Senate is going to interfere with the legislation? But the government refrains from taking steps so that they could place this legislation before the Senate and enable the Senate to consider it and so that they could charge them with the full responsibility of their act. I hope the government will make more haste this year than they did last, not leave it until the last days of the session and then blame everyone in the country but themselves for the fact that the legislation is defeated.
In this connection I want to say a word on a matter I have not heard discussed in the House and which sooner or later is bound to engage the attention of parliament, and that as the question of providing for those exservice men who through the technicalities of the law are denied a pension but who gave their sendees overseas and whose health in so doing was impaired. The time will come when that class of men and others in their old age will have to be considered by parliament and the people of Canada; we shall have to take into consideration those of our returned men who having given their services overseas now find themselves in a helpless and destitute condition, unable to provide for themselves. At that time it will 'be necessary in my judgment, and indeed it will be the duty of the people of Canada, to make provision for these men. I have advocated this before and I advocate it again to-night; and I trust that the government in considering legislation looking to this end will see fit to bring in some measure that will adequately take care of this class of our citizens. Finally, I would express the hope that the government will before long not only bring down those measures to which I have referred and in which the provinces are
interested and are waiting for some decisive action, but that they will show some decision in dealing with the many questions before parliament. I hope we shall have no more alliances between the government and our friends to the left, that the government will no longer show those hon. gentlemen undue deference, but rather that they will bring to the House legislation calculated for the welfare of the people of Canada.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
shall not endeavour to follow my hon. friend in all his meanderings through the labyrinth of figures which he has given to the House on the budget. My hon. and learned friend is a distinguished lawyer, and I could very well and easily juggle with the figures in the way he has done. But I am satisfied that no matter how he manipulates them he is bound to come to the same conclusion as the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has reached. One thing though that did surprise me, knowing the hon. gentleman as I know him, was that, genial companion as he is, he should put on the cloak of pessimism and treat this country in the way he did'. He made the statement that for some time past there has been a steady flow of Canadians into the United States. I have not taken the time to check him up in every detail, but I do know that the last report shows that 35,152 Canadians icame back from the United States in the period of eight months ending November 30 last. There is no steady flow of emigration from Canada into the United States. The hon. gentleman has said that one of the reasons why some of the European population did go there was that they were attracted by the news that came from that country. But it is equally true that some of our Canadians were attracted by the same news; although once they got there and spent a few months in the country they found it advisable to come back. For after all, as they found, there is no place like Canada to live in.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If 35.000 have come back
will the hon member tell us how many have gone over?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The balance is increasing on our side every day. The hon. gentleman will not dispute the statement that within the last few months they have been coming back at an enormous rate, and I for one know that in the city of Ottawa, where there was a scarcity of skilled mechanics two years ago, there are now more skilled mechanics than we can employ. The men

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
are coming back continuously. I shall not go any further with the remarks of my hon. friend. Before proceeding I should like to say how happy I am to join with all the other speakers who have preceded me in extending to the A-cting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) my congratulations on the budget he has brought down.
I shall speak only on one or two outstanding features of the budget, for as I .agree with what the minister has said it would be useless to labour it at any great length or to repeat what has already been brought to the attention of the House. The most conspicuous fact brought out in the budget is the improvement which it shows over last year, while last year was the first fiscal year in a very considerable period when the budget had been balanced. And not only is the budget balanced this year, but we have a surplus of 81,800,000.	In making that statement the
Acting Minister of Finance rightly said, that the people of Canada should feel justifiably proud of this result, and I believe myself that the Canadian people, irrespective of political allegiance, will be particularly glad to know that our finances are being stabilized and improved. I feel quite confident therefore that when again we go before the people they will place their confidence in those who in a very short term of years have brought about such an improvement in the financial condition of this country.
There is another feature that strikes us in all this avalanche of figures. Notwithstanding the fact that the taxes have been reduced by some $50,000,000 odd the national debt has been decreased by $36,000,000. That is an achievement of which the Canadian nation should be proud; only in a few instances has it happened that the national debt has been reduced.
One matter of outstanding importance which I shall touch upon is the magnificent showing of the Canadian National Railways. I am sure the people of Canada look with pride on our National Railways and that they are grateful to the administration for the splendid manner in which the system has been operated. I am not one of those who believes in state ownership; but when we found ourselves in the position we were in with our railways, and when the policy of the government was announced and advocated and the government decided to give the railways a fair and honest trial, I made up my mind to do them equal justice myself. I am not yet convinced however that it is a good scheme; yet we have been loyal in our endeavour to help out the National Railways. And in that we have been seconded by a very capable board of

administration. I am confident therefore that if we continue that trust and loyalty in the Canadian National railway system; if we continue that administration; and if that administration continues to manage the system as it has managed it in the past, very soon the railways will be on a sound financial basis and probably the Canadian government will not be called upon to assist them.
I desire now to turn to something more .parochial: the budget serves that purpose in a number of instances. I might not have referred to it but a number of previous speakers have spoken about the Civil Service Commission. I am not going to speak at any length on that subject because my views upon it are quite clear; I have expressed them on a number of occasions. And they are .particularly laid down in the report of the civil service inquiry of 1923 of which there are over 1,150 pages. Unfortunately, I am responsible f,or .practically half of that volume. I have laid down there What I thought to be the true state of affairs. I say that the Civil Service CommissiQn is attempting to administer an impossible law. I believe that those who inspired that law did not realize at the time the consequences that would flow therefrom. I cannot conceive that anyone imbued with an elementary idea of efficiency, of assuring promotions according to merit, in all cases, at all times and at the least expense, would put on the statute books a law of that character.
There are .many aspects of it. It is a cast iron law, there is no flexibility about it. The deputy ministers are deprived of a large amount of their authority and are rendered practically powerless. I cannot blame those who are now endeavouring to administer the act; but I do blame those who placed it on the statute book; I do blame those who, when any honest endeavour is made to Correct and improve the act, for some partisan purpose oppose every amendment; I do blame those who, moved by some sanctimonious sentiment, consider the Civil Service Act as a holy of holies, against which no hand should be raised, not even with the view of improving it. The moment we say that we want to improve that law they reply, "Thou shalt not touch it." It is something like old King Tut's grave, that if you .place an unholy hand upon it you shall die. And in a number of instances the Civil Service Act has proved to be a King Tut's grave to the ambitions of a large number of civil servants.
The Civil Service Commission may be viewed from another angle, and that is with regard to the present salary revision. I say that 98 per cent of the civil servants earn every cent of their salary, just as much as

The Budget-Mr. Chevner
98 per cent of the employees of any large corporation fully earn their salaries. I say without fear of contradiction, for I know whereof of speak, that the service is not underworked, nor is it overmanned, but I say also without fear of contradiction that the service is underpaid. I know a certain number of gentlemen here will not agree with me, but had they lived in the city of Ottawa all their lives, had they themselves been employed, as I have, as civil servants, had most of their relatives and friends been employed in the civil service, had they felt what the civil servants are feeling to-day, and what I felt then, they would not make the statements they are making derogatory of civil servants. The salary revision must be settled onoe for all, and it can only be settled when those who are charged with the administration of public affairs give it an honest and fair study. When they give to the Civil Service Commission and to the civil service that study which they merit, then those unwarranted attacks will cease, and those who came to scoff will remain to pray. They will say then just what the leading statesmen of Great Britain say about the civil service there; and the civil service of Britain is no better and no worse than the civil service of Canada. The British civil service is doing its work loyally for the country-just as much as the civil service of Canada is doing its work loyally by the country. The statesmen of Great Britain treat their civil service with the respect which it deserves; and the civil service of Canada is entitled to the same consideration. Now, what do the British statesmen say? I take this from the Ottawa Journal of April 2 1925:
The annual dinner of the British civil service recently took place in London and was as usual a brilliant affair. It was honoured with the presence of royalty and of the most illustrious personages of the realm. In the long list of distinguished guests were the Prince of Wales, the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the House of Commons, the Chancellor of Exchequer, the Foreign Secretary, the Lord Chief Justice, the Chief of the Imperial General Staff, and so on.
The Prince of Wales warmly eulogized the British civil service, and proceeded to say:
"It is difficult, if not impossible, for anybody to express in words the extent of the debt which this country owes to succeeding generations of civil servants, who, as government followed government, have never failed to serve with unquestioned loyalty and efficiency."
What difference is there between that and the loyalty and efficiency of the civil service of Canada?
In proposing the toast of "His Majesty's Civil Service," Premier Baldwin, after referring to the ephemeral life of governments and the permanency of the civil service, stated:
"It is a great pleasure for me to be present once more at your dinner and to be allowed the privilege of paying my tribute to the British civil service-the finest service of its kind in the world."
Had he seen the Canadian civil service he would have said, "One of two of the finest."
Amongst other things, Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, said:
"The British civil service upon the whole, and amongst many others, is the strongest and most enduring bulwark of the power and integrity of the British people."
Addressing himself to the civil service, Mr. Austen Chamberlain, Foreign Secretary, said:
"We remain to all eternity your grateful debtors."
And the Journal adds:
Such is the attitude of British statesmen towards the civil service. Very different is that of Canadian politicians towards our own civil service, which is the object of their constant attacks.
There is another paramount defect in the civil service law, in that the Civil Service Commission in their discussion of this salary revision are advised by their own officers, 95 per cent of whom have never had any practical experience in the working out of civil government, most of them having been taken into the Civil Service Commission without any practical knowledge of department work. Whatever knowledge they have acquired has been since they joined the staff of the commission. They are the ones that are charged with the reorganization, with the recommendations, with the determination of the accuracy of the reports. They are passing upon the qualifications of men and women, particularly of men, who have been in the civil service for thirty or thirty-five years, while these officials have been in their present positions probably no longer than since 1919. True, the deputy ministers, it may be said, are acting also for the civil servants and for the government. But theirs is a dual responsibility, and this brings me to what I consider to be a paramount defect-that the civil servants themselves are not represented in these deliberations that concern themselves most. I advocated the amendment of the act-it will be found in this report-to overcome this defect, but I am prepared to say that hon. gentlemen across to my left and to my right would immediately vote against such a resolution if I moved it here. I say that in all these deliberations the civil servants should be represented. I have advocated the introduction of something like Whitley councils. When I was in London I had a lengthy interview with the Speaker of the House of Commons, the Hon. Mr. Whitley, who inaugurated these councils, and I am corresponding with him. The main defect of our system is that in these deliberations everything is cut and dried and the civil servants

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
themselves, the very people who are most vitally interested, are never consulted. Some hon. gentlemen may say that it is hard to please a considerable number in so large a service. Why, if say sixty thousand people in any large industrial concern were not taken into the confidence of the employer there would be much less harmony, very much more discord, than there is at present in the ranks of the civil service.
This salary revision question is a difficult one. I have given it considerable attention. I do not know what the recommendation will be of the Civil Service Commission. They may have made a recommendation to council or they may not; I do not know; but I have my own views on the subject and I will give them for what they are worth. I have consulted a large number of civil servants; I have conferred with heads of organizations; I have digested all the evidence and have come to my own conclusions. In doing so I have had in mind the principle of equal pay for equal work. I have not disregarded the status of married civil servants, in other words, those who are considered eligible for household bonus. But I do believe there should be no discrimination; the range of salaries dhould be increased for all. I find, however, that it would cost a considerable amount of money to provide what I thought would be a fair salary range and I have been obliged to dwindle it down-. Of course my remarks may not influence the Civil Service Commission at all, but at all events I think they are justifiable. I do not believe any one should start in the civil service at less than $900. The next class should be $900 to $1,200; the third class, $1,200 to $1,500; the next class, $1,500 to $1,860; and the next $1,860 to $2,340-doing away with the bonus. Everyone in that case would receive not what I consider an adequate compensation for the work which is being done, but at all events something that would be commensurate with the loyalty of the services.
There is a third point upon which I wish to touch; and I quote now from one of the memoranda that was submitted to me in this matter. Referring to the superannuation law, it says:
Although it is recognized as a very generous measure, providing as it does a competent allowance for the maintenance of the retired civil servant and an allowance more or less generous to dependents, it is yet susceptible of improvement.
It could scarcely be supposed that an act could be framed that would at once make equitable provisions for all the intricate cases existing in the service, and it is reasonable to suppose that the government is prepared to receive requests that amendments should be made to the act.
IMr. Chevrier.]
And it was on that understanding last year that I gave it the study and attention that I did. I shall not go into the suggested amendments at length, but will just refer to a few of them. For instance, the retiring age is a very important feature; the authorities agree that about sixty-five should be the age of retirement, and superannuation should be at the option of the employee at any age after sixty. The act as it stands now makes it seventy-five, and the result is that avenues of promotion are blocked to a number of civil servants. But a very obnoxious amendment -and I do not use that word with any disrespect-was added to the bill last year; it is one of the most drastic changes in the act. The House passed the bill without any amendment but in the Senate the four per cent provision was made applicable to the arrears of contributions. With the permission of the House I would like to read just one letter, which is typical of many others but which puts the whole thing in a nutshell. I quote:
Under the present conditions we have the option of surrendering one half of our length of service,, instead of paying the accumulated arrears of the five per cent abatement, plus four per cent simple interest on the same. This surrender of one half the unpaid years of service of course very materially reduces the chances of ultimately obtaining full pension, unless the employee is fortunate enough to be of an age which enables him to serve on long enough to complete the required thirty-five years for full pension, or seventy per cent of his salary.
May I interject here that I honestly believe that when that amendment was introduced no one who took part an the discussion had the slightest conception of the difficulty it was going to create, of the hardship it was going to bring about, of the impairment it was going to cause in a law designed to retire those who had reached the retiring age. I quote further from this letter:
However, when a man reaches the age of sixty years this is almost an impossibility, because the retiring age is set for sixty-five, and in exceptional cases for the age of seventy.
Now, here is the case. This civil servant says:
In my own case I have put in forty years of service, during the first thirty-five of which I paid no five per cent abatement of any kind-was not permitted to do so; but for the last five years I have paid this five per cent of my salary. The accumulated unpaid abatements together with the four per cent interest thereon amount, in my case, to about $6,000, which of course makes it out of the question for me to pay, and consequently I have to take the option of the surrender of one-half of my unpaid service. This as above stated, is thirty-five years, so that I would have to surrender seventeen and a half years, leaving me'with a similar length of service, together with the five years that I have paid; so that after forty years' service I am only credited with twenty-two and a half years on which my pension can be computed, and I have to take chances on being able to carry on for a few years
! i t !TI

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
longer to try to attain as long a period of service for pension as possible; and as I am now in my sixty-first year the chances of obtaining the full thirty-five years of service for pension are almost impossible, as I could not serve for twelve and a half years longer even if I should be in condition to do so, as I should have passed the limit of seventy years of age.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did that official
not have the option of retiring under the Calder Act?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but as the distinguished hon. member is well aware, he was not entitled under that act to superannuation and the benefits attaching to it. He could have retired under the Calder Act, which was a generous measure, but that act had no superannuation features.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You mean, for his family?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. When I say, superannuation, I refer to all the features that go with superannuation. Under the Calder Act the civil servant was not given superannuation ; but superannuation means that he gets a certain amount every month and that after his death his wife benefits to the extent of one-half of what he had been getting. Under the Calder Act he got simply a lump sum.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I beg pardon, I am
wrong; the Calder Act was based upon the length of service, in relation to which a certain amount was given.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only difference between the Calder Act and the recent Superannuation Act is that the former did not provide for the family.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, we are agreed on that. But the Superannuation Act does so provide, so that there is an immediate benefit, and that is the reason why we struggled so hard to get a superannuation law to replace the Calder Act-because there were superannuation features for tthe dependents after the death of the employee which were not given by the Calder Act.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask, as a
matter of information, how that four per cent provision would affect the man who retires, not under extraordinary circumstances such jas have been mentioned by my hon. friend, but in the ordinary case where a man has completed about forty years' service?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It does not apply to the Calder Act. Nobody wants to take the Calder Act, or very few do, if they can take
superannuation under the other measure, but they will be driven to taking the Calder Act if they have to pay such exorbitant amounts to come under the new superannuation law.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Calder Act is now repealed?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have until the 19th of July, I think it is, to elect between the two.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought the Calder Act expired in November last.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am just going to ask that it be extended.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think we will see that you do not extend it.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am awfully soriy that my hon. friend should take an anticipatory view. Probably if I had given expression to some feelings, I might have said considering the success I have had in past attempts to modify the law, my proposition to extend it would have ended in King Tut's grave.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the case of a civil servant who has retired and is receiving a pension, and who afterwards takes a remunerative position, does the pension cease or continue?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He cannot take another position in the service.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Outside the service.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh yes, he can go outside and endeavour to earn his living. It was a bargain that after he had served thirty-five years, he would be entitled to full pension, and that if he had served less than thirty-five years but more than ten, he would be entitled to retire for ill-healtlh or on other grounds stipulated in the law. That is the bargain that was made and once the civil servant has done his part of the bargain, and once the government has complied with the terms of its side of the bargain, the civil servant may do as he pleases. He may go out and work and endeavour to increase his income, and his pension is not touched. I think that is only equitable.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he retires on account of ill-health does that also apply?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether he would be well enough to work. He might write a book, he might become an author or a member of parliament, and there is nothing wrong in that. He has served his country for a certain period and is entitled after he has served the time stipulated to receive his

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
pension. We are not the masters of to-morrow. A man may be ill to-day and unfit for service, and be well again to-morrow. So I see nothing wrong in that provision.
I will just mention another head-I will not discuss it-and that is with regard to unmarried contributors in particular, but of all in general. I would suggest that contributions should be returnable without interest to the contributor, his dependents or estate as the case may be, without limitation, at any time that he may quit the service. That is, this superannuation measure was brought in for one purpose, and that was to help in the elimination of those who had reached a certain age and could not give the full benefit of their activities in the same proportion that their remuneration came to them. But in order to achieve that, wie must not make it so difficult that they will refuse to take advantage of the terms. On the other hand, if we give them a superannuation measure and make it so stringent that people will be deterred from coming into the service because they know it is going to cost them too much, then we are more or less biting off our nose to spite our face, because the law will not work. In a number of cases, if this provision is allowed to remain, people who would feel like making the civil service their career will be deterred from doing so because they will argue: If I serve for nine years, and then for some reason have to get out, I shall lose all the money which I have paid in.
Now to come to the kind interruption of my hon. friend who asked whether the act had come into force.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman
takes up that phase, would he permit an inquiry? I understood him to say that he had had a conversation with Hon. Mr. Whitley on the operation of the Whitley councils in England, but I did not gather from what Hon. Mr. Whitley had said, whether he was satisfied with the application of the Whitley council to the civil service, or whether he was dissatisfied.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I was in England, I was there in no official capacity whatsoever, and I had, of course, no official status when I discussed this matter with Hon. Mr. Whitley. I was simply looking for information. He did not seem to think there would be any difficulty in the way of applying the Whitley council scheme, or probably some modification of it; he seemed to think that would be quite feasible, though not, probably, in the form of the Whitley councils as they

are known in England in their application to commercial life.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They have it already in the
service, have they not?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but of course,
Hon. Mr. Whitley, gracious as he was, was not going to say to me:	Undoubtedly you
can apply that to your service in Canada. But I gathered from his remarks that he saw nothing that would militate against it. Considering the present state of this new superannuation measure and the difficulties that go with St, I think the government would be well advised if they considered extending the time beyond the 19th of July next within which the civil service may elect to come under the act. If the government was to give some assurance that some of the amendments I have suggested would be considered this session, then probably the time would not require to be extended, and a larger number of the civil sendee would take advantage of the superannuation measure.
Mr. Speaker, I have said a few things about the budget; I have said something about what I consider very important to my own constituency. M'ay I now be allowed to say just a few words on what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Me-Quarrie) the other night said was a great privilege, and that was our visit to South Africa. I shall not be as lengthy as he was, not that I could not say as much, but because he has in a very able manner graphically described all that took place. I want to treat it from a different angle, and I do not propose to follow him up the meanderings of the Zambesi and along. May I in this connection say a word or two with reference to	the	Empire	ParliamentaryAssociation, the guests of whom we were on that wonderful trip. I take this from one of the reports of the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, who, as everybody knows, is the secretary of	the	Empire	ParliamentaryAssociation. Let me say that there is a vast difference between the Inter-parliamentary Union, and	the	Empire	Parliamentary
Association. I am now speaking of the Empire Parliamentary' Association:
The organization is upon strictly non-party lines.
There is a branch in each parliament of the empire, for the purpose of providing introductions and hospitality to every self-governing country of the empire for members visiting from other such countries, and also for providing for travelling facilities, special information, parliamentary privileges, meetings among members of parliament for the discussion of matters of mutual interest, and general machinery enabling parliamentarians both to hold more constant intercourse by

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
visiting other portions of the empire with a minimum of expense, and also to obtain the maximum of useful information they might require to collect in the time at their disposal.
It was the South African branch of the "Empire Parliamentary Association that organized this trip. I want to say just a few words as to our arrival in Durban. Hon. Senator Boyer, who represents the Vaudreuil or Soulanges district in the Senate delivered a speech at Durban, and presented to the city of Durban a photograph of the monument which is now to be seen in Montreal, of Sir Benjamin Durban, who founded Durban, and who died in Montreal. South Africa is a wonderful country. I do not want to go over the itinerary of the trip, as I said a moment ago, as that was so well done by the hon. member for New Westminster the other evening. However, I cannot resist the temptation of saying one word as to the things which struck me most forcibly.
As one looks back on South Africa he cannot forget the spell of the Karoo or the majestic grandeur of the Drakensberg, with the rapturous beauty of the valley of the Thousand Hills; nor shall I attempt any des-scription of the fascination of the Kalahari, the tranquil placidity of the Zambesi, flowing so calmly through the enchanting borders of luxuriant vegetation, nor the appealing and awe-inspiring spectacle of Victoria falls; nor shall I make any attempt to express to you the deep fascination of a night on the veldt, beneath the incomparable star-studded heaven, with the eternal breeze wafting over the veldt; that never-to-be-forgotten, peculiar odour of the dried, parched, sun-burned day, drinking the dew under the silvery beams of a moon, the like of which I am sorry to say I have not seen in Canada. Nor shall I attempt to picture the wonderful variety of flowers that bloom in myriads, twenty-four hours after the refreshing rain; and no one could describe the exquisite variety and beauty of birds that people the forests of Knysna, of Southern Rhodesia and other portions of that enchanted land. Those memories one may cherish, but they are beyond description.
But what struck me most was the fortitude of the people of South Africa. South Africa is not an easy country in which to settle and those men and women who did settle there had to pay a great price, but when they do pay that price the reward that South Africa brings is well worth fighting for. I think I owe a debt of gratitude to the Canadians who settled in South Africa, and they have not been mentioned. At Pretoria I met Mr. Pearson, who for twelve
years was an employee of the Royal Canadian Mint at Ottawa, and who is now Deputy Master of the Mint at Pretoria. At Salisbury we met Mr. Cleveland and his wife, who settled in Africa some thirty years ago. Mr. Cleveland came from British "Columbia and his wife from the Maritime provinces. They are now the owners of immense tracts of land, comprising fourteen large farms. Curiously enough, his son was in the employ of this government in the pension board and is now practising medicine in Vancouver. I also met Sir Charles Coghlin, who is now Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia, and he told me how happy he was at seeing the Canadian delegation, and particularly of meeting those he knew so well, the hon. Speaker of this House and hon. members, and he gave us details of that wonderful occasion in 1910 at the inauguration of the South African Union, when our distinguished Speaker of the House, representing Canada, delivered a wonderful oration. I met a number of people in South Africa who well remember that memorable day. We also met General Smuts at Rustenberg. who spent the whole of one day and an evening with us on the train. In the geological museum at Pretoria I was pleased to see quite a number of exhibits of Canadian minerals, and particularly a wonderful sample of mica from the Wallingford1 mines at Perkins Mills, just a few miles from here in the Gatineau valley.
As I said before, we were sixty-three days on South African soil. The British delegates, the Australian delegates, the New Zealand delegates and the Canadian delegates, with the South African delegates lived together either in close intimacy on the train or in the hotels, but particularly in the 'large centres, very much closer to the South African people. We were in close intimacy with the delegates and people of South Africa in that we shared their family life, slept under their roof, ate at the same table, and had a number of conferences with them, and discussed the many difficulties which confronted the administration of South Africa. In that way we really entered into their mode of thinking, we understood more readily their ideals, their ambitions and their desires. We came into close contact with their problems and difficulties, and appreciated in a better way the struggle which is theirs for continued advancement of their country, but above all, we were in a better position to appreciate the kindness, the warmth of feeling, and the generous hospitality of these people. We have learned to appreciate, to esteem and to love them. We

I desire to call the
attention of the government to the despatch which appeared in the press of Friday from Melbourne, Australia, as follows:
Melbourne, Australia, April 23.-(Via Reuter's.)- Premier Stanley M. Bruce has replied to a cable from Premier Mackenzie King of Canada on the matter of re-opening the Canadian-Australian trade treaty negotiations, the Commonwealth premier declining to do so.
Premier Bruce, in his reply, says he regrets his inability to agree to Premier King's suggestion that the discussion on the proposed trade treaty should be re-opened. The Australian Premier says he is now awaiting the decision of the Canadian Parliament on the treaty.
May I ask if the despatch fairly represents the facts, and if it does, if the government is in a position to make a further statement as to its purpose?
[Mr. ArchambaultJ
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister):	I decline to make any
statement based on newspaper reports. Certainly the despatch as read does not represent accurately the situation between Australia and Canada at the present time. The last communication I had from Premier Bruce made inquiry as to certain changes we were proposing to make in what was the original basis of our agreement. That telegram has not been replied to as yet, but it will be replied to very shortly. I may mention also that after Australia had made the changes in her treaty which she had agreed to make she also made certain changes with respect to the conditions under which goods would be admitted under the treaty, which conditions had not been discussed before. By order in council the Australian government adopted a condition that, Canadian goods might not be given the advantage of the changes made in the Australian tariff, unless-as I understand it-75 per cent, of the labour and materials were of British origin. That feature was never considered when the discussion relating to the changes in the tariff took place between the two governments, and until we get that phase of the question definitely understood we do not propose to ask this House to make any changes in our tariff, because it is a very material factor in the matter. I might say that the government has decided to have Mr. Ross, who was in Australia before, return to Australia to conduct further with the Australian government such negotiations as we may have with them, in the hope that we shall get matters so adjusted as to bring about a final arrangement that will be satisfactory to our government as well as to the Australian government.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
Africa is now manufacturing a very fine quality of cement. We were privileged to visit that exploitation field and we found that the cement manufactured there is about 98 per cent pure. While we were on the Mozambique coast we noted that the graphite produced on the isle of Madagascar is supplanting the graphite we produce here. So it is that when we are brought in touch with these facts it becomes our duty to bring them before the Canadian people in an endeavour to apply a remedy, and if possible to attract some other line in order to make up for what we are losing in that particular direction.
It is therefore certain that the preference is a definite determining factor in Canada's favour in respect to the following commodities: condensed milk, wrapping paper, rubber tires, canned fish, oatmeal, fencing, and binder twine. These are commodities which ordinarily could be obtained by South Africa to equal advantage elsewhere. In respect to the remainder of these principal entries the preference is undoubtedly of great assistance. Among lesser commodities the preference is of undoubted value to Canadian exporters of the following goods: paints, hardware, iron and steel bars and pipe, tools and implements, wood'enware and furniture, pumps and machinery, leather, chemicals, musical instruments, glass bottles, canned foods, knitted goods and brushware. These latter commodities I enumerate because they are general items which would benefit largely from an extended South African preference. None of these commodities is on the South African free list at the present time, and only four, namely, glass bottles, pipe, certain classes of machinery and leather are in class 4, on which 100 per cent preference is already given.
On the other hand, what is the value of the Canadian preference to South Africa? As I have stated, with gold and diamonds marketed under monopoly, wines explicitly excluded by Canada in granting preferential treatment, and wool, coal, mohair, wattle bark and maize on the Canadian free list, the value of a Canadian preference to South Africa is very seriously curtailed. The only commodities now dutiable in Canada which interest South Africa to any appreciable degree are dried fruits, fresh soft fruits, and to a very limited degree, sugar. As a matter of fact sugar may be more or less disregarded, because of the limited South African surplus for export and its high local manufacturing cost.
May J be permitted for just a few moments to deal with a few items that I think should be of interest from the point of view of the making of a bargain with South Africa looking to the promoting of trade with that country? Take oranges, for instance: the production in South Africa in 1923 was 1.009,000 boxes. The quality was comparable with that of the Canadian import. Canada used on an average about 1,000.000 cases and the source of supply for Canada was 95 per cent from the United States, most of the remainder from the British West Indies, and some from Spain. Could not some of that import be taken from South Africa? Of pears, the production in South Africa was 759,000 boxes, and the quality was comparable with that of the present Canadian import. Canada imported 17,800,000 pounds, and the source of supply was entirely the United States. In peaches the production in South Africa was
4,406,000	boxes and the quality was comparable with the best Canadian imports. The source of supply to Canada was entirely the United States. In 1923 Canada imported 13,-
406.000	pounds of peaches. Of plums South Africa produced 365,000 boxes, of a quality, however, not equalling that of the larger part of the Canadian import. Canada imported 140,000 bushels, entirely from the United States. Of grapes the production in South Africa was 15#,000 tons, of a quality comparable with the Canadian import. Canada imported 5,103 tons, the source of supply being entirely the United States. Of maize, the South African export was 1,128,314,250 pounds, the quality being comparable with that of Canadian imports. Canada imported 9,227.416 bushels, the source of supply being the United States. I cite these figures in the hope that when the conditions permit something may be done with a view to having trade arrangements in these commodities entered into with South Africa.
Now, let me deal for a moment with the question of oranges. It is entirely a matter Gr transportation. TIig dist-siico i*? not. t.oo great, and the quality and price are right. As to maize, any tariff concession on this commodity would be of extreme value. If all maize were subject to the 7i cents per bushel to which maize for distillation is liable, and this were accorded to South Africa as a preference, the result ought to swing this valuable business from the United States to the Union. So far as fresh deciduous fruits are concerned, given the transportation, this business could be developed either with or without preference, as Canada is paying more for her winter fruit at present than South Africa realizes in her principal market.
In conclusion I would suggest some action to induce the Elder Dempster Steamship Company to return to Canadian ports, and the
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier

establishment of a Canadian duty upon oranges and maize for the purpose of offering South Africa a substantial preference. A preference upon dried fruits comparable to the present advantages accorded to Australian dried fruits might also be advisable.
As I said a moment ago, While at Cape Town I spent some time in the office of our trade commissioner, Mr. Stevens. Mr. Stevens was preceded in that office by a very distinguished gentleman who is held in high esteem throughout South Africa and whose name I heard at Cape Town, at Durban and as far north as Salisbury; I refer to Mr. Egan, now Deputy Minister of Immigration. But Mr. Stevens is somewhat handicapped in the handling of the office down there. Mr. Stevens has not said anything of the kind to me, but so far as my observations have led me to conclude, I think he should be allowed a little more latitude, and particularly a little more in the matter of pecuniary assistance. I would have been delighted to have had the advantage of Mr. Stevens' knowledge throughout this trip in South Africa, and particularly if he had been allowed to accompany us through the peninsula. I think it is only fair, if we want to have our trade with South Africa or other distant parts of the empire develop, that when these questions come up we Should, not be too niggardly in the matter of the expenses that go with the administration of those offices. It is always exceedingly difficult to appreciate the difficulties that exist down there. For instance, to travel between Cape Town and Johannesburg or Pretoria, where the administration offices are, does not seem to us to be any distance at all, but it entails a considerable amount of expense and also a considerable amount of time.
Passing along, after leaving Cape Town, we returned to England about the 18th of November. It was my good fortune to spend a few weeks in London, and my greater good fortune to meet quite a number of times our distinguished representative there, Hon. Mr. Larkin, and I desire to assure everyone that our interests are very ably looked after over there by Hon. Mr. Larkin and 'his most efficient staff. I referred the other evening to Canada's status in the empire and to the talk of appointing an ambassador to Washington. I am one of those who believes that it is time, and high time, to appoint an' ambassador to Washington; I believe that is only consistent with Canada's dignity and importance, and I want it clearly understood that if I advocate the appointment of an
[Mr. Chevrier 1
ambassador to the United States, that does not in any way derogate from my fidelity and loyalty to the British Crown; but I feel that we have reached that stage of national development where we can have our own representatives in the other portions of the world. We talk of appointing an ambassador to Washington, and yet we have in London i but a high commissioner, and in Paris an agent. To my mind, there is an absolute inconsistency between these three terms. These two officers in London and Paris respectively are held by two Canadians of the highest distinction, who fill those positions in a way that reflects the greatest credit upon Canada, and it is with a feeling of pride that one hears their praise repeated by all those whose good fortune it has been to come in contact with them. But the same thing cannot be said of the premises wherein they do the best they can for the national development of Canada and for her reputation abroad.
It was my good fortune also to be invited to Australia House, when the Attorney General for Australia, Sir Lyttleton Groom, was in England on his way back to Canada and Australia, and really I was ashamed of myself and of the way Canada is looking after its representatives abroad when I compared Kin-naird House or the Agency in Paris with Australia House or the South African quarters. Australia House is within a stone's throw of Kinnaird House, and has the most luxurious, sumptuous reception halls.
It is a building all by itself, where one feels at home, and where the products of Australia are exhibited in a way that is quite as commendable as the exhibits one sees in Windsor station, Montreal, or in other places where the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National show the products of this country.
I was really surprised, and after having been received with the kindness and hospitality and warmth of sentiment that marked our reception at Australia House there was but one consolation, and it was that if our premises at Kinnaird House are so cheap, so poor, so out of keeping with Canada's status, at all events the warmth and cordiality of our reception by Mr. Larkin, both in our own building and later at his own house, not only was on a par but it did go much deeper to my heart than the reception we received at the other buildings.
That brings me to say a word with reference to the changing of our Canadian quarters in London. Something has been said with reference to the purchase of the Union club. Now I do resent and feel very deeply the remarks that are made by some hon. gentlemen

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
who whether they know whereof they speak, or, I will not say know not, but who speak without a Ml knowledge of the facts, in reference to the location of our quarters in London. I have visited the Union club building; I have seen what improvements are being made, and I am perfectly well satisfied, both as a member of this House and as a citizen of Canada, that what has been done has been done in the most commendable way, and that no expenditure has been made which should not have been made, and that it is a building consistent with the standing of Canada. I do resent the statement which was made that this building is situated in a blind alley. Statements like that should not be made. People who have visited London and are well aware of the layout of the city know that this club is not situated in a blind alley, but in Trafalgar Square, on the comer of Cockspur street, with the National Art Gallery at the back, and leading up to the Strand and Australia House. I was so impressed with what was being done while I was there that I made certain notes of my own, and asked for certain information which I will give to the House now. I have put this down in writing so that there will .be no misunderstanding as to the exact 'location, if any hon. gentleman wants to locate it afterwards.
The building is situated on the west side of Trafalgar Square and the frontage-120 feet- on the Square occupies practically the entire west side. The second frontage-72 feet- and chief entrance surmounted by an imposing pediment, will be on Cockspur street, which is the main thoroughfare of traffic from the city to the West End. The south side of Trafalgar Square is enclosed 'by Cockspur street. The corner formed! and occupied by the Canadian building is probably the principal site in the heart of the West End of London. If any gentleman says that this is located in a blind alley, he is the one who is blind. The National Art Gallery faces Trafalgar Square from the north and occupies the whole of that side. The South African government building faces the east side of the square and the Canadian Pacific Railway building from the south, which position was secured by that company many years ago.
In addition to these, the following buildings or office premises are located within a stone's throw of the Union club:
The Sun Life Insurance Company Canadian Pacific Railway offices Royal Mail Steam Packet Company's offices Cunard Steamship Company, Limited H. M. Government of Norway International Sleeping Car Company Canadian National Railway
Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Company Orient Steam Navigation Company, Limited Thomas Cook & Sons
Brown Bros. & Company, International Bankers The White Star Steamship Company and subsidiaries Credit Lyonnais The Carlton Hotel
On Northumberland avenue and the Strand, immediately opposite, are:
The Grand Hotel
Victoria Hotel
Metropole Hotel
Charing Cross Railway Station
Then within five hundred yards of this corner are:
Colonial Office War Office The Admiralty The Privy Council Foreign Office Home Office India Office Scottish Office Treasury
Ministry of Agriculture
Board of Trade
Ministry of Labour
Ministry of Health
Office of Woods and Forests
Then as to the accommodation we find there: At present the High Commissioner's office in ICinnaird house has 5,238 square feet; the emigration office on Regent street has 5,549 square feet; the pension office, on Oxford street, has 1,800 square feet; and the Trade Commissioner's office, on Basinghall street, 700 square feet. The four offices, absolutely unconnected one with the other, are on four different premises containing 13,287 square feet. The idea is to bring them under the same roof, and the new building will provide 26,971 square feet, which will give a surplus available for extension of about 3,700 square feet. I will not give the House the history of the acquisition of these properties, I will reserve that for another occasion; but the consensus Oi opinion in England, on the part of people who are not financially interested in this question at all, is that the 'bargain is a good one. My own impression is that it was a good bargain and that we should have no fear or apprehension or doubt about it. Personally I am prepared to say, after having seen the property, after having looked it over, after having heard what it cost, and after having heard what the rentals are in proportion to the other buildings ini the neighbourhood, that it was a good bargain.
It was also my privilege to spend a few weeks in France, and there I met Hon. Mr. Roy-not our ambassador, not even our high commissioner, but the agent of Canada. Not-
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier

withstanding his unimpressive title Mr. Roy is a man well qualified to shed lustre on the title of ambassador in France, just as Mr. Larkin reflects credit upon his office in England. But the status of Canada's representative in France is simply that of agent. There also I found that somewhat the same conditions prevailed as in London. I have no hesitation in saying that the offices of Canada's representative on the Boulevard des Capucines are far from being in keeping with the dignity which Canada should maintain on French soil. I make this Statement-and I make it without any fear of contradiction by any hon. gentleman who has been in France-that the room of Hon. Mr. Roy is far below the character of the quarters provided for a number of officers of this House; and that the room of many members of this parliament is far better equipped than the room of our agent in Paris. When one enters this long room one sees an old time-worn table in the centre and time-worn chairs along the sides, newspapers Strewn around, and foreign newspapers hanging on the walls. Fifteen people can hardly sit at ease in that room; and I Should like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) how he 4 p.m. felt when he was seated there studying the wonderful French language at the time of the negotiation of the French treaty? Would he not have preferred to have better quarters where he could have mixed with some degree of comfort with the distinguished French people whom he saw? Would he not have preferred to meet those people in a very much better place than where he did meet them? It certainly would have been far more in consonance with Canada's dignity.
In conclusion, I rejoice in the statement that has been made by the Acting Minister of Finance as to our present financial position.
I feel that the statement will be well received by the people of Canada; and I sincerely trust that in the administration of the affairs of this country no false economy will be practised, but that the high standard of national development at which Canada has arrived, coupled with proper economy, will not be marred or hampered !by the fear or the refusal to spend adequately-and I repeat the word "adequately"-in that connection. Ours is a vast heritage; it has been worth living for, it has been worth dying for. I have no other desire and no other ambition than to see Canada continue her national development, guided in her own way but remaining forever a component part of the greatest Commonwealth of nations.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at any great length in this debate which has been moving along rather slowly. I find that I am the eighty-eighth speaker since the debate started, and the twentieth speaker from the group of which I am a member. In looking over the columns of Hansard I observe that although there are a number of speeches that occupied almost three hours, the speakers from this group have not averaged more than half an hour each, and I do not intend to exceed that time.
In regard to the budget I must say that the proposals contained in it are not of such a character as to develop any enthusiasm on my part, and therefore in my brief remarks I shall deal with the budget from a critical standpoint. We were led to believe on a former occasion that the reductions then put into force were but the fore-runner of others to follow; but I am afraid the fore-runner must have, in some way, lost its connection with the main body. The budget has been dealt with from so many different angles that it is rather difficult to approach its consideration from any new point of view, consequently my remarks will be general in their character. While I criticize the government for its action-or possibly I should say inaction-I also wish to say that the high tariff policy of the Conservative party will find no foothold today in the prairie provinces, but-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You have not been there lately.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have just returned from
there. But permit me to say that a party like the Liberal party which has made no further advance, during the four years in which it has held office, to carry into effect its platform and published policy, will certainly not be received with open arms by the thinking portion of the electorate, especially in that part of Canada lying west, of the Great Lakes, and I wish to say that the people of Canada to whom that remark applies are now extremely alert. The haphazard easy going individual who believes everything he hears and tells everything he believes is now a back number. The thinking element have now commenced to see that in times .past they have been made use of for the benefit of other people; they are beginning to see that owing to the immense production, on a peT capita basis, of the value of the products of their farms, particularly in the case of the western farms, and from the fact that they are compelled to sell their products in competition with the world in the world's markets while at the same time forced.

The Budget-Mr. Knox
to purchase what they need for their own requirements in the restricted, protected, high priced home market, the time has come for a change. The conditions through which they have been passing are such as to compel all those men and women who have suffered from those conditions to do a lot of thinking. The result is that a great number are convinced that neither of the two old political parties is much interested in trying to help the farming community nor the communities which are entirely dependent upon the success of agriculture. Accordingly I am convinced of this, that in the west-in the prairie provinces at least-neither the policy of the Conservative party nor the policy of the Liberal party- judged by their actions during the last few years-will make any appeal to the thinking masses; and the man who is bold enough out there to argue that benefit is to be derived by the farming community from supporting either of those parties is likely to be only "a voice crying in the wilderness."
I have been impressed with the similarity of the position of the Maritime provinces, and the conditions there, to those of the western provinces. They too are more or less isolated and hampered in regard to traffic restrictions. They too are handicapped by a long, expensive rail haul, and they too are striving to develop their ocean ports without the sympathy and assistance which should be given them by centralized interests. It is quite plain that the Maritimes are also beginning to see that party politics is not getting them anywhere. I have been greatly interested in the addresses which have been delivered by Maritime men during this debate, particularly one by the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes). These addresses clearly show dissatisfaction with existing political and economic conditions, and the editor of Maritime Rights, a paper published in Halifax, in last Saturday's issue has the following to say in an editorial:
It has very often been said there is more party politics to the square inch in the Maritimes than in any other part of the world. It looks like it. What has it got us? Are we the most prosperous provinces in the Dominion? We all know the reverse is the fact.
Cut out the party stuff. No matter what side. Put on your war paint and go out after the things that will make these provinces prosperous and you will succeed. We have the country: we have the resources; we have the men; we have the money too; and what we do not have we can get. There is nothing wrong with the Maritimes. The trouble is with Us the People. Forget party and there will be a flow of life blood through your veins that will surprise you. Just look round and see the mess things are in generally and ask yourself who are to blame. The answer will be as plain as the nose on your face: you.
After reading this and knowing that no part of the Dominion has stuck to party politics so faithfully or long and without results as the Maritimes, I am convinced that the psychology of the movement at present in those provinces is precisely the same as it is in the west and in many parts ot Ontario, although, perhaps, not quite so fat advanced. I am also convinced that in theii hearts these Maritime men are not satisfied with the' present party system. Consequently I have no hesitation in giving to them the old Macedonian invitation to "come over and help us," or I might put it in more up-to-date language by saying; "Come on in, the water is fine."
I would ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, for a few moments while I revert to some matters which are more or less parochial, but which, while they may not at the present time be closely connected with the budget, may some day have a very direct bearing on the finances of the country. I would refer first to the necessity for a survey of the great hinterland in northern Saskatchewan lying around the south of lake La Ronge. I might point out that lake La Ronge is a lake of considerable size. I think it might possibly cover some 400 square miles. It is surrounded by a rocky formation. This rocky formation is a continuation of the Laurentian range starting in Quebec, running through northern Ontario, northern Manitoba and on into Saskatchewan. Prior to the present time, owing to its inaccessibility, this portion of the Laurentian range lying in Saskatchewan has been very little explored. Now, there is a wagon road constructed by the provincial government from Prince Albert to Montreal lake, a distance of sixty miles, and from there to lake La Ronge there is good water connection, in fact right into the Churchill river and on into A/fv -r>r*in +* ic that I would like that some attention be given to this matter in the shape of a survey of the shores of the lake, also that this be followed by an aeroplane survey such as has been undertaken in some other parts of the north country, so that prospectors going in there will have something to work upon. This part of the Laurentian range contains the same minerals, such as gold and copper, that have been found in other parts of it. But it contains another mineral that has not been discovered in any portion of the Laurentian range to the east, and that is coal. In proof of that I would read a couple of extracts from speeches delivered by Hon. C'has. A. Dunning, Premier of Saskatchewan, in the legislature there. The
The Budget-Mr. Knox

first was delivered on the 23rd November, 1920, and will be found in the Sessional Papers of that year at pages 40 and 41. He says:
I should refer at this point to the preliminary northern exploration which was made in the past summer. Some publicity was given to the matter. It was the intention of the government to make arrangements to either confirm or disprove the rumours which had been persistent for many years, circulated by Indians, trappers, Hudson bay men, missionaries and so on that coal existed in the neighbourhood of lac la Ronge. Arrangements were made for an exploration party to go into that district and to verify the existence of coal and also to bring back samples.
I have stated the tremendous economic importance of the presence of good coal in that portion of the north. The presence of good coal in that portion of the north would mean tremendous development. In addition to investigating coal the exploration party made a reconnaissance survey of a considerable area of the north-eastern portion of the province, the trip embracing all told over one thousand miles north and north-east of Prince Albert.
Naturally the party could not, in covering such a large amount of territory, do a great deal of detailed prospecting. That class of work must still be done by the prospector who is prepared to wander off with his pack on his back and his pick and shovel and take chances on what he may find. No government organization has ever arranged to take the place of the prospector in the search for precious metals.
I have the major part of the report of this party at the present time.	Lieutenant-Colonel Garner was
in charge of the party and I have his diary which makes interesting reading and gives a good deal of information as to what is to be found in that section of the north. The reports from the geologist and mines expert of the province representing coal I have not yet received but as regards coal I can say that it is there. It is a kind of coal similar in character to the coal which is found in the south and therefore a low grade lignite coal. As to whether it will be possible to create out of it a commercial commodity in the future it is difficult to say but while I do not want to be too optimistic, the situation of the coal, the nature of its overlay and the nature of the material underlying it is such as to lead to the hope that somewhere in the vicinity of this seam there may be coal of a considerable better quality. In the bottoms of some of the streams drift coal is present also.


I have in my possession a sample of sand brought back by the party from a large deposit of pure white sand. It shows on analysis 99 per cent pure silica which means an excellent glass sand. The deposit is 150 miles north of Prince Albert but it is a valuable resource. The only other raw materials needed for the manufacture of practically all grades of glass are sulphate of soda of high purity and some lime. Sulphate of soda and fuel are available in large quantities in our province and there seems to be the opportunity in the future for the establishment of a glass industry.
The second extract from Mr. Dunning's speeches is under date of January 24, 1922, also dealing with the same matter. Mr. Dunning says:
This summer the government picked out what appeared to be the most logical place for intensive survey work and the party was asked to devote its attention to that particular area, the Wapawekka lake and Bear hills, immediately south of Lac La Ronge.
I do not think the country covered had been explored 
previously. Travel in the north is largely restricted to water ways and in portions of the country covered by the party this summer they are satisfied that even the Indians did not know the country intimately.
The party did not find any great coal deposits or oil. The thing I would most like to find in our north land is coal, rather than gold or copper. The best guarantee of immediate development of the north, from the railway and agricultural point of view, would be the discovery of good coal beyond the present range of settlement. It would mean immediate railway development. The discovery of coal of good average quality, for smelting for instance, would mean a tremendous industrial development because of the copper deposits on the boundary between Manitoba and Saskatchewan which are handicapped by reasons of the fact that their ore must be ship-ped to Trail in British Columbia for smelting. The discovery of a coal suitable for smelting purposes in the north would mean industrial development similar to that which took place in northern Ontario under similar or even more difficult conditions than in Saskatchewan. I had been hoping that the result of the trip of the party would result in the discovery of good coal. A year ago the party confirmed reports of coal, which had been made prior to settlement in this country, by Indians, prospectors and travellers. It is true that coal is there.
I should like to read a brief extract from the report of Mr. J. B. Tyrrell, in the Geological Survey report of 1892. Mr. Tyrrell is a noted explorer and geologist. It is in reference to an examination he made of a deposit of drift coal on the banks of the Saskatchewan river 7 miles east of Prince Albert, at a place called Red Cliff. In connection with that examination he sayS:
This sand is composed of grains of quartz in layers, interbedded with layers of fragments of black lignite, the latter occasionally in well rounded pebbles an inch or more in diameter. There is a great quantity of this lignite, the bed of sand, whose thickness could not then be determined, being often composed largely of it.
These rounded grains and pebbles of lignite have clearly been washed some distance by the water, and deposited alternately with the heavier quartz grains as the current varied in strength, but the quantity present would seem to be too great to permit of its having been washed from any of the known coal seams on the river, the lowest of which is near the mouth of Egg Creek, 400 miles higher up the stream. It is much more likely that these fragments of lignite have been washed from a deposit, not at any great distance, which is now covered.
In order to determine whether such a deposit of coal exists in the vicinity or not, also whether the Dakota sandstone is here tar-bearing or not, as well as to ascertain the exact nature of the cretaceous section in this district, where the surface appears to be almost everywhere covered with drift, it would be of the greatest service to make a boring down to the underlying Palaeozoic rocks. If either coal or oil were met with the value of the country would be enhanced to many times the cost of the boring.
My point is that it would be a great advantage to this northern country if a survey such as I have suggested were made, so that prospectors going in there could secure maps of the country and know where they were going, and I would urge that this survey be included in the programme for this year We

The Budget-Mr. Knox
have the engineers already in the employ of the department, and we have the aeroplanes already doing this class of work, so that I am not asking for any further expenditure.
Another point to which I would refer is in connection with the soldier land settlement; and I might say that I have always had and still have same hope for this scheme working out to the advantage of the soldier settlers, but there is no question in my mind that a readjustment in value, such as was suggested by the special parliamentary committee last year, will have to be brought about, and there is no excuse for leaving this in abeyance any longer if the confidence of the men is to be retained. A short time ago there was some mention of closing the soldier settlement office at Prince Albert and transferring the work and supervision to one of the other two offices in the province, in spite of the fact that the Prince Albert district has more men under the board than either of the other two. It may not have as much money lent out, but following out the spirit under which the act was first introduced, the welfare of the men, and not the money, should be the first consideration.
I also find that the Prince Albert office controls more acreage under the act than either of the other two offices in the province, the total being 756,410 acres for Prinoe Albert or 226,005 more than Saskatoon and 88,923 more than Regina. In regard to acreage, Prince Albert is fourth largest in the Dominion, in which we have altogether thirteen districts.
As regards the number of men settled under the act, Prince Albert has 3,145 or 579 men more than Saskatoon and 201 more than Regina. In this respect it is again fourth in the Dominion. As to the number of total repaid loans, Prince Albert heads the list with a good lead as far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned. It might be interesting to know in what portions of the Dominion the soldier settlers under the act are showing up to best advantage. This is easily discovered by looking up the adjustment or salvage cases which may be looked upon as the failures. In this respect the Prince Albert district has a much smaller percentage of failures than any of the other twelve districts in the Dominion.
I might say I am not surprised at this, because I have farmed in this district myself for the last thirty-five years, and I do not hesitate to say that last year was the only year that could be called a real set-back in all that period. I have figured out here
the percentage of failures in the thirteen different districts. They are not given in percentages in the report of the Soldier Settlement board, but I think these are perfectly reliable. I find that the percentages of failures or of salvage cases at Prince Albert was 11.7. I am giving these in their order of merit, starting with the lowest number of failures and working up. The next in order of merit is Prince Edward Island, 17.11. Saskatoon follows very closely with 17.14 and Vernon, British Columbia with 18.21. The percentages are as follows:

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
