Just for information, is the
percentage based on the whole, or on the number within the area?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
In the different districts.
I was giving the percentage for that district, with Prince Albert as I said very much lower than any district in the Dominion, being 11.7, while the next was 17.11. This is largely based on local conditions.
There is one other matter which I propose to touch on very briefly-I refer to the conversion of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in favour of the Hudson Bay railway. During the many discussions, Mr. Speaker, an which I have taken part in regard to the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, I have often wondered why the hon. minister could1 not see his way to give us his influential support. But the mists were cleared away a few days ago when, in the course of that memorable three-hour speech of his, he informed us that after his trip up the line as far as Kettle rapids-which by the way is still ninety-two miles from the bay-he was an out-and-out believer in the scheme, and that Hudson bay was the logical outlet and inlet for the prairie provinces. Up to this point he gave us encouragement. Then he showed the real
The Budget-Mr. Knox

thought in his mind by informing the House that the engineers, navigators and other qualified officials who had investigated the comparative merits of Port Nelson and1 Fort Churchill had made a grave mistake by selecting the wrong port and spending over $5,000,000 there, and that a truce should be called for another indefinite period while further investigations might be undertaken to determine which should be the tidewater terminus. I am sure the House will agree with me when I say that it is most regrettable that the hon minister did not visit Kettle rapids years ago. But why did he not continue on to the bay? He could not learn anything about the suitability or otherwise of the present terminus while he remained at Kettle rapids, because he was still ninety-two miles from tidewater. We are almost forced to the conclusion that he had his line of action already decided upon before he started for Kettle rapids. Such a statement coming at the present time to me looks somewhat fishy, too much of the red herring variety -a further excuse for further delay. I hope, Mr. Speaker, to have an opportunity of speaking further on this matter in the near future.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to answer the observations of my hon. friend who has just completed an excellent address, further than to say, if I may do so without offending my good friends across the way, that I hope some day his grandson will Come to this House and still have an opportunity of advocating the completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
My only excuse, Sir, for entering the debate, which has already been excessively prolonged, is my desire to press upon the government consideration of a suggestion which, in my humble opinion, is of vital importance to Canada. It has to do with the National railways, and while I realize that the time for debate on the railway probably would be more opportune when the estimates are under consideration, yet certain observations have been made from this side of the House with regard to the disposition of the Canadian National system that I feel should not go unchallenged. I desire also to discuss very briefly a few other matters which come more properly within this debate. At the outset let me say that I am not a pessimist regarding the future of Canada, and I have no sympathy with those who, perhaps unwittingly, by their observations in this House are doing something to destroy the reputation and the credit of Canada abroad; and, what is infinitely worse in my opinion, are destroying the confidence of Canadians in their own country. Our debt, Sir, is enormous, our

annual obligations of some $340,000,000 by way of taxation constitute a very heavy burden; but it would be folly for members on this side, and almost treason on the part of members of any party, to exaggerate unduly the gravity of our financial situation; nor would it be wisdom to deny that it is grave. I propose to do neither, but to the best of my ability to make some reasonable suggestions as to what the government can do to remedy the situation.
I congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon his presentation of the budget. I do not do so in the ordinary stereotyped manner that is sometimes expected of a supporter of the government. The budget gives some reason for satisfaction. In the face of falling revenues it comes as a surprise and a gratification to the people to know that instead of being confronted with a heavy deficit we have a small surplus. True, our friends diagonally opposite, and perhaps some of our friends directly opposite, have figured that with the capital expenditures on our National railways we have a very heavy deficit. But my position with respect to that has already been made quite clear, and I am not going to take time by discussing it now. In congratulating the government on the budget, I do not mean to say that I agree with all that has been done or that has not been done-for there are in my opinion some errors of omission. I should have liked to see the entire abolition of what are sometimes called the nuisance taxes. From the very first day when the stamp taxes were introduced by the former government I was opposed to this form of taxation. I believe they are properly named nuisance taxes. If taxes were ever devised to annoy the public, you could hardly conceive of anything to better fulfil that purpose than the imposition of stamp taxes. The tax on receipts comes in the same category. In my opinion that form of taxation is absolutely illogical and has only the one recommendation-that it produces the revenue.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Which tax?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The taxes on cheques, receipts and commercial paper generally. I should also like to have seen a reduction in postage rates, and I believe that a return to the prewar figure would not have resulted in loss of revenue. In that connection I should like to quote from the Canadian Milling and Grain Journal the following article:
To stimulate business
Following the change of government in Great Britain, the Manchester Guardian Commercial, circularized fourteen of the leading business men of

The Budget-Mr. Euler
that, city, asking each to suggest how best the new Baldwin administration could stimulate trade. The replies indicated that while many of the writers had strong and original views on the subject, there was a measure of agreement among them, which should not be without interest in Canada. Seven out of the fourteen declared that if the government would remove the taxes on cheques and receipts and reduce postage rates to pre-war level, then business all over the kingdom would receive a great impetus. There may be a suggestion somewhere here for Ottawa.
I would draw attention also to one or two weaknesses, as I see them, in the present sales tax. A wholesaler or a manufacturer, under the Sales Tax Act, is made the collector of the tax. He puts the amount of the tax on the invoices which he sends out to his customers, and makes his monthly remittances-
I think they are monthly-to the government. In many cases he has not yet collected the tax from his customer when he forwards the .account to the government at Ottawa. It has occurred quite frequently, and I know some eases in point, where manufacturers have sold large quantities of goods to retailers in other provinces, paying the tax to the government, and later these retailers failed in business and did not pay either the principal amount of the invoices nor the tax. Yet the government holds the manufacturer responsible for the payment of that tax. He is in the unfortunate position not only of losing his principal, his capital, but of paying the tax when he was not really intended to pay it. In cases of that kind, it seems to me that if the manufacturer has not been reimbursed he should receive a refund or rebate of the amount paid in respect of that tax.
There is one other weakness in the law, to which I would like to refer. It is a discrimination which I consider unjust-and I should not like the members of the House to think I have any personal interest in the matter at all. It refers to the printing business. We have on the statute book a law which exempts from the operation of sales tax all printers who do a business of less than $10,000 a year. A man who has a business, we will say, of $9,990, escapes paying the sales tax, while the man who does a business of $10,010 is subject to the payment of the tax. It seems to me that is a gross injustice and should not be continued. I see no justification whatever for it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Would the hon. member accept it as an axiom that the people object to taxation according to their understanding of the tax?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am not sure that I get the meaning of the hon. gentleman's question.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The objections of the people to taxation are greater according to their understanding of the tax in question. That is, they can see more distinc' y through the principle of direct taxation t an the principle of indirect taxation.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am taaling entirely with
direct taxation in this particular instance. I see no reason why one m in who does a little smaller business than another should be excused from the payment of a particular tax while the man with the si ightly larger business has to pay it. There is no reason why anybody should be exempt from sales tax, in the same line of business at l'.ast.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My idei was that a person studying the principle ol taxation will more readily understand the pri iciple of direct than the principle of indirect ta xation and will consequently object to the latter more quickly.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: With reference to the sales tax on the printing business, what change, if any, does the hon. member suggest?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think that is very obvious:
I should say they should all be taxed. I would like to make reference to some of the remarks made by hon. gentlemen "angularly opposite,'' as they have been described. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), who, I am sorry to observe, is not in his seat, made a very excellent speech some weeks ago. H I had any criticism to make of what he said-and of course I have no authority to lecture anyone-I would say that t/he severity of his language did not add anything to the strength of his argument. I think also he was a little careless with his figures, but I am not going to go into that just now. His speech was interesting. I was rather surprised that he should quote in support of his contentions such a man as President Coolidge, who, after all, is an American and not entirely unprejudiced. He also made some very interesting references to historical events; and his references to my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) were not just as courteous as they might have been. I remember one interesting allusion he made to ancient history: he spoke of Nero fiddling while Rome burned, and he drew a comparison with the action of the government in that regard. I was almost sure when he did that that he was about to lead up to another interesting historical incident and make a comparison with that well known occasion when the Gaul was at the gates of Rome and the cackling of the geese saved the people of that city. He also criticized the lack of
The Budget-Mr. Euler

unanimity on the part of hon. members on this side of the House. His remarks in that respect had reference chiefly, I think, to differences of opinion on this side with regard to the tariff and with regard to the principle of public ownership. He is quite right in that. There are members on this side who are protectionists; there are some-two or three, perhaps-who are free traders; there are others who believe in a tariff for revenue, or, we will say, moderate protection. But the same thing exists among our friends diagonally opposite. I think I can remember last year the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Doucet) moving a resolution with regard to higher tariffs. I think I can also remember that this year when the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) moved a resolution in favour of the reduction of the tariff on automobiles, the hon. member for Kent voted for that proposed reduction.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit me, the amendment of last year declared for tariff consistency, fiscal stability-a consistently maintained tariff policy; and this year the resolution to which my hon. friend refers dealt with the reduction of a duty which is higher than that on any other article imported into this country.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not finding any particular fault with my hon. friend for voting either one way or the other. I am merely pointing out that it was a case of the pot calling the kettle black. We also had other members from the Maritime provinces, even a member of the former Union government- the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter)-voting for a reduction in the tariff. So did the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Jones). I am not finding fault with them, but the fact remains that members of the House will vote according to their own interest, whether it be on the question of tariff or not; and occasionally they will vote against the attitude taken by their own leader.
I might make some reference also to the other question in respect to which hon. gentlemen opposite say we have been inconsistent, that of public ownership. Members on this side, I am sorry to say-a great majority of them, I believe-are opposed to public ownership, while some of them, including myself, are believers in the principle of public ownership. On the other side we have heard very little with regard to public ownership; so far as I can remember, only one hon. gentleman, the member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has this session said one word in 
favour of that principle, although scattered among the members of that party are those who in former days supported it very strongly.
We have the amendment now-and it has not been discussed to any considerable extent-for the reduction of the sales tax. In theory, Sir, I am in favour of the amendment. We also saw in the press before the session opened a suggestion on the part of the leader of the opposition that we should have a reduction in freight rates both east and west. The thing that I desire to point out in connection with both these suggestions is that both must mean a reduction in the revenues of the country, and I have heard no practical suggestion as to how those revenues are to be replaced.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury condemned such arrangements as the Crowsnest pass agreenient. He stated,-he is not here and I shall not do him any injustice, but I think this is correct-that he was entirely opposed to any special agreements that would give preferences to one 'class of the people or to the people of one section of the country as against those of another. That is a very sound principle; but in the very same speech he also stated that it was necessary that the people of the Maritime provinces should receive special consideration so far as freight rates were concerned. I see no consistency in that attitude.
There are many things I should like to discuss, Mr. Speaker, but I khall deal only with the subjects which to me seem of greatest importance at this time. It is true that business stagnation exists in Canada. I do not believe it is more serious than it is in the United States, but I would like to deal briefly with what I consider to be the causes of that depression, and to suggest as far as possible some remedy. I would say that there are three chief causes: over-industrialization; lack of confidence on the part of business men-for reasons which I shall examine a little later-and last, and greatest of all, high taxation.
With regard to over-industrialization, I would say that during the prosperous years of the war, and later, in 1920, the manufacturers of this country-I am not blaming them for doing it-extended their businesses more than was warranted by the business that was offering in this country itself, and with taxation becoming high, costs became greater, and people not having the same purchasing power as they had before. These two are the causes of over-industrialization. We have factory plant in this country which is more

The Budget-Mr. Euler
than sufficient to supply the needs of the Canadian people. Now if I am right in that statement, then it points clearly to the necessity of developing foreign markets, and I am glad to say that this government is doing something in that direction.
But, Sir, if foreign markets are to be developed they must be developed in a systematic way. I do not believe in paternalism as a principle of politics, but in my opinion the government, or the Department of Trade and Commerce, ought to have in every country where some trade may be looked for commercial agents to advance the business interests of this country.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
While I agree entirely with
the remarks that are being made by the hon. member, would he kindly explain-I am asking just for information-how we are going to compete in foreign markets when we are continually being told that Canadian manufacturers are unable to compete in foreign markets owing to the low cost of production in these other countries?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is falling into this very common error. When we speak of foreign markets and low cost of production, we are not saying that that obtains in all countries of the world. There are certain countries in Europe to-day manufacturing certain lines of goods in which it is utterly impossible for Canadian manufacturers to compete at this time; but there are some countries in which we can sell things, as witness the proposed trade agreement with Australia, and the suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) that we should be able to do more business with South Africa.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I want to put myself right.
I do not believe in those arguments myself. I only put them up to you.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have no fault to find with
the hon. gentleman's objections to my argument.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I do not mean your argument, but the argument that we cannot compete with other countries. I think we can, if we go about it right.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would just put this up
to my hon. friend-and I would not like him to think that I am in any sense an extremely high protectionist: I think he will admit that in some countries of Europe at least, and of Asia as well, the cost of labour is very much lower than it is in Canada or the United
States. If wages are higher in the United States than in Canada, Canadians will naturally drift to the United States. I think that follows.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If the cost of living in the
United States is no higher.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Well, we will say that. I
think the cost of living is practically the same in Canada as in the United States. Now, if wages are higher in the United States than in Canada, Canadians will naturally go to the United States. If wages in Canada are as high as they are in the States and if they are lower in Europe, I say it is very difficult for Canadians to compete with the low-paid labour of Europe. I did not intend, Mr. Speaker, to go into a lengthy dissertation on the tariff to-day at all.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman stated that one of our difficulties in Canada was that we were over-industrialized. In view of the importation last year of $140,000,000 worth of iron and steel products, does he still contend that Canada is over-industrialized in that line?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would not say that of
iron and steel, no; my statement is made in an entirely general way. As for the United States, Mr. Speaker, I think it is high time indeed, both for commercial purposes and for the sake of our national self-respect, that we should appoint a representative at Washington. I remember very well that an appropriation for that purpose was made under the former government. No appointment ever was made by that government, and that neglect has been continued by this government. For my part, I cannot understand why there should be such a long delay when the desirability of such action is admitted on all sides. We may as well admit that our interests are inevitably bound up with those of the United States. The United States does not admit it, but she must ultimately realize that she cannot prosper permanently unless she obeys the well-known economic law that she cannot hope to sell if she does not buy. A well-known American economist has given it as his opinion that if we Canadians survive for another ten years, which, of course we will, the United States will have 135,000,000 of people, and she will then purchase all the foodstuffs that Canada can produce. We ought, I say, to put ourselves in a position to meet those conditions as they come, and one of the things we should do is to appoint a Canadian representative at Washington as a necessary step in that direction.
The Budget-Mr. Euler

I spoke of lack of confidence. Our friends of the official opposition say that the tariff is not properly adjusted, and that the uncertainty as to its stability -causes the waning of enterprise and a lack of -confidence in every way. I think there may be some justification for that statement. My position on the tariff is, I think, pretty well known. It is the same as it was last year, it is the same as it was the year before, and it is exactly the same as it was when I entered this House some eight years ago. I am not going to review all that again; I shall content myself with saying that I favour such a tariff as will ensure that .at least a fair share of the 'Canadian home market shall be preserved for Canadian workmen and Canadian industry. I voted against the budget last year, not because the reductions in the tariff were great or startling, not because any industry of -my ridinig was seriously injured; but 'because I believed then as I believe now, that before changes in the tariff are made there should be the most -careful investigation as (to the effect of such -changes. I urged then the appointment of a tariff board, not a partisan body of men but a body of men selected with one object-and only one object-in view, a body of men who have the ability to go into the business places of this -country, with the power necessary to find out exactly the condition of those businesses, and to obtain knowledge and to bring information to this government and to parliament which will enable an intelligent revision of the tariff to be made.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How would such a commission determine costs in other countries? The hon. gentleman may have read how the tariff -commission of the United States attempted to ascertain costs in Germany and France, and how unsuccessful they were, and how they threw up their hands in despair at making the actual cost basis a factor in the tariff schedules.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Costs, of course, would be only one feature.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Bu-t a very important feature.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If you want to search out the books of a company or find out the costs of any manufacturing enterprise, I do not think it would be very difficult for expert accountants to go to those places and find out exactly what the costs are.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: In foreign -countries?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Not in foreign countries.
There they would be entirely at the mercy of the people of that country.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Then you have no comparison.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Under the former government, where the dumping clause was supposed to be applied on the basis of what goods cost in the United States, it was found impossible to enforce that clause because Canadian officials would not be permitted to go into United States factories and make investigations.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: They do it now.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I think you would find a great deal of difficulty in sending any Canadian into a United States factory, a man who has no particular -business -there, and who does not represent Americans, -and get them to give him free access to their books to ascertain anything he may choose to obtain.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The Customs Inspection department -check u-p the cost of goods now in exactly that way.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think all they check up is this: If they think an invoice of goods -coming into Canada is too lp-w, all they do is to go to Boston, New York or some other place of business and check up the prices named in that invoice with the regular prices at which these things are sold throughout that country.
Mr. ROBB. They find the fair market value.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes, the fair market value. I congratulate the Prime Minister and the government upon their decision to create such a board. We 'have had the statement of the minister that upon that board shall be certain experts from the department. I have no fault to find with that, but I should 'like to urge upon the government as strongly as I can, that upon that board there should be a preponderance of independent men chosen entirely for their fitness -for the work to be done and clothed with ample power to do it properly.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You will have to import them.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
In that case we will put a
tariff against them. Unless what I have suggested in connection with the tariff board be done such a board may very easily do more harm than good. On the other hand, if the personnel of that board is what it ought to be a great deal of good will come from it. I believe such a board will inspire a good deal of confidence because our 'businessmen will know that before changes in the tariff are made they will at least be given an opportunity to present their side of -the case; and in that way-although not entirely, because I believe the responsibility for taxation and the making of tariffs must always remain with parliament and with the government-we may, to some extent at least, keep the tariff out of politics.

The Budget-Mr. Euler
Now I am going to refer to another feature of the tariff with which probably many members will not agree. I took the opportunity last year-I think twice, both in the debate -on the Speech from the Throne and in the debate on the budget-to refer to what is known as the British preference. Our friends angularly opposite are in favour of higher tariffs. I would say to them that nothing else would be more properly and more nearly to their hand than action to abolish the British preference. My reason for being opposed to the British preference rests entirely upon the commonsense basis that if protection-if you want to call it that-or a tariff for the maintenance of your industries is right and proper,
I do not see why there should be any qualification at all one way or another. Tariffs are a matter of business and not of sentiment, and the sooner we proceed on that basis the better. For my part I see no reason why the British preference should be maintained if the tariff is to be used for the preservation of Canadian industry, in which I believe. If a Canadian industry is ruined because of competition from Britain I do not think it makes it any more bearable for the Canadian who is ruined if that result has been brought about by a British industry rather than by an American industry; and one of the defects, one of the abuses, in reference to that preference is that large quantities of goods come into this country under the preference as British goods that are not British goods at all. They merely come from other countries via Britain and get the benefit of the preference.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: More than we sell to them7

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Possibly. I was going to say that if our friends opposite, the members of the official opposition, are sincere-and I am not questioning their sincerity with reference to the tariff-I would suggest that if the leader of the opposition will submit a resolution to this chamber for the cancellation of the preference I shall support it with my vote. If he does not I rather think he owes an explanation to Canadian industry.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I think you are perfectly safe in making the suggestion.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Perhaps so. But, Mr. Speaker, while these things are factors in the business depression that exists, the greatest of all is the matter of high taxation to 5 p.m. which I propose to devote my remarks now. We have the sales tax, the income tax, the stamp taxes, and the excise taxes of various kinds including the luxury tax. All these increased the cost of production and result in high prices, and so 158
limit the power of the people to purchase. High taxation without a doubt is to-day the chief obstacle to national prosperity. And what, Mr. Speaker, is the remedy? Our friends opposite suggest economy and a higher tariff. Well, Sir, I am in favour of economy, of course, as is every other member of the House, and a reasonable degree of protection. The government has made some progress in the direction of economy, although that is denied. But economy in administration is admittedly very difficult. Still there may be room for improvement, and perhaps the one direction in which some improvement might yet be made is in that much abused arm of the service known as the civil service. Now, I do not believe that civil servants as individuals are overpaid; in fact I am certain that a good many of the men in the service are underpaid, and we very frequently lose them because we do not pay them as much as they are worth; but I have a suspicion or more than a suspicion that it is still true that the civil service is overmanned, and we have had statements of ministers of the crown to that effect. Consequently it occurs to me, and I have said this before, that if some survey were made of the other departments such as was made in the case of the Printing Bureau it might be found possible to effect some economies there. But when all is said and done there is still a large residue of expenditure which is uncontrollable. Our debt, exclusive of the railways, is nearly two and' a half bdlions of dollars; I think we realize just a little more accurately what is meant by that when we say it is two thousand five hundred millions of dollars. Pensions are practically uncontrollable, and the cost of the ordinary administration of the country's affairs cannot be reduced below a certain minimum. I he interest on the war debt is enormous, and while something can perhaps be done from time to time by way of careful refunding, as was done last year by the Acting Minister of Finance, that burden must remain heavy. We had a reference the other day to the waste that took place in connection with the war. I have nothing to say with regard to that, but after all I think our friends of the opposition should not be hypercritical in regard to war debt, and perhaps with regard to taxation. After all, our debt was created largely when our friends opposite were in office and the most of the responsibility is theirs. Wars are costly and their burdens continue to rest upon generations to come.
But there is one large item of our tax burden which in my opinion can be wiped out if the government has the inclination and

The Budget-Mr. Euler

the courage to grapple with the problem. That item is the loss suffered each year by the National Railways. Now I have no criticism to make of the head of the National Railways; rather would I say a great deal that stands to his credit. He came to us less than three years ago. He found a series or group of railways more or less disorganized; and I think the House will admit that he has welded them into the very efficient system known to-day as the National Railway System. Those of you who travel over the line, and you all do, will admit freely that the service on the National to-day is not excelled in Canada and I think that means on the continent of North America. I had the pleasure of a trip over the National railways last fall from Toronto to Prince Rupert, and throughout the whole of that system the service was such as would make any Canadian proud.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Should we be proud of that or should we economize?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am proud of it. I am quite free to say that I am proud of the service that is being given by the National; and if Sir Hentry Thornton has done nothing else, he has created a spirit of esprit de corps among the employees of that road that is simply admirable and is not excelled by the employees of any other railway, and I should like to say to my hon. friend that that costs the country nothing.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the question of unjustifiable luxury.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It also stands to the credit of the president of the road that in a year which was a bad year he has been able to cut expenditures in operating the road some $14,000,000, and has showed a net operating revenue of $17,000,000. Yet in the face of all that the loss each year is very high. The National railways owe to the government of Canada the sum of $560,000,000, not including interest on that debt for some years. The interest upon this sum last year was $31,000,-000-I am giving only the millions-which has to come out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada. That sum of money forms part of the consolidated debt of Canada and it is taken care of in the annual estimates of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). In addition to this item of $31,000,000, we had to contribute on last year's account some $21,000,000 towards paying fixed charges on the bonds of the railways owned by the public, that is not by the gov-
[Mr. E-ilarl
emment of Canada. That makes a total amount upon the taxpayers of Canada of the $31,000,000 plus the $21,000,000, or $52,000,'000 each year.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is for interest?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes. I am not referring to the amounts put on capital expenditure which my hon. friend also treated as a loss and deficit. Upon that point I cannot agree with him.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Temporarily.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Until the business pays and then it all becomes a surplus?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what the hon. member said the other day.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Until it becomes active.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I believe we might carry out a plan by which, instead of having a loss of some $50,000,000 a year we could show a surplus of some $50,000,000. I am sure that will appeal to hon. members, and in a very few moments I desire to go into that a little more fully. That really is my reason for rising to speak to-day.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: A Daniel come to judgment!

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Thank you. Before doing that, I should like, for the sake of discussing the matter intelligently, to give a number of essential figures in connection with the National railways. First, the investment in road and equipment is about $1,837,000,000. The total assets of the road amount to about $2,074,000,000.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How are those assets figured?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what has been charged up as the cost. They may not be worth that now. Loans from the government, as I stated a few minutes ago, amount to $560,397,957.64. The interest on the loans is not included in that sum.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There are other Capital
amounts besides that, not included in that amount.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Interest on loans by the
government amounted to $31,000,000 last year. The debt to the public of Canada, not the government, but outside bond holders, many of whom the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) says are foreigners, is $913,913,082.80. The fixed charges or interest on that debt amounts to $38,361,704.14. Taking

The Budget-Mr. Euler
then fixed charges of $38,361,704.14 to the public and interest on the moneys owed by the railways to the government of $31,000,000, we have a total in round numbers of $69,000,000 of fixed charges on the National Railways. From this we deduct the operating revenue of $17,000,000, leaving, as I stated before, a net deficit of $52,000,000. I think it is only fair to say at this point that this is not fairly chargeable to public ownership of railways. I will read just an extract from the Toronto Globe which bears on that:
A large part of it represents the mistakes and extravagances of governments and private owners and promoters in the past, and is not based on replacement values. It is announced that the management will submit before long a consistent statement of the case for writing down the capitalization. It will be a highly important question for parliament to decide, as the writing-down process would involve an increase of the national debt. The advantage of lower fixed charges would be that it would give the National Railways a definite financial objective which they might hope to reach within a few years.
I quite appreciate the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) some time ago that writing down of the capitalization of the National Railways is not going to wipe out the debt. The debt will remain, of course. That is somewhat elementary, I think, but this will give the National Railways, under public ownership, just the same chance as private ownership would have had if those roads had been organized under a new company and had been conducted as a private corporation.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It means simply that you are transferring to consolidated fund so much interest that has to be paid, instead of charging it against the railways. The interest there is exactly the same.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not questioning that
at all. We are not going to save any money by doing it, but we are going to give the principle of public ownership as fair a chance as these railways would have under private ownership. These things were piled up under private ownership, and if these railways had been taken over by a privately organized company, the hon. member knows that they would have been reorganized; that these amounts would have been written down, and that they would have gone on with a capitalization more like that of the Canadian Pacific, about which my hon. friend knows more than I do.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not. We would be
simply deluding ourselves into a false position. In other words, we are making a bookkeeping entry and putting on one side certain millions 158i
of dollars and imagining, for it is purely imagination, that as regards the railways we are paying less in fixed charges. That is the point I make.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am quite willing "to let the House judge what is desirable. I think the House understands what I mean.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman give the House the amount that is carried by private parties in bonds?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I gave that before.-$913,913,-082.80.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
What is the
interest paid on that?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What percentage is that?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It varies. I cannot give
that exactly. I spoke last year about the duplication and waste involved in the operation of these two great railway systems. I did so at that time as chairman of the select committee on estimates for the National Railways. In our report at that time appeared this paragraph:
Your committee desires to direct the attention of the government to the apparent unnecessary competition and duplication of services between important centres by the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways and to suggest that the railways be invited to consider the whole question with a view to elimination, wherever possible, of unnecessary duplication and competition, so as to conserve the revenues and resources of both companies while still rendering adequate service to the public.
We have heard within the last few days- and I think it is gratifying to all members of the House-that the heads of the two national railways, together with their officials, are getting together with a view to eliminating, as far as possible, duplication of services. That is well worth while doing if we are going to continue as we are. But I think there is a better way, and the hon. member for South York and myself, in the debate on the ocean freight rates resolution, made reference to it. Last year I said-and I said it again in the course of that debate-that I had it on the highest possible authority that a saving of from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000 could be made each year if the two railways were amalgamated and welded into one system. I say now-and again I say this upon the highest possible authority-that if the two roads could be amalgamated, there could be saved the colossal sum of $100,000,000 a year. That is nothing less than a staggering statement.
The Budget-Mr. Eider

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Which system would do the amalgamating?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am coming to that. I know we are going to have a difference of opinion.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is the rock on which we split.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If that sum were saved each year to the people of Canada, it would pay the national debt in about twenty years.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman's calculation include the saving that would be made on the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific, or on the Canadian National Railways alone?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The total saving effected by the amalgamation of the road. That would relieve the heavy burden of taxation. This was the suggestion I was going to make; if we combined the two roads it would immediately solve the ocean freight rate .problem with which we are now wrestling. The president of the National Railways is reported in the paper-1 am not permitted to make any reference to the committee-as stating that the savings would be enormous and would be sufficient not only to pay the operating expenses of the amalgamated roads, but the fixed charges on the debt to the public and in addition to that the interest on the money loaned by the Dominion of Canada to the National Railways. Lord Shaughnessy in his famous proposal figured out a saving of $56,000,000 by amalgamation, and he was calculating on the basis of a condition under whioh the Grand Trunk Railway would not be included. He was ready to cut the Grand Trunk adrift and let that road do the best it rjould for itself. The 'Grand Trunk was added :;o the National system after Lord Shaugh-nessy's .plan was first submitted. I submit ;hat this .matter of the railways and the savings that could be effected is the most important question before parliament and the country to-day, barring none. I say that it is of tremendous importance. If $100,000,000 can be taken off our tax levy each year it will have an effect on the industry of the country that will be simply incalculable.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not crediting the $100,000,000 to the reduction of taxes, when possibly half of it would be a saving to the Canadian Pacific Railway?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It depends on whether you are going to have the railways run by the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian National after the amalgamation is effected.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If the merger took place, would the service be as good?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You could apply to the railway commission to reduce the rates if the railways were merged, the same as you do now.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes. If parliament decided
that it would sooner have the railway rates reduced than have the taxes reduced, that could be done according to its judgment.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement that $100,000,000 would be saved is naturally of vital interest to the country, but a statement made on the responsibility of the chairman of the committee ought to be accompanied in some way with an explanation of where the saving was to come from, and how the figure was arrived at. My hon. friend cannot furnish that.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
expect to present to the House an itemized statement of where the savings could be effected.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am not so unreasonable as to expect that an itemized statement Should be given, but I suggest a statement from the chairman of the special railway committee that $100,000,000 going out to the country is of first class imoortance, and ought to be accompanied at least by some geheral intimation of how the figure is arrived at.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The general impression is- and I think it is evident to every hon. member Who travels on the railways of Canada- that there is a tremendous degree of duplication of service, absolute waste, lines paralleling each other, duplicate stations and duplicate offices in almost every city in Canada. It seems to me that without any great explanation the principle of the thing must be apparent to everybody. As to the amount, I cannot give my hon. friend any information in detail, and I do not know whether those in authority would be prepared at the moment to give it in detail. But I would say that the men who are most concerned in the conduct of the National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway are agreed that a saving nearly as large as the figure I have mentioned can be made by a merging of the roads. The amount of $100,000,000 as a saving-and I expected to be asked my authority for that statement-is given to me by the highest authority in the land, or at least as high an authority as we have in this country.

The Budget-Mr. Euler

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would not like to throw
cold water on sudh an alluring proposition as my hon. friend presents, but would my hon. friend see no danger, if this proposition were carried out, of the Dominion of Canada coming under the powers of a private corporation on the one side, or on the other side, of the whole thing being controlled from a political point of view? These are the things that are in my mind. Outside of that, I think the idea is a splendid one.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The thing I desire to bring
before parliament is this: the saving would be $75,000,000 or $100,000,000. Parliament and the people of Canada would have to decide whether it is worth while to put all the railways of Canada under public control with the possible danger of political influence; or on the other hand to put all the railways of Canada under the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway, with all the danger of private monopoly, which I would not like for one moment to support.
In my opinion-and I may as well say it now-it would be in the interests of the Canadian people if these roads were combined under public ownership, so that the country would get the benefit of the saving made, and not the private corporation, which would enjoy a monopoly of the railway business in Canada. I know that this estimate of $100,000,000 sounds like an extreme statement, but I am not making it without reason, and if it is well founded, it transcends in importance all other matters before us at the present time, and I think it becomes the duty of the government to take some action.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the hon. gentleman for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) made the statement the other day in the House that there were five transcontinental trains running between Montreal and Vancouver, and that each one of those trains cost the taxpayers or the people of the country $9,000,000.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I was not present when he
made that statement, but I would say that there is a partial answer to his question as to how those savings could be effected.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is looking
at me. I am not from Vancouver South, and I did not- make any such statement.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I was not here when the
statement was made. I assure hon. members that the people of Canada are beginning to take a very great interest in this matter, and I -would urge it upon the consideration of the government. I am not trying to be
dogmatic on this question. I have my own opinion with regard to what ought to be done, but I believe it becomes the duty of the government to at least make an investigation as to whether this statement of the savings which can be effected by the amalgamation is founded on fact or whether it is not.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: In this saving of $100,000,000, does the hon. member take into consideration the amount of interest that would be assumed by buying out the Canadian Pacific Railway?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Certainly. Suppose for the
sake of argument, the Canadian National took over the Canadian Pacific Railway, we must assume that the Canadian Pacific stockholders and bondholders would continue to receive the return on the investment.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
And you would be
assuming a very much greater liability than you have at the present time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: But look at the income. The saving is supposed to be $100,000,000 over and above what the two railways are now able to accomplish.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How would the hon. member fix the dividends to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member is going into details which are rather premature.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Any such amalgamation
would have to be by the consent of the directors, and the shareholders, too, of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Perhaps so; and I for one
am inclined to believe that it might just be possible that the shareholders of the company would consent to an amalgamation.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not questioning
that at all1.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My point is this, Mr. Speaker, that if the statement I have made be true, then it should be at least worth while for the government to take the initiative and make some investigation with regard to it, and then take such action as may seem suitable,

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member not fear that this estimate of saving $100,000,000 was based on the thought that when the competitive element was taken away it would be possible to reduce the service to the public not only to the point where duplication was cut out, but where the public would not care to stand for the reduced service?
The Budget-Mr, Euler

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have absolutely no reason whatever to believe that that thought was in the minds of those who made that estimate. I would also add, though, that I believe it would be possible, if there were no competition, to cut out a great deal of the service that we are now receiving and that is entirely unnecessary.
Now, Sir, I realize there would be a decided difference of opinion in this House, and perhaps throughout the country, as to whether the combined systems should come under the control of the Canadian National Railways or of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In that connection I should like to correct an inference which might be drawn from a statement made by the Border Cities Star, which seems to be taking quite an interest in this question and which is urging very strongly that the railways be combined under Canadian Pacific management. The paper has spoken of the great economies that could be effected, and of the great waste that obtains just now, and it continues:
There is only one way to meet it-the situation- and that is for the people of Canada to adopt the course that the president of their railway system has practically advised them to follow. The acquisition of the Canadian National Railways would be a tremendous advantage to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I leave it right there, with this remark, that there is no ground for the inference that the president of the Canadian National Railways is in favour of combining the railways under the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Nothing he has said at any time, so far as I know, and nothing he has said upon which the articles in the Border Cities Star are based, would justify the paper in making that interpretation.
Now for my part, Mr. Speaker, I hold it "unthinkable that a private corporation should have a national monopoly of a great public Utility such as the railways of Canada. If there is to be a monopoly, it must be held by the people themselves. Some of my fellow-members on this side of the House sometimes express surprise that I should be in favour of public ownership. Well, I am from a city and from a part of Canada where public ownership has been made a great success. I might refer to the hydro system, which I have already done on other occasions, but I will confine myself to my own city of Kitchener. We have there under public control and public ownership our electric plant, our gas plant and our municipal railway. Never yet have the ratepayers of that city been called upon to pay one penny in taxes to carry on these businesses; never yet have they paid a cent in taxes to discharge the debentures as they

fell due and the interest; never yet has tihe commission that manages those concerns found it necessary to do any refunding, and at the present moment, after some twenty years of operation with a five-cent street railway fare, we find the public utilities of Kitchener in this condition, that even with low rates for electric current, gas and street railway fares, they have built up a surplus of $1,000,000.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Did they reduce the capital expenditure hs well?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
As the debentures fell due
the principal and interest were paid out of earnings, and in that way they have built up a surplus of $1,000,000.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If public ownership
of hydro has been such a success in Ontario, will the hon. member explain why they have seen fit to advance the rates?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That does not necessarily
say that public ownership is not a success. The probabilities are that if it were not publicly owned and operated the rates would have been advanced still more. In any case there are those who hold a theory, for I think it is only a theory, that a publicly owned and operated road is not so efficient as a privately managed one. That theory, Mr. Speaker, is in my opinion no longer tenable. We need only look to the conduct of the National Railways to-day. I can call no better witness than my hon. friend for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) who is antagonistic to public ownership and who the other day said on the floor of the House that the service on the National Railways is excellent, and he added that it wras the best in the world. The National Railways are giving an excellent service, a service that is improving steadily, and no one of late has charged that politics is playing any part in the management.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You cannot improve the service; it is the finest in the world.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend agrees with me. The usual objections to government operation are, as I have said, that you do not get the same efficient service as under private operation. That, I think, has been disproved. The other objection to the amalgamation of the Canadian Pacific Railway with the Canadian National under government control is that it would cost a great deal of money to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not profess to have any particular financial ability like my hon. friend for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), but I would say that it would not require the expenditure of any money what-

The Budget-Mr. Euler
ever to take over that system. I should think that the bondholders and stockholders of the Canadian Pacific! Railway could be given securities in the National Railways and draw their dividends or their interest just as they are doing now. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier was strongly opposed to the Canadian National Railways, and he advocated just as strongly that the road should be combined with its rival under Canadian Pacific ownership and management.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would say to hon. gentlemen that at the time our friend made that speech he gave us a great deal of interesting information and afforded us some amusement, and he reminded me of this little story. An old Englishman was sitting in his cottage and was being belaboured by his loving spouse, but he took it with perfect equanimity. One of his friends happened to walk in and expressed his surprise that he could take such treatment so calmly. The old man replied, "It pleases she and it don't hurt I." I felt the same way about my hon. friend. We had a good deal of enjoyment listening to what he said and, after all, what he said did not hurt the National Railways at all. But, after so much publicity being given to what was said by that hon. gentleman, and also by my hon. friend for St. Lawrence->St. George, who also advocated the acceptance of something in line with the Shaughnessy plan, I think it would be well to make some reference to that plan. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier admitted to the leader of the opposition the other day that the merger of the roads now under the National system was good; that to merge them was the only thing to do-although, mark you, at first he had been very strongly opposed to that course. Perhaps he will admit at a later stage that a similar merger of the Canadian Pacific with the National Railways under public ownership would also be the only thing to do.
But let me get on with the Shaughnessy plan. To my mind the Shaughnessy plan was a most excellent proposal,-for the Canadian Pacific. It proposed first of all that they keep out of the merger all their ocean steamship lines; keep out the express companies; keep out the hotels; keep out the lands and land contracts; keep out their railways in the United States; keep out their mining interests and certain other things. The Canadian Pacific Railway proper, then, was to take over our National system holus-bolus with the exception of the Grand Trunk, which came into our system afterwards. Now, what
the country would get for this was the reasonable certainty, according to Lord Shaugh-nessy's own figures as taken from his proposal-and I think the right hon. leader of the opposition will know whether or not I am giving it correctly, because it was addressed to him-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: There might be an inference in what the hon. member said that the plan involved subsequent acquisition of the Grand Trunk. It did not; the Grand Trunk was to remain as a separate road.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If my right hon. friend will search his memory I think he will find that Lord Shaughnessy's proposal was that the Grand Trunk should stay out and be allowed to shift for itself.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what I said.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is correct; and I made reference to that before in my observations. But what the country would get would be a reasonable certainty of an annual loss of $55,000,000 under the Shaughnessy plan, and the loss of our railway besides. Let us see how it works out. First of all, the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were to be guaranteed fixed dividends forever by the government of Canada. The rate is not specified, but I presume it would not be less than seven per cent, which is what they are receiving now out of the railway proper.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend in his argument has already admitted that.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Exactly; I am explaining the purport of the agreement. First of all the Canadian Pacific shareholders would be guaranteed fixed dividends forever by the government of Canada. On the basis of the 1920 business-that was the year used by Lord Shaughnessy in his calculations-the combined systems would have a deficit of $80,000,-
000.	Lord Shaughnessy thought, however, that the savings which could be effected by amalgamation-and perhaps this may have some force with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre-an amalgamation in which there would be no Grand Trunk railway, by the way, would reduce this deficit to $24,000,000. In other words, the saving would be $56,000,000-a very substantial sum-according to Lord Shaughnessy's calculation. These figures are based on the business of 1920, which, he said, was a bad year; a good year, he thought, might reduce the deficit to $11,-
000.000 or $12,000,000. But as he is definitely taking 1920 as a basis I think it is fair to adopt his estimate of $24,000,000. Now, Lord Shaughnessy was very careful not to say any-
The Budget-Mr. Euler

where that his new company would pay the interest on the advances made by the government of Canada to the National railways, in principal some $560,000,000 in all, involving annual interest charges of $31,000,000. Thus we would continue to pay under his plan the annual interest charge of $31,000,000, plus the deficit of $24,000,000, or a total each year, as I said before, of $55,000,000. Is that an attractive proposal, Mr. Speaker-to continue to pay out of taxation $55,000,000 a year and to give away our railway besides?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I think it is only fair that my hon. friend should point out that it is now over five years since this suggestion was made, and circumstances have altered considerably since that time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am quite willing to accept that for what it is worth, but I do not know just what value I can place upon it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
And also that the figures
in that plan were estimates; similarly are the present suggested figures estimates. *

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Certainly; that goes without saying. I have not given any hard and fast calculations; these are estimates-it is all we can possibly base our argument on.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend's hard and fast arguments are his own view of public ownership.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am sorry, Sir; I had hoped to get through in not more than an hour, but as my hon. friend himself said once before, Others are making a speech for me. We are actually doing just a little better than that now-and I would like hon. members of the House to note this; we are doing just a little better than we would do under the plan suggested by Lord Shaughnessy. We lose the $31,000,000 by way of interest on the moneys advanced to the National Railways, and this year we failed by some $21,000,000 to pay the fixed charges on the debt owing by the National Railways to the public, or a total loss of $52,000,000. That is what the railways are costing us this year as a loss; so I say we are actually $3,000,000 better off than we would be under the Shaughnessy plan, and we still have our railways and the control of them.
In addition to this-and I think this is of prime importance-the Canadian Pacific under the Shaughnessy plan, would get all the benefits of the savings effected by amalgamation, over and above the required $21,000,000 to pay the fixed charges on the debt owing to the public; which would amount to 
the trifling sum of from $60,000,000 to $75,000,
000	a year. Mark you, the Shaughnessy plan also says that in addition to the fixed dividend which shall be guaranteed in perpetuity to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific, if the profits of the combined system warrant i't, the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific shall receive further dividends. There is nothing in his statement to suggest, I repeat, that the people of Canada shall have interest paid on the moneys advanced to the National Railways, or any profits that might accrue under an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific to be carried on under Canadian Pacific control.
Nowr, Sir, I am almost through with what
1	had to say. I consider that the proposal of amalgation under the ownership of the Canadian Pacific Railway should not be considered at all. The Toronto Globe-and I do not always take the Toronto Globe for my guide-thinks it is hardly worth while discussing that proposal. The Canadian people, Sir, will never permit a monopoly of the railway business in Canada by any private company; if they must have a monopoly it must be a public monopoly. We are not going to place ourselves at the mercy of a private concern in the matter of the railway business of this country. It is said that the railway commission will protect us if the Canadian Pacific has a monopoly of the railway business of the country. Yes, the railway commission can control rates, but within the four corners of their right to operate, and entirely outside the practical powers of the railway commission, I contend there lies the whole field of service, and that service may be good, bad or indifferent. I leave it to the good judgment of the House whether any private corporation where there is no competition, no matter how good the intentions of the management may be, is not more apt to give indifferent service than anything else. Here is the difference in theory between the two plans: The privately owned business always has as its primary purpose the making of money, the making of profits, whereas a publicly owned business always has or ought to have in view the primary purpose of service to the public.
I believe the people of Canada would destroy any government that would dare to hand over the National Railways to a privately owned corporation. I believe they would wipe out the candidates of monopoly, although possibly some of my friends who come from the city of Montreal might escape; but I doubt very -much whether the sober common sense of the French-Canadian people would

The Budget-Mr. Euler
tolerate the suggestion that the railway business of Canada should come under the control of a private monopoly. Certainly from the Ottawa river west, and I think I know whereof I speak, not a baker's dozen would come back to parliament on that issue. I marvel, Sir, at the boldness of the man who made the Shaughnessy suggestion. It was not a compliment to the intelligence of the people of Canada or to the intelligence of parliament, and certainly not to the intelligence of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), who then was Prime Minister of this country, and who I am glad to say never apparently considered the proposal. I can only understand the acceptance of this plan by my able friend for St. Lawrenee-St. George and my good friend for George Etienne Cartier on the assumption that they did not realize quite what was involved in that suggestion, or else they were so influenced by their antagonism to the principle of public ownership that they let their prejudices run away with their usual good judgment.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Let me say quite clearly to my hon. friend from North Waterloo that I have not entirely accepted the Shaughnessy plan at all in any way.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You mentioned it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The Shaughnessy plan was to me a tentative proposal, nothing more or less. I have never analysed the figures of the Shaughnessy plan in any way, but what I say is this, that some plan should be devised and proposed to this country that will effect the savings that are necessary. If any other plan is as good as the Shaughnessy plan, I for one am quite prepared to accept it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Always, I presume, if it be a plan for the Canadian Pacific Railway taking over the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Not at all. Let me correct my hon. friend there also. I am not at all wedded to the question of the Canadian Pacific Railway taking over the Canadian National Railways. I want to see the railway deficit stopped in this country, first of all.
