maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am very glad the hon. member and I are quite agreed on one point.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend is speaking like a partisan.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I will leave it to the judgment of the House as to who is the partisan when we come to the question of the railways.
Sir, the union of these systems under national ownership offers a good deal more than the
Shaughnessy plan. It gives to the country the benefit of the savings effected, and not to the Canadian Pacific. When I remarked the other day that Sir Henry Thornton believed that union would result in the paying of all fixed charges, including the interest on the moneys advanced by the government of Canada to the railways, the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier rather ungraciously remarked that Sir Henry Thornton was a good promiser. I would just like to draw attention to this, that Lord Shaughnessy was also a promiser, and that the one promiser represented private interests, and the other promiser the Canadian people, and I would like to ask: Which one would the members of this House as the representatives of the Canadian people consider the more disinterested?
Now we have the three alternatives. We can continue as we are, run our roads in as close co-operation as possible with the Canadian Pacific Railway, making savings wherever we can, but running as two independent systems. I believe much can be done that way, and with a reasonably good year I believe that we will come very 'close to paying fixed charges to the public. If we continue in tha* way I believe that something should be done by way of writing down the capitalization of the National Railways so that they will be placed on some sort of basis that will enable them to go on as they would be able to do under private ownership.
Then we have the second plan-combine under Canadian Pacific Railway ownership. I am not going to discuss that any more, because I think it should not be very seriously discussed.
Third, combine the National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway into one great public-owned system. That in my opinion is the proper solution, a solution which seems perhaps impossible, may I sa}r, because of its apparent magnitude or because men's minds have not learned to adjust themselves to so big an undertaking, but which, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion will be forced eventually by tho logic of facts. If anyone had said ten years ago that five great railway systems in Canada would now be combined into what is known as the Canadian National Railways, he would have found very little credence with the Canadian public; but we have them combined into one system to-day.
Let me repeat, Sir, if $100,000,000 can be saved to this country by a union of the two great railway systems, it constitutes a challenge to parliament and to the government, and I believe the people of Canada will expect some sort of action, even if it be only investigation of what I say. I think it can in duty do
The Budget-Mr. Euler

nothing less, and if it finds it true, its duty is so clear that the neglect of it, I think, would be inexcusable.
In conclusion, let me summarize what results we can expect if we grapple courageously with the suggestion to settle this question as it must one day be settled.
First, it will enable the government to reduce taxation by nearly one-third, or at least one-quarter.
It will restore confidence, and encourage the Canadian people to go ahead, knowing' that light is breaking at last on our financial horizon.
It will stimulate trade. It will lower the cost of living. It will encourage enterprise and lead to the more rapid development of our natural resources. It will at once solve our ocean freight rates problem.
And finally, on \t could be based a practical scheme for the extinction of our enormous public debt, to which may be attributed most of our difficulties.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) I very seldom take part in the debates in this House and therefore have no apology to offer for occupying a brief period of the time of hon. members this evening. The hon. gentleman in question mentioned a statement as to the cost of a sitting of the House, and if I remember correctly he said it was at the rate of about $18,000 per day. A statement somewhat similar to that was made by some hon. member during one of the previous sessions of parliament, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) last session made a statement which placed the matter right, and as it is more favourable to those who are rather inclined to indulge in long speeches I feel perhaps justified in giving his figures. He stated that the cost of a session of the House was about $55,000 per month, over and above the regular permanent charges which must be paid in any event. Figuring twenty working days to the month that would make the cost about $2,700 a day, very much smaller than the figure mentioned by the hon. member to whom I referred. So that I feel the situation in that regard is not as bad as it might be after all, and possibly I may be disposed to take a few minutes longer than if the cost were $18,000 a day as represented.

Before proceeding with the matters that I intend to discuss I should Like to refer briefly to the very interesting address of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who finished his remarks just before six o'clock. The hon. gentleman always has something interesting to say and speaks with a knowledge of his subject. To me the remarkable feature of his address to-day was the extent of his criticism of the government. He found fault with the taxes. He called some of them nuisance taxes, criticized the sales tax, thought the income tax should be lowered, and was not altogether complimentary in his references to the dealings of the government with the railway proposition. One would expect that after all this volume of criticism he would not be quite comfortable on that side of the House. His criticism covered many subjects and was of a wide range, but I notice that the hon. gentleman sat down without stating how he was going to vote in connection with this budget. One would scarcely expect, in view of the criticism indulged in, that he could possibly support the government on this budget; we will await with interest his action when the vote takes place.
The budget, of course, is the subject of discussion at the present time. There have been many attacks upon it, attacks from many angles, and few of the members seem to be able to understand it. Many confess that they are unable to do so; and it would appear that if the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) had endeavoured to present a statement that was confusing and hard to understand he could not have possibly succeeded better than he has on this occasion. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) says that he cannot understand the statement, and other members, as I have stated, take the same position. The distinguishing feature of this budget is that it lacks clarity and, worse still, lacks candour. The Acting Minister of Finance admits an increase in the public debt for the last fiscal year amounting to approximately $14,000,000. To arrive at this conclusion he adds to the estimated cash surplus of revenue, amounting to approximately $1,823,000, the sum of $4,000,000 due from Roumania and Greece for interest on certain loans, although this sum has not been paid and possibly may never be paid or received by the Dominion of Canada. Assuming, however, that payment will ultimately be made this item should be treated as an asset, and .there is no justification whatever for its addition to the revenue pending actual payment. If this proper course had been adopted the increase

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
in the public debt for the last fiscal year would have been approximately $18,000,000, an increase which I think most hon. members admit would in itself be rather alarming in view of the high rate of taxation prevailing in this country particularly as compared with the rate prevailing in the United States. It must be remembered too that the $18,000,000 above mentioned) does not include moneys borrowed for the Canadian National Railways, the repayment of which has been guaranteed by Canada. The amount thus provided for the last fiscal year is approximately $64,000,000. On this basis the total increase of public debt, including moneys provided for railways, is $82,-
000.000 and in addition to that we have $18,000,000 provided for the National Railways for branch lines. Therefore, if that is taken into consideration, as I submit it should be, the total increase in our national debt during the last fiscal year is approximately $100,000,000. As against the moneys advanced to the Canadian National Railways, there may fairly be set off the increase in capital assets. But as is admitted all around, that already these railways stand in our books at a very much larger figure than their real value and tftiere is a contention from different parts of this House that the capitalization should be written down, very little comfort is derived from the mental process of endeavouring to estimate how much our roads have been increased in value by these expenditures. This government appears to have done its best to confuse the statement and conceal the facts; but an analysis of the figures forces any competent authority to a realization of the serious condition that confronts the Canadian people. The question is: How long can we afford to go on increasing our national indebtedness at the rate of approximately $100,000,000 a year, and how long will the Canadian people tolerate a government that carries on in this way?
What is the cause of the confusion on the part of members in this House as to the actual state of affairs in .connection with these accounts? This may be found in a reading of the budget speeches of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and comparing them with the speech made by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in delivering his second budget. I wish to quote briefly from Hansard of the session of 1922, volume 3, pages 2106 and 2107, where the Minister of Finance made the following statement dealing with the public debt:
I want to call attention now to the increase of our public debt. Against the gross debt are set off what are called the assets of the Dominion. In
former years practically all our assets are treated as good. When the amount was not very great in proportion to our business, .perhaps there was no need for any discrimination, but when these assets, under the operation of our railways, grew to very large figures, it became desirable or necessary that there should be discrimination. My predecessor in office, very properly I think, made that discrimination by dividing those assets into active and nonactive. It makes no difference with regard to the general expenditure, but if only the good assets are set off against the gross debt we get a fairer statement of the real debt of the country. Now, we are continuing this method of treating the assets: we treat these railway moneys as loans. Perhaps there can be some just objection to that. The Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern are now virtually owned by the Dominion of Canada, and when we advance money to them we are, in a sense, lending money to ourselves. When we represent these debts as assets, a keen critic might find some fault. But it may be that it will be necessary to continue that system; we are following out the accounts for 1922 in that way. There may be an advantage and a convenience in separating the railway operation from the rest of our expenditure. However, there is another view of the matter. We have a justification for charging to capital or to a special account some particular thing-the building of a railway for instance. Various classes of public expenditure having permanent results may .properly be classified as assets, may properly be classified under capital account; but if from year to year we are to provide for the ordinary expenses of the railway; if we are to provide for the deficits, the difference between receipts and expenditure; if we are also to provide large sums for interest on the bonds and other securities of these so-called railway companies -if we are to do that unfailingly every year, with a reducing figure we may hope, it will be open to some to say with much justice, that this is no longer a special account but part of the ordinary expenditure of the country; and if so, that ordinary expenditure should be included before we undertake to declare a surplus. However, as I said a moment ago, there may be some advantage in keeping the accounts of the railways for the present as separate and apart from others. If we clearly and definitely understand the nature of the transaction, I suppose there may be no serious objection to it.
Then, dealing with loans, he said:
During the year four Canadian government loans have been floated. Three of these have been in the names of the railway companies and one a direct government obligation. We still keep up the theory of corporations in regard to these railways; the railway loans are issued in the names of the railway companies, with guarantees by the government. As a matter of fact, the government to-day are both makers and endorsers of those securities; so that practically they are now government loans.
In 1923, the Minister of Finance, dealing with income and expenditure, made the following statement, as reported in Hansard, volume 3, page 2641:
We turn now to the year 1922-1923 which closed not many days ago. We have not the complete accounts before us, but there is sufficient information to enable us practically to announce the result. Ordinary revenue amounted to $393,619,000. These are estimates as the figures are not absolutely final. Ordinary expenditure amounted to about $331,780,000. As between those two items, there was then a surplus of $61,839,000. Capital expenditure, howe/er, represents $14,500,000; adjustment .of war claims,
2484	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
$6,700,000; cost of loan flotations, $3,050,000; these representing in all $24,250,000. There was thus a surplus over ordinary, capital and special expenditures, of $37,589,000. But again the railways have to be taken into account. We had to advance during that year $92,190,000 for railways, and $6,060,720 for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, making in all for that charge, $9S,250,720. This, of course, takes up ail the surplus I have mentioned and leaves a large balance on the other side of the account. If we take everything into consideration for the year, the net result was that we added to the public debt in the year just closed $49,293,086. The receipt of something over $8,000,000 from the British government on exchange account helped us to keep down what otherwise would have been a larger addition to the public debt.
The point to which I wish to call the attention of the House in these two budget speeches of the Minister of Finance is that he dealt explicitly with loans to the Canadian National Railways and clearly stated that they must be taken into consideration in dealing with the national debt. He went almost so far as to say - that they should be taken and included in the expenditure for the year. Just let us see how the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his first budget speech departs from this practice which, I submit, is entirely sound. I am quoting from Hansard of 1924, volume 2, page 1214. In dealing with railway loans, the Acting Minister of Finance speaks as follows:
I may say when loans are made by way of cash, under the arrangements made by the former Minister of Finance, they are treated as non-aotive assets and are, therefore, not taken into account when determining the net public debt. Moneys raised by way of guarantee, which places the government in the position of an endorser, do not presently affect the public debt in any way as they are indirect obligations.
I do not think that contention will commend itself to the best judgment of the members of this House, and it is quite in opposition and quite different from the position taken by the Acting Minister of Finance. I think it is absolutely unsound, and reminds one of the practice of our old friend Micawber, who gave a note and said the debt was paid, and that was the end of it. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in dealing with this matter the other night also made it very clear in the course of his remarks that these guarantees were part of the national debt and must be taken into consideration in dealing with this question. At page 2335 of Hansard he says:
That is not the point in question. The point in question is this, as to how much of those bonds emitted year after year, have to be added, using that argument, to the net consolidated debt or, if you put it in another way, to the combined debt of the country. In other words, hon. gentlemen have complained that in a certain year we paid out a great deal of money in cash on account of the railways and we charged that in the net consolidated account. Consequently, the deficit was very large.

Now, they say, you come along and say to us:	We
do not intend to pay out cash, but we intend to finance by way of bonds. Consequently your net deficit is very much less or you may have a surplus as the case may be. There is a good deal in that argument and it has to be fairly faced. The question of policy is one which does not make any difference one way or the other in the financial arrangements. Whether the railways are financed by way of cash or by way of bonds, it matters not, all the obligations of the railways are our debts and have to be taken into consideration in some way or another. If $20,000,000 is issued, guaranteed or unguaranteed, in any particular year, that is reflected in the debt of the country, perhaps not for book-keeping purposes in the consolidated debt, but in the combined debt of the country. We owe that money and we have to pay it. Of course, as against it, we have the assets, if any, purchased by the funds or proceeds of those particular bonds. Therefore, in the last analysis it does not make any difference whether we pay cash or issue bonds, for practical purposes we have to take into consideration the net result which is obtained.
That is a position which I submit, Mr. Speaker, is quite different from the position taken by the Acting Minister of Finance in his address. Nearly every speaker has spoken of the high taxation that prevails in Canada. I do not know that we always realize how high it really is, and we can only get at this by a comparison with taxation in other countries. We all admit it is too high, and that it should be reduced if possible. We are apt to think of England as a country in which the taxation is exceedingly high, and figures have been quoted in this connection; but if you take into consideration the taxation in the Dominion of Canada, including our federal, our provincial and our municipal taxation, we find that it is a little higher in Canada than it is in England. An authority dealing with this question quotes the taxation in England as $80, and in Canada our Dominion taxation amounts to $38. In the province of Ontario our provincial taxation is $13 and our school and municipal taxation $30, making a total of $81, just approximately $1 in excess of the taxation that exists in Great Britain.

Let me quote a statement made by President Coolidge, which I .think is just as applicable to Canada as to the United States. He said:
All experience shows that a larger amount of money can be collected from large incomes at a moderate rate than at a high rate. When the Tate is too high large incomes disappear, leaving all the burden of taxes on the wage earners, and people of small means.

We are a young country, with illimitable natural resources, but no great accumulated wealth. A burden which could lightly be borne by an old country, with its great capital resources, is one which might strangle the future development of a young nation.

When we come to the tariff we at once get on controversial ground. We have had a good niany debates on the subject, even since the introduction of this budget, and no subject has been the cause of more prolonged discussions during the last quarter of a century than this same question. I do not, however propose to deal with it exhaustively to-night; I hope another opportunity will be presented when the resolution standing in the name of my leader comes up for discussion to go into the subject more fully. Let me briefly review the record of the government upon this important question. The government was elected upon a platform of a downward revision of the tariff; that was clearly set forth at the convention of the Liberal party in 1919 and was enunciated in this House by the Prime Minister when leader of the opposition and by all of his supporters during the last election campaign. When the government came into office their first budget showed a slight reduction in the tariff, so slight that it was entirely offset by an increase in the sales tax. Recognizing that this did not in any way amount to a fulfilment of their preelection pledges, they told us to be patient, that this was a beginning, that it was a step in the right direction-"Wait until you see us next year." Next year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), to the surprise of all, announced that we must have tariff stability, that it would not be right or proper to be always tinkering wfith the tariff, particularly as our tariff was only a moderate one anyway. I commend his statement to those hon. members who are accustomed to speak of our tariff as high. It is not a high tariff; it is a low tariff compared with the tariff of other countries, particularly since the war. In the third session of this parliament, notwithstanding that announcement by the Minister of Finance, the budget contained considerable reductions in the tariff, reductions which disturbed industry and alarmed capital, and resulted in no corresponding advantage; in fact it would be hard to imagine any advantage that could compensate for the injuries caused by these reductions. We were told that the government were carrying out their programme, which they would persist in until finally we had that all-round downward revision which had been promised in

Shortly before the opening of this session the Prime Minister, in the course of a speech in Toronto, announced that there would be a pause in the downward revision, that after all there would be no serious tariff changes in the next budget. What do we find to-day? In this, the fourth budget of the government, instead of carrying out the earlier programme of a downward revision, we find there is an increase in the tariff on coal, and we have a sort of promise-for what it may be worth-that a tariff board is to be constituted.
The member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), in dealing with this proposed tariff board, intimated that he thought it was really something that would enable the government to avoid responsibility, a sort of smoke screen behind which they could hide for protection. The proposition is so hazy, so indefinite, and the government have so frequently resorted to royal commissions of one kind and another to escape responsibility upon every vital issue that has come up, that I do not wonder at the member for Springfield looking upon this tariff board as a similar device. I think it would be possible to erect a commission that would really be helpful to the government and to all concerned in tariff matters; but this proposition is so vague, there is so little detail presented, that we are unable to judge whether such a board would be of any real service or not. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this proposal is put forward on the eve of a general election to enable the government to escape from the difficulty in which they find themselves. Is it not intended to make the tariff issue a free for all, to enable their candidates to preach high protection where it suits, to preach low tariff where it suits, to preach tariff for revenue where it suits -in short to suit the tariff policy of the government to the particular constituency, so that some of their candidates may pose as supporters of a tariff for revenue only, others as protectionists, and still others as free traders-ready to ring "the death knell of protection?" I submit that the proposal is open to this interpretation in view of the action of the government on this vital issue. But, Mr. Speaker, these tactics will not save the government. We had hoped that the government would bring down before this time its policy upon this important question. Surely the time has come when this agreement, which operates in such a way as to work a serious discrimination, should be terminated and the whole matter turned over to the railway .commission for the framing oif a fair and .proper system of railway rates, based on such instructions as may be given it in any policy laid down by this parliament.

If a conference between the heads of these railways fails to bring about the desired result, then I submit the matter should be sent to the railway commission and. if necessary the Railway Act should be amended to enable the commission, upon application of either of the railway companies, of the Minister of Railways, or of the Governor in Council, to deal with this matter and! to make such order as will bring about an elimination of this needless competition.
Another matter which I desire to deal with very briefly is that of hydro electric power, and my reference to it is suggested by the imposition of an export duty on power. Hydro electric power is the most potent attraction for industry and development on the face of the globe to-day, and the province of Ontario is more interested in this than in any other future or possible development. It is an asset of almost inestimable value to Canada, and particularly to central Canada, because of the use of a vast quantity of coal and the extent to which electricity is taking the place of coal for power purposes and domestic use, both urban and rural. The development of hydro electric power, the extent of Rs use, and its successful transmission for long distances, is one of the remarkable developments of the last quarter of a century. A few years ago there was considerable anxiety with regard to the question whether a sale could be found for the large volume of power the development of which had been undertaken and was assured. Any fears in this direction have been entirely dispelled by the constantly increasing use of electricity for so many purposes, and the difficulty that now presents itself is to meet the demand, which has overtaken and overrun the supply. If there is any national asset which with
peculiar advantage may be retained and developed for the Canadian people, it is hydro electric power.
The passing of an order in council under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act imposing an export duty of $1.95 per horse power per year raises the question as to what our policy should be. On a previous occasion I pointed out to this House the importance of this matter and urged that hydro electric power should not be exported but should be retained for the use of our people, the development of our natural resources, and industrial enterprise. At that time I was speaking with particular reference to the proposed development on the St. Lawrence, and urged that this government approve the plans filed by the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario and allow the province to proceed at once with this new development to furnish power to supply a shortage which already existed and to meet the demands upon the Ontario system. I now wish to repeat that request and to condemn the imposition of an export duty. We should not, Mr. Speaker, export our power at all If export is now allowed difficulties will develop when we find it necessary to discontinue the export. Contracts will have been made and vested rights acquired, and many objections will be urged against the cancellation of export licenses.
Our experience in connection with the diversion of water by the Chicago drainage canal, made without permission or license, has been very unfortunate and has led to years of expensive controversy between Canada and the United States. A severe lowering of the level of our lakes and harbours has taken place because of this unauthorized diversion, with millions of dollars of consequent loss to shippers and a large expenditure of public money in deepening the channels of navigation and our harbours. The end is not yet. We must wait for years before conditions become normal, and in the meantime make additional large expenditures of public money. The .complications that are sure to develop in the export of hydro electric power are likely to cause a situation equally serious and difficult of adjustment. Let us take warning from our past experience and avoid future difficulty by preserving this asset intact for the benefit of Canadian agriculture, Canadian industry, Canadian labour and Canadian railways.
A similar policy should be adopted in connection with our pulpwood, either by the imposition of an embargo, or perhaps better still by a good stiff export duty, increasing

We have heard a great deal, Mr. Speaker, about conditions in Canada. We have heard it urged by some that conditions are not satisfactory, that we are not prospering. Others have controverted that and said that we are doing pretty well, after all. Well, you can imagine the effect that a two-hour address by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) would have on a man who is out of work and seeking employment. You can understand how far his address would go towards giving a man in those circumstances satisfaction.
What is really wrong with Canada at the present time, because I think we all admit that conditions are not as they should be? What is really wrong with us, after all? We are suffering from dislocation of business and general confusion following the war. For this the government is not to be held entirely responsible, but the government must be held responsible for its failure to take such action as is best Calculated to overcome these handicaps. Canada is debilitated, run down, weak hearted, because of her repeated overdoses of tariff reduction. We need the stimulus that has been adopted by nearly every other civilized nation since the war, namely, the adoption of a policy of preserving the home market for our own population. Canada stands alone as the one nation adopting the opposite course of opening her markets to foreign competition from highly protected countries, from whose markets we are excluded. It will not be a cure for all our troubles and all our difficulties, but it is a first step necessary to restore confidence and give employment, and stop the exodus of our best workmen and young men from Canada. What does Canada really need at the present time? I have a few headings here which I think will suggest a good deal to the hon. members of this House.
First, we need thrift on the part of the Canadian people. Second, we need economy by all governments, federal, provincial and municipal.. Third, we need the adoption of a proper tariff policy and stabilization of our tariff. Fourth, we need readjustment of railway rates and removal of duplication in our railway services. Fifth, we need a readjustment of taxation, particularly income and sales taxes.	,
Now with regard to the first item, thrift. A great many people in Canada are suffering to-day because of extravagance and unnecessary expenditure. I am 9 p.m. afraid the Canadian people have to a large extent forgotten how to be thrifty as our ancestors were. The

people of the older countries, particularly Scotland, knew how to be thrifty, and they practised thrift to their own good and to the national advantage. Thrift keeps people out of debt; it makes them independent; it gives them confidence and corn age; it enables them to meet unexpected reverses. Economy on the part of governments is necessary. Governments, just like the people, have lost perhaps a sense of economy in large measure. In the old days the idea was that to be popular a government must be a spending government, but Mr. Speaker, for the next few years the government that will make good with the Canadian people will not be a spending government, but a government that practises economy, a government that sets aside all unnecessary public expenditure and that calls upon those who are demanding it to wait until we are in a better condition. This government pretends that it is practising economy. It has not succeeded in any large measure. I think when you look at the large number of commissions it has appointed, you will find that there is a failure to practise economy. What about the pulpwood commission that cost Canada $75,000, and that has enabled the government to dodge this question and that brought about no practical result? What about the grain commission that cost us $170,000? What about the abortive lake freights investigation that cost $41,000? What about the ocean rates investigation. by Mr. Preston, which report has finally been discarded and a contract made entirely independent of it? What about the purchase of the Union club for $2,000,000? What about the purchase of the Scribe hotel for $3,000,000? What about the raising of the Auditor General's salary from $6,500 to $15,000? And so on with a large number of other items I could mention. When the supplementary estimates come down, if, as last year, they disclose a large expenditure on public works, we shall find there very little evidence of economy on the part of this government.
I spoke of the adoption of a proper tariff policy for this country, a tariff policy that keeps our workmen at home, and that preserves our home market for our own farmers and our own people. I have gone into the question of the railway rates and the readjustment of taxation.
The government claims that we are prosperous in Canada. The Prime Minister spoke about two hours quoting statistics, and I think he must have been convinced that he had failed to satisfy the members of this House and the people of Canada because the Minister of Labour spent another two hours

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
endeavouring to accomplish the same result. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, to this government some of the things that I think most clearly indicate a lack of prosperity in Canada. First, our falling revenue. There has been a decrease in the revenue as compared with last year of approximately $52,000,000, partly due, undoubtedly, to a reduction in the sales tax and the lowering of duties. The Acting Minister of Finance last year estimated that our loss of revenue in this direction would amount to about $24,000,000, but it is double that amount showing that there is a falling off in the volume of business from which the revenues of this country are to be derived. There is a decrease in the amount received from income tax in 1922 as compared with 1924 of about 31 per cent. There is a decrease in the gross railway earnings for 1923-24 of the two national systems. In the case of the Canadian Pacific the decrease is about $14,000,000, and in the case of the Canadian National Railways about $17,000,000. Is there any evidence of prosperity in these decreases? Then there is a continued exodus to the United States annually of at least 150,000 of our best people, of which number only about one in four return.
These, I submit, Mr. Speaker are facts which show that Canada is not prospering as we would like it to prosper, but that on the contrary it is going in an opposite direction. Prosperity is its own best witness, and when it comes to Canada all the Canadian people will recognize it and gladly welcome it. We shai! not require long speeches by ministers of the crown to let us know when it is here. Prosperity will not come under an administration such as we have had for the last three years under the present government. Its policy has no stability upon any vital issue, particularly upon the tariff. The government's policy has been sessional, it has gone forward and then backward'; it has stood still; it has sidestepped, wobbled, and pussyfooted until it has become dazed and confused, and does not know in which direction to move. It has introduced anti-dumping legislation, and then has itself dumped its own legislation. But the great dumping act will take place at the next election when the Canadian people dump this government. Some people will vote against it because it has not fulfilled its pledges; others will vote against it because it has tinkered with the tariff-sometimes raising it, sometimes lowering it, sometimes pausing in its programme of ringing the death knell of protection, and now proposing a commission behind which to take refuge for 159
at least another session; others will vote against it because it has mud led our finances and increased our taxes and pubic debt; workmen will vote against it because many of their number are out of work and others have been forced to emigrate to the United States to secure employment; capital will vote against it because it has destroyed confidence; farmers will vote against it because it has refused their reasonable request for a fair measure of protection against the large volume of products of 'the United States, and because they are in a large measure losing their home market. The government's sole desire has been to retain power at the expense of principle. In its confusion it does not know what to do, how to lead. Prosperity will come in Caqada when we adapt a sane, stable tariff policy that will protect agriculture, labour, industry and capital, and will give to the hundreds of thousands of Canadian workmen employment in Canada instead of in the United States. Prosperity will come when we adopt a policy that will preserve our forests and our resources of field, mine and water-power for the benefit of Canadians and those who may desire to become Canadians. This policy will solve our immigration problem by retaining our own people and attracting desirable immigrants. By doing this and providing additional freight for our railways deficits will disappear, and our burden of taxation -will be lightened. The Canadian people are longing for the adoption of this policy, and realize that they must look not to the present government but to a new government with courage, with capacity and with determination to face the present difficult situation fairly and squarely.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first matter that naturally presents itself in this discussion is the amendment by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). That amendment recites that conditions in Canada demand a reduction of taxation, especially of the sales tax, and deplores the fact that the financial statement does not show the economy necessary to enable the government to do this. I apprehend that we are all agreed that a reduction of taxation is desirable, that it is a "consummation devoutly to be wished"; on this point we are all in accord. While this is true, Mr. Speaker, I have a theory that the Canadian taxpayer gets more value for the dollar he pays the tax gatherer than for any other dollar that passes through his hands. I believe that is true. I believe that he gets the most substantial value-in the way of items that are inestimable and beyond price-for the money he pays the tax gatherer. The great burden of taxation is represented in the amount paid for the war debt, for the expenses incidental to that great struggle. When we consider the scope of the catastrophe which we escaped can we rightly estimate what that victory meant to us? Can we, in any way, conceive what would have been the disaster if the victory had gone to the other side and Canada to-day was under the German flag, or the heel of the military despot was on our necks and we were paying reparations beyond all measure while our own obligations were postponed? No. we should pay that tax and pay it thankfully that we had escaped the disaster that threatened us. Do we begrudge the money we pay our wounded soldiers? I think not. I think that tax is a sacred duty and that we pay it willingly. We are told that we are burdened with our railroad deficits, and that is true. We are told that our railroads are overbuilt. We probably do not need them all at the present time; but the time was when these railroads were all needed, when every acre of land that they developed and brought under cultivation was required. During the war we saw long trains sweeping across the prairies and over the mountains loaded with our soldiers, with workmen from China and the Orient, with supplies gathered from all quarters of the earth, with the golden stream that flowed from the prairie provinces

The Budget-Mr. McConica
over the prairies across the mountains and over the sea to our soldiers and our allies. Those railways were absolutely necessary; we needed them badly in those dark days, and we could not, in all probability, have succeeded without them. I still think there was something almost! providential in the fact that they were built and that the land in the west was developed as it was. No, we needed those railroads then and our railway situation to-day is improving. The condition is far better to-day than it was when I came to this parliament. We are gradually evolving towards the light. I am satisfied that some plan will be arrived at by which the deficit will be met, it may be by the plan of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), or that of the venerable Nestor of the House (Mr. Maclean), or that of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). The day will come and it is not far distant when we shall meet that deficit. The time will come, in my opinion, very soon when we shall remember those dark days and the memory will be a pleasure to us.
Then we have the tax for the ordinary expenses of the government, a comparatively small portion of our expenditure, not very much more than we spent prior to the war. We have a list of the public utilities and public services rendered in our estimates. Ye go over them carefully; we look at them individually, and we decide that each one is worth more to the taxpayer than it is costing him; that it would be a distinct loss to tihe country to discontinue them. The time may come when it will be necessary to discontinue some; but let us remember that Canada is a going concern and that we must not curtail those things the curtailmennt of which will inflict a loss beyond the loss we are suffering in the taxes we are paying. We examine these estimates fairly carefully. It is charged that there is great waste. I do not see just exactly where it is. We look over the estimates; we decide the purpose for which the money shall be expended; we decide the amount that is to be spent, and if there is profligate and extravagant waste, we, as members of this parliament, are responsible for it. We cannot hide behind the skirts of the government. Every man here is responsible if there is wild extravagance in the expenditure for the current demands of the government. I do not think there is sudh extravagance. It would be a marvel if some money did not get away; but upon the whole, considering the magnitude of the enterprise I am of opinion that it is not very good business to be trying to convince the people 159i
that they are being unmercifully taxed and that money ie being recklessly squandered. I do not think that is a very patriotic thing to do, and I do not believe it should be done. The people are meeting their obligations manfully. They know they must pay heavy taxes; they realize the condition of the country, and they are meeting their taxes with little grumbling. We hear more of it in this House than we hear anywhere else. More fuss is made in one day here about taxes than in Saskatchewan in a year, and I do not think it is patriotic to perpetuate this sort of propaganda.
But our friends to the right tell us that a reduction of taxation is desirable, and we agree with them. How do they propose to bring this about? Take a dollar off the sales tax and1 add four dollars to the indirect taxation 1 Take a penny off a man's tax bill and add a pound to ithe cost of his coat, for it takes four dollars paid by the consumer .'to put one dollar into the treasury. If we take a dollar off the sales tax, we must make it up by the tariff, and wre pay four dollars to make up the deficit. That is not the kind of taxation relief that the country needs, and I do not believe the taxpayers are looking for that sort of benefit. This is like the relief which the vulture gives to the lamb when he covers and devours it. Four dollars on for one taken off! That is the philosophy of our protectionist friends.
To what end is this to be done. In order that we may keep our manufacturers busy. What is the trouble with our manufacturing enterprises to-day? Is it that the home market has gone? Why, our imports fell off by the million last year. If there is any market here, we have it for our manufactures. The trouble with the protective proposition is that the thing has undermined itself. It has sapped the purchasing power of the country until our workmen are living from hand to mouth in rented houses, our salaried men are just able to live, our farmers are working on mortgaged farms with impaired and worn out equipment, and there is no purchasing power. You may galvanize it with all the high protection imaginable, and you cannot sell a single dollar's worth of goods more than you are selling today. The trouble is not that our factories cannot manufacture under the present tariff. The only trouble is that they cannot sell. They tell us that we are over-industrialized. I suspect we are. We are told also that money is not being invested in manufacturing enterprises. Certainly it is not; it was not before the chan re in the tariff. It has not been invested in manufacturing enterprises since the war, and there is no call for it.
The Budget-Mr. McConica

I was rather interested in the pathetic story told by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in his speech on the Address. He told us that there were large amounts of iron ore within half a day's ride of Vancouver, and large quantities of splendid coking coal in the immediate vicinity. He intimated that if it had not been for the reduction in the tariff there would have been iron mills and steel plants out there and that country would have blossomed into a hive of industry. I do not doubt that these minerals exist. I have no reason to question the hon. gentleman's accuracy on that point. I have no doubt they are there, and they have been there for some time. They were put there before the morning stars sang together, and for fifty years we have had a tariff, and during much of that time we have had a bounty on steel; during a great part of that time we had in power a party in favour of increasing the tariff if asked to do so. And yet during all those fifty years not a ton of that ore was smelted and not a ton of that coal found its way into a blast furnace; yet the hon. gentleman would have us understand that if we had not taken just a shaving off the tariff at that particular time, just an infinitesimal amount, that whole country would have blossomed into a busy hive of industry, the hillsides would have been speckled with workmen and the valleys would ramble with rolling mills and great fumes of black smoke would be shooting up from those factories until they had tarnished the very stars of heaven. But that little change was made in the tariff, and that stopped the whole proceeding. Now, Mr. Speaker, if that enterprise was so weak and wabbly that that trifling change in the tariff was going to kill it, it was better that it should stop in embryo, in my opinion,- better that it should have stopped before it was born; otherwise we would have had another lame duck on our hands asking for more protection.
It is said that no money is now going into new plants, and yet we are told that just across the river a new concern is to be started, with a capital of $27,000,000, quite a considerable amount, more money than I have seen for a month. They are going to start manufacturing, and they are going to employ Canadian workmen. They are going to use Canadian raw materials and Canadian power. They are going to compete with the pauper labour of Europe and the massed production of the United States. They are going to turn out goods and sell them in the markets of the world. That is the kind of factories we need.

What they can do others can do. As the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) said, electrical power in this country is the great attraction. Now, why under heaven manufacturing cannot be carried on in Canada where we have an abundance of the cheapest and best power in the world, and more that can be developed easily is difficult to understand. Why we cannot manufacture with the raw material at hand, with the best workmen, or as good workmen as are to be found in the world, just as skilful, just as industrious and efficient, and why we cannot compete in the markets of the world is something I cannot understand.
If we are to develop a manufacturing nation we must compete in the markets of the world; otherwise we cannot consume the products of all our factories nor the products of our farms. We must have a foreign market, and in order to sell abroad we must buy from abroad. One trade brings another and we cannot simply ship our produce across the ocean and bring back the money. We must take goods in return or else we will find no market. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) tells us that market gardeners need protection. He would like to protect the market gardener, and starve the people for ten months of the year with the hope that they would eat more during the other two months. But at would not have that effect. The fact that in April or May I eat strawberries that were raised in New Jersey early in the spring is no reason why I will not eat them in July if they are raised in Ontario. A man's dinner is not like his coat. It does not last him three or four years. He must have at least one dinner a day. I have a theory that the market gardener should be supported for the people instead of the people for the market gardener. But that argument is as logical as any of the tariff arguments we hear. The theory is, make the people take what you want to give them and when you want to give it to them, charge them a good round price for it, and if they grumble and object to it they are not patriotic. I will not prolong this argument. I am glad to know it only costs me $2,700 a day and I do not want to pay for very much extra time.
This tariff situation is an important matter. We are going to have a vote on the budget. I do not propose to vote for the amendment. That is quite settled in my mind. Now, how about the budget? My hon. friends to my right are going to vote against it because the tariff is not high enough. My friends to my left are supposed to vote against it because it is too high. If I vote against it and my friends on my right vote against it, are they

The Budget-Mr. Robitaille
voting with me or am I voting with them? Or are we trying to hitch up a team and puil the government from the seat of power, with one horse pulling east and the other pulling west? And if we succeed, who is going to get the credit and who is going to take the responsibility? That is the question I would like to have settled in my mind. What would be the issue in the next campaign if we were to put the government out of office on this vote? Would it mean that we were in favour of a higher tariff or in favour of a lower tariff? That is a question for hon. gentlemen to try and settle one way or the other. I have been thinking at over pretty thoroughly, and I am going to keep on thinking for a little while, and listen to the balance of the discussion.
There are some questions I should like to have threshed out. I think it was a great improvement when they amended the dumping clause. I supported the Progressive amendment with enthusiasm because I especially objected to the dumping clause. That clause, I am glad to see, is to be eliminated. I hope there may be some other eliminations. I am in favour of a lower tariff. I khould like to have seen a reduction in tariff at this time not on the items reduced last year but on other items. I believe that we should gradually come down to the point where we have a tariff for revenue. I do not believe we can walk on industrial stilts to the end of time, and get them longer and longer all the time. If we do, we are bqund to take a tumble. I believe we should get down to the ground, and stand on a firm foundation where we can manufacture and sell in the markets of the world. I believe we can do that. Until we do, we will not have an industrial Canada.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my sorrow for the illness of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), which deprives us of his presence in the House. Even if I must wound the modesty of the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), I want to congratulate him and express to him my admiration for the way he administers both the Department of Immigration and the very responsible Department of Finance.
I shall not thresh out the budget; other members better able than I am have clearly shown its nice points and advantages, and the country, I feel sure, is well satisfied.
I cannot pass over in silence the remarks of the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet) in regard to the French language. It is unfortunate, that he was not a member before, he might have been able, perhaps, to infuse
in his leaders a few principles of equity and justice towards the French Canadian, for he cannot have forgotten that the province of Quebec had almost always been ignored under the Borden-Meighen government. The hon. member for Kent must not have forgotten that his present leader, when Prime Minister, only invited or was only forced to invite French Canadians into his cabinet in the dying hours of his government; however, the province of Quebec, faithful to its motto, remembers.
The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fontaine), in the course of this debate', has shown that the present government had always endeavoured to be fair to French Canadians and he gave proofs to support his contentions.
One could add further proofs. For intance, it was a French Canadian that the present government chose to negotiate with the French Republic, on behalf of Canada, a parcel of land which would serve to commemorate the glory of our brothers fallen on the battlefield, and it is you, Mr. Speaker, who obtained from France this grant of land on Vimy ridge.
The hon. member for Hull forgot to mention all the positions to which our people had been appointed and which, perhaps, would be too long to enumerate. Fie neither mentioned that at the door of every office in this building, we notice, this year, for the first time, bilingual inscriptions engraved on brass plates.
The friends of the hon. member for Kent, have never shown much enthusiasm for our language, if we are to judge from the answer given to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) to questions he put to the government on May 5, 1920:
1.	Why is the calendar of the Clerk on the table-of the House of Commons in English only?
2.	Is it the intention of the government to have also on this table a French calendar?
3.	If so, when?
4.	If not, why?
Sir George Foster: My reply to the question asked by my hon. friend the member for Charlevoix and Montmorency is this:
In placing that calendar on the table of the House of Commons, traditions of former years since the origin of Confederation until our days have been observed. Under these circumstances, I do not deem it necessary either to replace it with another one or to put another one on the Clerk's desk. What was sufficient for the Fathers of Confederation should surely satisfy us, for we are not less intelligent nor more patriotic than our predecessors.
I think, Sir, that it is befitting to say a few words regarding the political campaign being waged by the friends, old and new, of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), in the province of Quebec. Important ques-
The Budget-Mr. Robitaille

tions are being discussed: tariff, British preference, protection, etc. In the "et cetera" is included conscription, of which the right hon. leader of the opposition has proclaimed himself the father. They reproach the 65 members of the province of Quebec for not having this act repealed. Is 'there a more low and despicable campaign than this one? I think, they are men connected with the law, barristers, who discuss this question in public. They have certainly forgotten an important factor; it is the views of their leader, who for them, is infallible. Allow me to remind them of it. On April 3, 1922, the present Premier (Mr. Mackenzie King) speaking on this question, among other things stated, what follows, which will be found on page 640 of Hansard:
If the statutes were being revised, Mr. Speaker, the commissioners would simply drop this act altogether. For us to proceed any further would be to take action which is wholly unnecessary.
To the above Mr. Meaghen answered immediately :
Of the correctness of the position taken by the Prune Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) there is no doubt whatever. The act has no present force and effect; there is no room for legal dispute of any kind on that ,point. The act plainly applied to the then war, and to no other; it could not by any government be applied to any other emergency, contingency, or war whatsoever. Consequently, on the termination of thaA war, the act became obliterated so far as actual operation at any time is concerned.
The 'hon. Speaker put an end to the discussion in the following manner which will be found at page 644 of Hansard:
In any judgment this discussion is out of order. Any resolution presented in the House must have something positive as to its effect. If a motion is made or a bill introduced with a view to repeal that legislation must be in existence. From the opinions -of the Law Officers of the House of Commons and -of the Deputy Minister of Justice, and, after the 'opinion expressed by some of the leaders on both sides, I come to the conclusion that the Military Servioe Act, 1917, cannot be repealed, because it Shas exhausted itself, and is considered as non-existent at present in the statutes. Therefore I give it as my opinion that this bill should be dropped and that the discussion should not proceed and I so rule.
In spite of this fact, the friends of the hon. eader of the opposition continue at their neetings, to use this question for purposes of political capital by seeking to lead the people of our province astray. Tariff, protection and national policy are also discussed. What did they do with the tariff when they were in power? Did they alter it? Did they do anything to help trade and the labouring class? No. Yet these gentlemen charge us with ruining the manufacturers. Have the latter to complain of the changes made to the tariff 	.
by the present government? Far from complaining they are well satisfied.
Now, we are told that if business is at a standstill it is due to the British preference. In a brief article which appeared a short time ago in the newspaper La Patric it was stated that the manufacturers of boots and shoes of Maisonneuve, were not satisfied with the figures quoted by the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) in his address on the budget, in regard to imports of boots and shoes, and they hoped that I would make the necessary corrections. I wish to state that I have received no protests on the part of the manufacturers of boots and shoes of my electoral division-and you are aware, Sir, that they are numerous-I am further informed that many are not affected by the British preference. Yet, this preferential tariff exists since a number of years-since 1907, I think. We heard of no protests when the Conservatives were in power; it is only within the last few years, since the Liberal party is at the helm of affairs that a great stir is set up in regard to this preferential tariff. I have a few official figures in hand; they are far from gainsaying those of the hon. member for St. Denis. It was thought in certain quarters, that the figures quoted by the hon. member for St. Denis only applied to imports of leather footwear, while in reality they included imports of all kinds of boots and shoes: leather, canvas, rubber and footwear made up of leather and canvas.
However, what is most important to us, what concerns the most our manufacturers and our leather workers, is to know exactly the figures of imports in leather footwear, that get the benefit of this preferential tariff. I have before me the statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce which give the following figures for each fiscal year: 1914, imports $4,349,587-no mention is made of the years 1914 to 1918, they are exceptional years; 1918, imports $3,179,138; 1920, $2,731,591; 1921, $2,200,121; 1922, $1,338,775; 1923, $1,220,734; 1924, $1,546,216. Well, Sir, if figures speak, it is certain that the criticisms of our opponents are uncalled for when they state in our manufacturing centres, that the Liberal government's policy is on the eve of closing up all the factories. Far from closing their doors, our factories are working quite normally. I understand that quite a number of people are out of work; but if the boot and shoe manufacturers are unable to operate

The Budget-Mr. Coote
their factories to their full capacity it is clear the preference tariff in vigour since 1907 is not to be blamed for it, as we are importing to-day far less goods from England than in 1914 and in the following years; it is rather due to the overproduction in evidence under the extravagant administration of our adversaries. Moreover, these imports are bound to decline, on account of the pound sterling being now at par.
Allow me, however, to make a suggestion. I understand that if we favour the importation of British goods it is certainly not for the sake of the mother country, it is because we have mutual trade relations, and we grant certain advantages to England because we are getting something in return. Now, under the Act at present in force, imported goods must contain at least 25 per cent workmanship and! material of British origin, whilst Australia demands that at 'least 50 per cent of the workmanship and material be of British origin. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we would do well to raise our ratio to 50 per cent at least.
The necessity for economy is another point insisted on by our opponents in the cities. They falsely contend that economy is not practised by this government. It is all very well for them to urge economy! It is all very well for these gentlemen to say: Do as I tell you and not as we do or have done. After squandering millions and billions, they now advocate economy 1 What they have saved does not amount to much, unless it be daylight, through their daylight saving enactments.
Now, Sir, I shall take the liberty to point out an anomaly in the Income Tax Act: it is that the consorts under the community of property clause are less favoured than those whose regime is separation of property. The incomes of consorts living under the community of property clause are considered as forming a whole, while those of consorts married under the separation clause are figured separately. In the last instance, the husband and wife benefit by the statutory exemption while the consorts living under the community regime are entitled to a single exemption.
I am of opinion, Mr. Speaker^ that the present discrimination that is being made in connection with the income tax of Public Utility
Companies providing gas and electricity should be done away with. Private companies are made to pay the tax while public ownership companies, like the Hydro-Electric of Ontario go scot-free. This is a disadvantage for the labouring class and citizens at large of Montreal and other cities similarly situated, since private companies invariably recoup themselves at the expense of the consumer.
Of course, taxes of whatever nature they may be, are not popular, and a further grievance is the lien retained by the government on the property of tax-payers in arrears. I think the government would perform an act of justice if it would cancel this section of the act which may be detrimental to the real estate business.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the government would be well advised to establish a free section in the port of Montreal. That would be a great help to promote trade. If the plan proved profitable, a free section might be provided in the other harbours. I think these recommendations should be considered by the government, and I am satisfied that if carried out they would greatly further the progress of our country.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my chief reason for taking any part in this budget debate is a desire to place before the House and before the country the present condition of the farming industry in western Canada. I want to deal with the question as it affects western Canada particularly, because I do not pretend to be very familiar with conditions in eastern Canada. I make no apology for discussing this particular industry, because I think it is the most important in Canada. It employs more capital than any other industry in this country; it gives employment to more people; it provides the greater proportion of our exports. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), speaking a few days ago, referred to the amount of our export of agricultural produce. I think there was some mistake in the figures which he quoted. I have here a table taken from the trade report showing just what part agriculture plays in the matter of our total exports; I will not read this statement, but if I have the permission of the House I would like to place it on Hansard.
The Budget-Mr. Coote

The statement is as follows:

It will be seen from this statement that our total exports were $1,045,000,000 odd. Of that amount the export of wheat and flour was valued at $330,541,000. Wheat and wheat flour together constitute 31 per cent, Canadian field crops 40 per cent and Canadian farm products 48 per cent of our total exports. That shows that agriculture .plays a larger part in providing the exports from this country than any other industry.
Agriculture is very important also to our manufacturing industries in Canada. I have a statement here, copied from the Canada Year Book for 1922-23, giving the value of the products of forty of the leading industries in Canada, and the following will show the value of the products of the first four of these industries:
Value of Product
Slaughtering and meat packing	$ 240,000,000
Flour and grist mills	 239,000,000
Pulp and paper	 236,000,000
Lumber, lath and shingles	 207,000,000
These first two industries are entirely dependent upon our agricultural industry. I believe there is a general impression throughout Canada that a .big crop or a big yield .means prosperity to the farmer or to the man producing the commodity in question. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, I think, made a statement, two years ago, that one or two good crops would mend conditions in western Canada. Well, we have had two of the 'biggest crops western Canada ever had; 1922 and 1923 were two of the beet years we have ever seen in that part of the country, but the conditions there are not yet anything like ideal. I have before me an article from the Financial Post headed, 'A half size crop but more revenue in Saskatchewan". It goes on to show that the proceeds from this year's crop are practically

the same as those from the crop of 1923, although the yield is only half what it was in that year. I have another article from the same paper-and I like to quote articles from the Financial Post because it is generally highly regarded by many who are not engaged in the farming industry. This article is headed, "Farmers' profit based on prices more than yield". It goes on to show that in some of the years when the farmers have had the smallest crop they have had the largest financial returns. Let :me read just Ithe last two sentences of this article. It says:
Comparing the years 1920 and 1922. we find that in 1920 the total value of agricultural products was $550,641,471 while in 1922 it was $505,318,966, although in the latter year the wheat yield was 250,167,000 bushels, or very nearly two and one-half times as great as in 1920. Taking the years 1919 and 1921, the figures furnish the same undeniable proof that it is the price and not the volume of production which makes for prosperity in agriculture. In 1921 the farmers' total (income was $444,937,773, the smallest during the five years, but the wheat yield amounted to 201,347,483 bushels as against only 89,993,685 in 1919.
We have often heard in this House and we have often read in the press statements regarding the cost of producing wheat in Canada and in the United States as found by the United States Tariff Commission. This commission made a very extensive inquiry to determine the cost of producing wheat in both countries, and I think it would be interesting to this House to know something of what that commission did report.
I have here another article, again from the Financial Post. It is headed, "Costs ninety-one cents to grow bushel of western wheat, but there are objections to calculations of United States expert." It goes on to say:
It cost according to the Tariff Commission of the United States which spent a good many thousand

The Budget-Mr. Coote
dollars to find out, 91 cents a bushel to grow wheat in western Canada in the three years from 1921 to 1923 inclusive. That is the cost of wheat at the elevator.
Further on it says:
But next you have to make an adjustment on account of taxes. Taxes were left out of consideration by the Tariff Commission, but they can in no wise be left out of the calculations of the farmer. You can estimate those for the period reviewed by the commission at from five to ten cents a bushel to be added to the 91 cents.
Further on, alter drawing attention to some other discrepancies in this report, it says:
Let us call it one dollar a bushel, and to recall the statement that many farmers have repeatedly made in the past two years, that if they could be assured of a dollar a bushel net at the elevator for their wheat, before paying handling and transportation charges, they would be content.
I have here a statement prepared by the Bureau of Statistics, showing that the farmers of the three wesltern provinces produced in the years 1921, 1922 and 1923, 1,107,552,000 bushels of wheat, and that they received for that $826,-
376,000.	Now the total production as I have stated was 1,107,552,000 bushels, and taking the cost price alt $1 per bushel, as figured out by the Financial Post, it gives you a production cost of $1,107,552,000. If you deduct from that the $826,376,000 that the farmers received, you will find that the farmers of the three prairie provinces lost in those three years in the production of their wheat crop $281,176,000.
We have heard a good deal, Mr. Speaker, of the losses that some of our other industries have sustained, but I would like to know whether any one of them has sustained such a loss in its production as the farmers in western Canada on their wheat crop.
If you object to these figures in the Financial Post, and take rather those as set out by the Tariff Commission, of 91 cents a bushel, you find that the farmers of the three prairie provinces lost in the production of those three crops $181,496,320.
I have here a statement taken from an immigration pamphlet issued by this government. It is entitled " Canada, the New Homeland," and is issued by the department of the hon. the Minister of Immigration. It says in part:
Evidence was given in 1923 before the United States Tariff Commission to show that the Canadian farmer was able to produce a bushel of wheat for 46 cents less than the United States farmer. The per bushel cost in the United States in that year was $1.49; in Canada $1.03.
In 1923, according to the statement of the Bureau of Statistics, we produced 452,260,000 bushels of wheat. At $1.03 a bushel the cost
of production of our total crop that year wfis $465,827,800. The amount that the farmers received for this crop, as given by the Bureau of Statistics, was $294,686,000, showing a loss to the farmers on their wheat production for 1923 of $171,141,800. I would not like to say that this statement of the Immigration department was right, but on the other hand,
I do not think they have overstated the case. I do not think it can be fairly shown that wheat can be produced for less than the cost per bushel which they give here. This article which I have taken from the Financial Post goes on to say that the writer started out on his calculations with the spending power of the farmer in mind. He says:
We have calculated away the profit or devoted it to the payment of debts. Has the farmer's purchasing power vanished in the calculation? Not at all. It is the current turnover of this business of farming that is important.
In what other business, Mr. Speaker, is the turnover considered as important? In every industry discussed in this House, it seems to me, except agriculture, it is the profits that are the determining factor. If profits can be made and dividends paid, that is the supreme end to be attained, but according to these financial papers, with agriculture it is different. The important thing, it says here, is the turnover. It says:
A business with a total cash return of $350,000,000 is a pretty important thing to other business even if the whole receipts are eaten up in the living of the proprietors and their families, and the upkeep of their establishments. You do not calculate the importance of an industry to the country by the amount of dividends drawn out.
I hope when we come to discuss some of the other industries in this House that point will be borne in mind, but I have never seen that statement in the Financial Post or in any other financial journal in regard to any industry except agriculture, and it cannot be wondered at by financial men in this country that the farmers finally decided to send farmers down here to speak for them in this House, and demand of this House a little bit of fair play. It says further on:
The business is going on again next year.
That is the business of producing wheat, whether produced at a profit or a loss:
The business is going on again next year, again with a necessary turnover of from three hundred to three hundred and fifty million dollars. Some debts paid off this year will simply mean the re-establishment of credit for another year's operations. maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Could my hon. friend point out to those who desire to try and get some knowledge of this subject what his reasons are for this drop in price? I am merely asking for information not to combat my hon. friend's statement.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: There are quite a variety of causes. The chief one was I think, the deflation which hit us in the year 1921; then a poor crop which made feed very scarce. The western farmer in many instances as a consequence was compelled to sacrifice his cattle because he did not have feed for them. In other cases he was forced to sell-either by banks, loan companies or some other creditors -and there seemed to be nothing to uphold the market. Prices went down until one-half the cattle were sold for their value for canning purposes.

speechtext: Was there about the same kind of cattle in 1921 as in 1922?
