No, I think the class exported in 1922 were not quite as good as those exported in 1921, I should say that in all fair-
The Budget-Mr. Coote

ness. The reason for that was, as I say, that in 1922 cattle were 'being forced out of the farmer's hands on to the market for a variety of reasons. Many of these cattle of course, were young and not finished, and that partially accounts for the big decrease. The increase in duty under the Fordney tariff, or tihe emergency tariff that was in force I think at that time, was also very largely responsible. We had the home market to ourselves, as an hon. member sitting near me suggests, but the home market was not sufficient to absorb the production.
I have here a little item from the report of the telephone department of the government of Alberta for the year just ended and I think it will give some indication of the condition of the farmers in Alberta at the present time. In the year 1923 we had the biggest crop in our history, but it would be along in the year of 1924 before a great many of those fanmers would have received the value of that crop so that its purchasing power could be felt. In 1924 although we had a short crop the price was the biggest we had received since the closing of the war. Yet I find that in the year 1924 there was a drop of $4,508 in rural phone revenue; a total of 1,937 rural phones were removed during the year; and 1,318 phones were added showing a net loss of 619 rural phones. In exchange phones there was a net gain of 904 during the year, showing the difference in the condition between urban and rural districts. There is now a total of 54,000 phones in use of which 20,000 are rural. There are said to be 75,000 farms in Alberta, so that apparently less than one-third of those farms can afford to own a phone. Now, this certainly shows the reverse of prosperity after having had in 1923 the biggest crop that Alberta ever produced, a bigger one than we may naturally hope to produce for some years to come. Just what use is there in this country deluding itself with the idea, in the face of these actual conditions, that the farmers in the west are overburdened with prosperity? I am not expressing my opinions here; I am trying to give some actual facts to this House. I sometimes think this is useless because, as a rule, the budget speech of a back-bencher like myself is not listened to with very much attention. I am a little surprised that somebody has not already risen and suggested that we should try mixed farming. I have endeavoured to show this House that there is very little hope for the farmer in raising cattle. We have increased our production of butter in Alberta during the last year when I find the production was 21,500,000 pounds as compared with

17,800,000	pounds in 1923. I remember, about a year ago, being told that our trouble in the west was that we were all grain farmers and that we did not keep any milch cows or poultry or pigs on the farm. I was a little surprised the other day to find that Alberta now stands second, I think, of the provinces with reference to the number of poultry on farms, the average number in that province being 80 as compared with Canada's average of 63.9. I also notice that Alberta's egg exports grew 33 per cent during 1924. I have figures here, but I will not take time to read them to the House showing that the total grain crops last year were less than one-half the value of our agricultural production. Therefore, hon. members will see that the Alberta farmers are trying, not only grain raising, 'but any avenue of production that they feel is open to them at all. The question will naturally arise, how the farmers can go on producing wheat at a loss, as I have already shown in my statement tonight. The first reason is that they are working for less than a living wage. Not only that, but the wife is helping to earn the living. She is trying to keep things going by raising poultry and milking cows. If there are any children in the family, they are pressed into service and they are encouraged to raise hogs, ' calves, chickens, and to help to milk the cows. In fact, the whole family must work hard in order to keep the home going.	As I go
through Canada from one end to the other, it strikes me very often that in no other industry do we see the women helping to earn the living. I remember noticing a statement in a paper here recently in reference to some noted farmer in western Canada who had been to the Old Country, I think under the auspices of the Immigration department. This paper was telling how well this gentleman had done in the west, and I noticed one thing that it stated in reference to his wife was that she had at times cooked for twenty-four men. Any man who has a wife capable of cooking for twenty-four men, helping to earn the living, surely should make some progress. He should be able to make enough to get a trip to the Old Country once in a while.

But there are many women in western Canada who have cooked for a number of men for many years and who are not yet in a position to take a trip to the Old Country. If there is one thing more than another that makes me wish to stay in this farmer's fight for a fair deal, it is the con-

The Budget-Mr. Coote
dition of many farm women in western Canada. I have not been to Nova Scotia to see the shacks that the minere are living in there;
I believe some of them are very poor affairs; but I have seen people living in shacks in western Canada that, I think, are not any better. Some of these shacks are one-ply of boards covered with tar paper, and both the boards and the tar paper were protected by a very substantial tariff. That is just on the side. I do not want to dwell on this too long, so I must hurry on. One reason why the farmers are able to continue producing at a loss is that the farms are depreciating. Buildings and fences are not being kept in repair and the land is becoming weedy. They cannot afford to hire sufficient help to do all these things. Neither can they afford to buy the necessary paint to keep their buildings painted.
Then, the cost of raising wheat varies in different localities. This statement of the United States Tariff Commission to which I have referred shows that some of this wheat was produced at a cost of about sixty cents per bushel, but in other localities the cost ran as high as $1.40 per bushel. In those districts where they receive more than the average crop, they are able to go on producing under present conditions, but in those districts where they are receiving less than the average crop, the farmers are gradually going deeper into debt. Because so many of these farmers are going into debt and have got into debt in the past through no fault of their own, I want to urge upon the government that one of the first things they should do when this budget is finally disposed of, is to bring down some amendments to the Bankruptcy Act, such as were recommended by the Banking committee last year. The government refused to bring in legislation to give effect to those amendments. I do not know all the reasons that may have deterred the government from bringing in this legislation; but it will cost this government absolutely nothing to bring them in and if they refuse to do so, we are going to lose another few thousand bankrupt farmers who will go to the United States to get rid of their debts. If they were given an opportunity of going through bankruptcy, I think they would remain here, and in time they might again become successful farmers. They are far better citizens for us to have in this country than many of the immigrants brought in from Europe to take their place.
I want to urge the government to revise the Canada Grain Act at this session. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low)
I understand-I did not happen to be in the House at the time-stated that he did not intend to proceed with the act this year. I want to urge the government to proceed with that act. I think the present act caused a loss of millions of dollars to the farmers in western Canada last year, and that loss could have been avoided, I believe, under a proper Canada Grain Act. As the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Stewart) pointed out the other day, we have large wheat pools operating in western Canada, and the Grain Act, needs some revision to allow these wheat pools to operate fairly with the old grain companies that are doing business there. I do not think this House should prorogue until the Canada Grain Act has been revised, regardless of what else we do.
I wish to urge upon the government some action in reference to establishing a system of rural credits. I am not going to -argue the subject because I think it is pretty well understood in this House. But I want to impress upon the government -and the House that western farmers cannot continue to carry on under circumstances such -as I have pointed out here and pay from 8 to 10 per cent on long term loans and from 8 to 13 per cent on short term loans. But the most pressing thing is the long term loan. Many of our farmers now are just on the very edge of going into bankruptcy or keeping out of it. Some men will say that the farmers have had too much credit, and I will agree that many of them have had too much credit. It has been the ruination of them. But it costs a farmer no more to carry a loan of $8,000 at 5 per cent than to carry a loan of $5,000 at 8 per cent. That is just where the difference comes in. The farmer possibly can make use of two or three thousand dollars if he could obtain it at 5 per cent, but if he has to pay 9 per cent he had better do without it. Many of these farmers are in a position where they now owe the money they obtained by a short term loan at 9 per cent. I mean a four or five year loan. But a man in that situation has very little purchasing power. Every cent he can make must go on the mortgage. I do not think we can do anything in Canada which would stimulate business more than establishing and putting into operation a proper system of rural credit. It would mean a reduction of 2 per cent in the interest rate, and that would be equivalent to three or four cents a bushel added to the price of the wheat. It is pretty difficult for us to devise means of increasing the price of wheat three or four cents a bushel. Two per cent reduction of interest would ba
The Budget-Mr. Cootc

equivalent to that increase. Just here I want to refer to a matter which possibly may seem very small to the Acting Minister of Finance, but I desire once more to urge it upon him; that is that he should abolish the war stamo tax on notes. I have here a statement made to me by a banker in Alberta showing one loan current since 1919, as follows:
Loan account current since 1919, various amounts which have not been paid and which now aggregate in the neighbourhood of $10,000-total revenue tax $42.89. This loan is in addition to temporary borrowings for current expenditures, et cetera and as the party is unable to pay any part of the loan the revenue tax was added into each renewal thus increasing his loan more rapidly.
I have a statement of another loan current since 1919, various amounts aggregating at the present time in the neighbourhood of $20,000, where the revenue tax amounted to $101.38. I wish to ask the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) if he thinks it is a proper method of taxation to tax a man who is hopelessly in debt. We heard a great deal from the hon. member for North Waterloo about the nuisance taxes, and I heartily agree with most of what he said. I believe that we may have to put up with the nuisance tax for a while but surely the tax on notes could be abolished, or reduced to two cents, the same as the tax on receipts. The man who has received payment can afford to pay a two cent tax, but in the case of the man who owes the debt and is forced by his creditors to put a stamp on his note of four cents a hundred dollars it seems to me nothing less than robbery.
Then I urge the Acting Minister of Finance to place the farmer's income tax on a three year basis. There are many cases where a man has produced three or four crops at a loss, and sometimes he does not get a crop at all. Then a good year comes and he makes sufficient profit to render him liable to assessment for income tax. In some cases a creditor would have a lien on all his crop and the man would have absolutely nothing to pay his income tax, although he was liable for it.

I seem to have mislaid a statement I wanted to give the House in Tegard to the textile industry, because the member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson) bewailed the condition of that industry and I wanted to make some reference to it. However, I should like to draw7 the attention of the House to the fact that the common stock of the Dominion Textile Company when this merger was formed was $5,000,000, but the money invested in that stock was only $500,000. That is, it was sold	at $10 a share.	The	earnings on thisstock	have certainly	been	very	handsome.A few years ago the stock had risen to $213	per share. As	that	made	the stockhard	to trade in on	the market	there was
a split, up of three shares for one, and now the common stock of that company stands at $15,000,000. They have paid dividends on

The Budget-Mr. Coote

this common stock for many years. I think I gave some statistics about this company two years ago, so it is not necessary for me to go into it further now; an investment of $500,000 some years ago has now become $15,000,000. We have here, I think, a good example of how capital is created.

speechtext:
I believe it was Mr. Daniels. I would like to point out now how capital is created. I have here a statement of the Sun Life Insurance Company, issued a year ago, and in a printed list of their investments I find that they hold common stock of the Dominion Textile Company for $1,007,656,23. The money which the people of Canada have paid to this insurance company to provide for their widows and orphans would surely be considered actual capital, and we now find this money invested in this common stock. So I think it can fairly be claimed that this $15,000,000 is now actual capital. The men who originally purchased this stock I presume will still control at least 51 per cent of it. They have received handsome dividends, because some years ago I saw a statement made
IMr. Coote.]
that this common stock had returned in dividends ten times the amount originally paid for it. They have sold a large part of this common stock to the public, and they now have several millions of real money invested in the common stock of this corporation. I am sure they feel perfectly secure, knowing that the public will now protect them because as I have shown the public are vitally interested.
I could show, too, that this insurance company, one of the largest of its kind in Canada, has $350,000 of the common stock of the Canadian General Electric Company, and $1,965,000 of the General Electric Company, as well as common stock in several other companies.
I do not wish to deal with the tariff any . further, Mr. Speaker, except to refer very briefly to the question of protecting the farmer through the tariff. I't is rather strange that a tariff on wheat does not increase the price of wheat, whereas a tariff of 35 per cent on automobiles affects the price of automobiles to the extent of 40 per cent. The tariff will increase the price of goods if those who are producing the goods are few enough to get together in a combine or gentleman's agreement and fix the price. A tariff on boots and shoes will not hurt us very much in this country if the boot and shoe men do not take advantage of the tariff to force up their prices, nor will the tariff on any other article increase the price very much under those conditions. The producers of wheat are too numerous to get together and force up the price of wheat, even if you did put a tariff on it. I admit that some farm produce can possibly be advanced in price through the tariff. That the price of apples can be advanced through the tariff has been demonstrated to be a fact; that is the way it has worked out. But it will not work that way with wheat and cattle because the men producing them are too numerous to get together.
I have here a little article from Commerce and Finance, a financial paper issued in New York entitled, "Congress, Coolidge and the Farmer." It deals at some length with the situation of the agriculturists in the United States. It mentions the desire of the government and of the public men in the United States to improve the financial position of the farmer in that country. It devotes considerable space to the McNary-Haugen bill, which would create a government body to handle wheat and charge the American consumer about 42 cents a bushel more for wheat than was charged to the buyer in foreign countries. It goes on to say that this bill was killed in

The Budget-Mr. Coote
congress for certain reasons. It then says that the bill will be up again, and if that bill is not put into effect some other marketing agency will likely be created in an endeavour to assist the farmer in marketing his products and in charging the American consumer more than the foreign purchaser of wheat. It also states that in the United States they are endeavouring to persuade the farmer to limit his production, but the writer of this article says:
Whether the remedy be production or marketing the starting point is production. If this first step is omitted, the experts and the congressmen may mill
around in circles, but will never arrive at any goal.
I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Immigration to that fact. If he goes on endeavouring to fill up the vacant lands in this country with farmers, what are we going to do with that production? This article is by James E. Boyle, Professor of Rural Economy, Cornell University, who has made a particular study of this subject. This is what he says about the tariff:
I am no defender of the protective tariff. I agree with the official findings of the American Farm Bureau Federation that our present tariff is costing the American farmers three hundred millions of dollars a year.
I do not think I can leave the question of the tariff with any better quotation than that. That is the last remedy I am going to suggest to the Acting Minister of Finance for the position the farmer in the west finds himself in to-day. He might reduce the tariff -on a few necessities which the farmer has to purchase.
I have here a little pamphlet published by the Edmonton Journal, which, as you all know, is generally regarded as a Conservative organ. They are advocating a " Canada Forward " policy. They evidently have discarded the old National Policy. They say:
A Canada Forward policy should recognize frankly that agriculture is and must be for some time Canada's basic industry, and that there can be no general or permanent prosperity in this country except under conditions that make for a prosperous agriculture.

speechtext:
They go on to say that if there are certain industries in Canada which cannot stand on their own feet, they have 160i
got to be eliminated, or something to that effect. He says here in part:
If Canada is to compete with other nations our agricultural methods and our industrial processes must reflect the latest achievements of agricultural and industrial science. Much of our agricultural products is sold in the world market where tariffs cannot avail, and Canada cannot afford the luxury of tariff protection for industries that are not one hundred per cent efficient in their industrial processes.
And I think on another page he does advocate a gradual tariff reduction.
Now I want to refer to certain remarks made by ithe hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) in his speech two days ago. He said in part^-page 2432 of Hansard:
My submission is that it is entirely because of the Progressive party, and very largely their views from a purely economic view are sound. They say: We produce wheat in our country; wTe sell in the markets of the world and we buy in a protected market; therefore if we can eliminate the protective duties we may get our goods cheaper and have a bigger margin of profit or be able to sell more wheat in the markets of the world. That is a hard argument to answer from the economic point of view.
Later on he says:
The value of w'heat and wheat flour exported was $327,000,000, or 22 per cent of the total agricultural production. So that this 22 per cent, representing the views of the prairie provinces through the Progressive party in this parliament, are dominating the government and the fiscal policy of this country. There is our trouble.
I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver South -the statement of the Premier of Ontario, made I think about a year and a half ago, and as near as I can repeat it it was that Ontario had always dominated the politics of the Dominion. I thought at the time that the Premier of Ontario had made a very correct statement, and I should like to suggest to the hon. member for Vancouver South that he might confer with the Premier of Ontario and see whether he is not, after all, mistaken. I feel that Ontario, and possibly we might add Quebec, has dominated the policies of this country and I think, possibly, will continue to do so. It is only natural for them to expect that they will, because they are the populous parts of Canada and return a majority of the members of this House. But I should like to refer you again to some of the words used by the hon. member in question. He says the Progressive argument is a hard argument to answer and he admits that it is hard to answer our argument from the economic point of view. But he goes on to point out that we are in the minority and asks why should our views prevail-why should they influence this government? If our views were influencing this government I
The Budget-Mr. Coote

for one would support tie present budget; but I do not think this is the ease, and I am going to vote against the budget not simply because our views are not influencing the cabinet, but .bycause I think the policy laid down in the budget is not one that I can support; it is not in line with the platform on which I was elected and I intend to stand by my principles. But when the hon. member was elaborating this point that although we might be economically sound and we had a hard argument to answer we represented only 22 per cent of the people so why should we influence the government-I looked on the mace-the glittering mace we have on the table-and I thought the hon. member was simply advocating the policy that had been in force in this country for many years; the policy of using the big stick on the minority although they might be economically sound in the views which they were advocating. What I would advocate, Mr. Speaker, is that this mace should be removed from the table; we should not have big stick government in this country. In place of the mace I would place on the table the figure that I think all members have seen where the goddess stands with the scales weighing out justice to all. That is what we must have in this country instead of having a big stick waved at the minority. "You may be economically sound," we are told, "but then you are advocating something that the majority do not want, so we will just take the big stick to you and you can climb down."
We hear a great deal about national unity; we have heard more from this government than we ever heard on the subject before. Why have we heard it? We would hear very little about national unity if all sections of Canada were getting justice. You are not going to get national unity until something more nearly approximating justice is granted than is the case to-day. There are two schools of thought in this country, Mr. Speaker, at least on this particular subject. One is that the west-I should not say the west-but those who are advocating lower tariffs cannot get their wishes carried out; that we are going to have protection, and that if we put the Conservatives into power we will get higher protection than we have now. Therefore we must continue the present government in office at all costs because they will not raise the tariff. Well, I cannot subscribe to that doctrine; I believe in justice to all. If our views are economically sound and our argument hard to answer but nevertheless we are denied what we are asking for, then it is up to those who are opposing us to show in

what way our demands may be fairly met. Are the people of the west to remain in this position forever, advocating something that is economically sound but being denied it because they are in the minority? Surely confederation cannot be held together on such a policy as that. I have listened in this House to a great many speakers on the budget, and on other subjects, and I have yet to hear a suggestion from any hon. member as to what way or in what manner any quid pro quo for this protective tariff is to be given to us. On the other hand I have heard admissions from many members that the protective tariff is of no benefit to us, that in fact it is a hinder-ance. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) this afternoon in a very well reasoned speech advocated the wiping out of the British preference on the ground, as nearly as I can recollect it, that he did not believe in sentiment influencing our economic policies in this country. Well, is it taken for granted that sentiment will persuade the west indefinitely to continue under a policy which is economically unsound for it?
That is the point I want to impress upon this House; there is no use our trying to gloss it over. This feeling of injustice has been bearing particularly hard upon the west while we have had adverse conditions and poor prices to contend with. So long as the people are prosperous they will put up with a wrong economic policy, but when it begins to bear hardly upon them they must seek a remedy. There is no use disguising the fact that there is an agitation in certain parts of western Canada to get rid of this domination of the east in some manner, and I think it is the duty of this House-I do not think it is too strong a term to use-it is the plain and bounden duty of this House, to see to it that that feeling of injustice is no longer * allowed to grow. There is a demand, as I say, for some action which will relieve us from this position. If some action is not taken, if we are allowed to go on as we are going to-day, I believe that feeling will grow in spite of all the talk upon national unity that can be handed out to those people.
Before I sit down, I should like to say in regard to this point which I have been bringing to the attention of the House, that as long ago as 1910 this feeling was very strong in certain parts of western Canada, and the late Mr. Bramley-Moore issued a little book entitled "Canada and her Colonies or Home Rule for Alberta". I do not think the late Mr. Bram-ley-Moore's loyialty could be questioned at all, as he was an Englishman who, when war broke out, although he was a member of the

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
Alberta legislature, enlisted, I think, as a private, went overseas and was killed in the Great war. But Mr. Bramley-Moore, in his book, endeavours to point out-and I think he makes a very good case-that as regards the western provinces, they were being treated by, I would say, older Canada in regard to this tariff in the same manner as Britain, Spain and Portugual treated their colonies years ago. He makes this statement:
Hitherto no colony of the Anglo-Saxon race has rested content in being made subordinate and subservient to the interests of the Mother Country. It remains to be seen whether western Canadians have lost the s>pirit of their fathers. In these days when state interference with individual liberty of action is becoming more and more pronounced, we may be tending to acquire the mental characteristics of the orientals who bend their patient backs beneath a government's tyranny with a proper self-effacement and equanimity.
I do not want to keep the House any longer; but surely the time has came when the people of western Canada particularly should be told whether this is the tariff that they have to put up with or not. If this is the minimum tariff that the Liberal party, who are the traditional low 'tariff party in this country, are prepared to endeavour to put into force, that should be made dear to the west. As I have said already, if there is any quid pro quo to be offered to western Canada, I think that should be done at this session of parliament.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few observations on the present budget, it is my intention to follow the example set iby members in this part of the House and to be very brief. I said some two years ago that any remarks that I would make in this House would not be much longer than twenty minutes and I intend to close within that time to-night.
First, I desire to express my regret at the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) through illness. I am sure we all miss his presence in the House and we all hope for his speedy recovery. I also wish to thank the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) and the Minister without Portfolio, the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin) for the visit they paid to the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this House. I am sure the electors of Provencher appreciated their visit. I think members of the government and every member of parliament should acquaint themselves with the different problems throughout the various parts of this country. There is only one way in which they can do so and it is by paying visits to the different parts of Canada. One of our chief difficulties in solving our national problems is that the knowledge of a great percentage of the members centres around their particular constituency and province, and until the members know the whole country, it is impossible for them to give justice to the various national problems that we have to solve.
On September 1, 1921, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) made a speech in London, Ontario, before 3,000 electors, announcing a general election. He stated the main issues, and I would like to read a few extracts from his speech as published in the Montreal Gazette of September 2, 1921. Tihe right hon. gentleman said:
But there is an issue. Here are 3,000 people! You have watched the shaping of events and the movements of political forces for the past few years. Is there one of this whole 3,000 who does not know as he sits in his seat to-night that there is something that Canada must decide and decisively decide before we square away for the journey ahead? I do not think there are two opinions in this hall as to what we have to decide. It is the tariff of Canada.
Then he goes on:
But there is a challenge from the official opposition under Mr. Mackenzie King. They adopted two years ago in solemn convention a resolution that bound them to place on the free 'list nineteen classes of articles including foodstuffs, farm implements and machinery and lumber of every kind, and to increase the British preference 50 per cent and to substantially reduce the tariff on boots and shoes and articles of consumption.
The point I want to make in reading the remarks of the then Prime Minister is that the tariff was a well-defined issue at the last general election. The Liberal party covered this whole country, going from coast to coast, preaching low tariff. The Progressives did the same. They all preached low tariff, and the Conservatives went from ocean to ocean and preached protection. On the 6th day of December, 1921, the electors gave their verdict, and the verdict given by the electors should be taken notice of and respected. The electors on the 6th December, 1921, elected with large majorities 186 members who preached low tariff throughout this whole country, and they returned only 49 protectionist Conservatives. What was the meaning of that verdict given by the electors? There is no denying that it was a mandate to the government who took office substantially to reduce tariffs on the implements of production and the necessaries of life. This government has been in power now for four years and this is its fourth budget. I do not want to be too. critical, but in my opinion we have had three stand-pat budgets and one with slight reductions on the implements of production. Is the government prepared to

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
go back to the electors and say to them: We have taken no notice of the mandate that you gave us in 1921, but return us to power and we shall see what we can do? I say you cannot fool the electorate all the time.
What has been the result of the government's failure to keep its promises? It has been to produce the present conditions of business depression and industrial stagnation. The government cannot take any credit for the improvement in agricultural prices. They have no control, for example, over the price of wheat. Nothing they can do would cause it to rise or fall. The farmers' returns are determined, broadly speaking, by world conditions which no government can affect; but with general business and industrial activities the condition is different. The government may help or hinder these interests. If the government had last year devoted its surplus revenues of some $24,000,000 to reducing the general tariff, business and industry would be to-day in a more flourishing state. The taxes remitted would have added to the purchasing power of the people, and in addition to the gain to the consumers of the country by the reduction of the tariff taxes paid to the exchequer, something like $3 for every $1 of revenue collected would also have been saved to the farmers and the consumers generally, by the reduction of the concealed bonuses paid to the manufacturing industries of the country under the protective system. Thus, instead of $24,000,000 of additional purchasing power something approaching $80,000,000 or $100,000,000 would have been available.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me a question? I wish to ask him how he can explain that, on the one hand, the Conservatives tell us that the stagnation in business is due to the lowering of the tariff, and that, on the other hand, a good Progressive like my hon. friend, asserts that the depression is due to the high tariff maintained by us?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is, himself, well aware that the reason *why business is at a standstill, and factories Slot producing as much as they should, is that she people have not the necessary purchasing power, and as I have just stated, for each dollar of revenue turned over to the Treasury, the people have to put up three dollars.
This huge sum spent by the people at large upon the implements of production and the necessaries and comforts of life would have brought about a stimulation of industrial and business conditions. We should to-day see far

less unemployment and far greater prosperity if the government had the foresight and the courage to live up to its promises to the electors to reduce the tariff.
This year no reduction of taxation is proposed. Thanks to trade depression the revenues have fallen off. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has, it is true, a surplus on paper of $1,820,000, but the figures on which this surplus is based are, after all, only estimates.	'Comparison of the minister's
estimates of expenditures at the beginning of the fiscal year and his estimate made a month before	the end of the year
show a difference of $9,386,300.07. It i3 somewhat remarkable that the minister who would be entitled to Plaim credit for so considerable a saving on the year's administration did not do so. It would be interesting to know just how and where these apparent savings accrued, but we are not afforded the information.
Everybody admits the need for economy. The need is the greater since revenues have fallen so alarmingly, and there is yet no evidence of their recovery. Reduction of taxation is a prime necessity and it is evident that it can result only from savings in public expenditures. The ministers cannot reasonably contend that reductions cannot foe made in the expenditures for which they are responsible. The record of the United States in this respect is one that they might profitably emulate. Writing in MacUean's Magazine of April 1, 1925, Mr. J. Herbert Hodgins makes the following comment:
Federal estimates in the United States provide for the spending of $3,062,277,407 for 1925. President Coolidge wants the amount to an even $3,000,000,000.
Then a statement by General Lord, who is the director of the Bureau of the Budget, as follows:
General Lord has counselled all federal spenders: " Go over your estimates with a microscope in one hand and a 'pruning knife in the other. If there is doubt whether a cut should be made-cut, resolve every doubt in favour of the taxpayers."
Further on in this article Mr. Hodgins says:
President Coolidge, with the active help of the director of the Bureau of the Budget, has given the United States lower taxes, "a material reduction of about $2,000,000,000 yearly" as he, himself, stated in Washington on January 26, 1925. Which, after all, touches the average citizen in his most sensitive spot, his purse, and convinces him of the worth-whileness of the national effort.
In a previous article I quoted figures that were presented by President Coolidge to show, how in four years, 1921-1924, there was the remarkable cut in the United States public debt of $3,198,000,000. This reduces the annual interest from $999,000,000 to $865.000,000-

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
a saving of $134,000,000, or a sum within one million dollars of Canada's annual interest bill.
President Coolidge has saved the United States more than $5,343,000,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if they can do that in the United States, if they can reduce the expenditures of Great Britain, there is not the slightest reason why we cannot reduce our expenditures in Canada. I might oiler a few suggestions as to how we could reduce our expenditures. I do not think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) would agree with me in this respect, but I think we could make a reduction in the expenditures for experimental farms. We have too many experimental farms in this country. I know that these farms have been a benefit to Canada; I am not denying that, but they do not reach the farmer to-day, or else the farmer does not reach them. I think the government could reduce the expenditure on experimental farms by a large amount, and devote a certain percentage of that saving to research work.

speechtext: That would not reduce the expenditure.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No. I said that we
could spend a certain percentage of that reduction in research work, which would be of greater advantage to the Canadian people a3 a whole. We might reduce our public printing. I go down to the post office in the morning, in the afternoon, and in the evening and it is always full. It contains many government publications some of which are beneficial. With reference to the others, most of the members throw them in the wastepaper basket. We might reduce our expenditures on national defence. I see the minister is in his seat just now.

If it is of public
importance I would.

It is not a
question of "if"; is the hon. member in favour of it?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If the Canadian .people are ever to reduce their national indebtedness, with its accompanying annual payments of interest, some thrift must be exercised and the old-fashioned policy of cutting our coat according
to our cloth must be made effective. To the people of western Canada, Mr. Speaker, this budget is disappointing. Not only because it does not reduce taxation, but because it does nothing to fulfil the promise held out to them of relief from the unduly high cost of the instruments of production and of the necessaries of life. Agriculture must be made a profitable industry if this country is to be fully and properly developed. It can be made so only by the removal of the handicaps it suffers from excessive taxation and from the protective policy.
This, Mr. Speaker, brings me to another point,-the lack of facilities for obtaining adequate loans on favourable terms, which is a serious disadvantage to our agriculturists. In his latest report, Dr. H. M. Tory says:	.
The question of agricultural credit is not one coming by accident out of the peculiar conditions of to-day, and therefore requiring only a temporary solution, but it arises out of conditions that are permanent and require to be dealt with on a permanent basis.
This statement, I am sure, will be endorsed by everyone who has given any attention at all to western conditions. The financial difficulties of the western farmers fall into two classes-those which are of a very pressing but quite temporary character, and those which will remain after all the immediate difficulties have been overcome, and which require the permanent remedy indicated in Dr. Tory's statement. Many of our western people could derive no benefit at the present time from a permanent scheme of rural credits because they are too heavily in debt; they have no credit left. Under the influence of circumstances, largely outside their own control, they have become deeply involved financially, and some way must be found to relieve their immediate financial necessities and to put them in a fair way to prosperity as well as to make their industry profitable. Then, and then only, will they be in a position to make proper use of rural credit facilities.
One of the chief instruments in assisting the heavily indebted farmers to place themselves in a more advantageous position for the pursuit of their industry is to be found in the Bankruptcy Act. At the close of last session certain amendments to that act were recommended to this House by the standing committee on Banking and Commerce. These amendments were drafted with the object of making the administration of the act more equitable and more effective so far as farmers are concerned. The government was pressed at that time to pass legislation along the lines recommended, but was unable to do so owing

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
to the advanced stage of the session. But no effort seems to have been made in the present session to give effect to the committee's recommendations. We on this side of the House would urge upon the government the necessity for immediate action in this matter. If the process of debt adjustment and of relieving bankrupts from their impossible situation could go ahead with greater freedom, there would be some prospects that hundreds of farmers would be retained upon their farms who otherwise will be driven off their land and probably out of the country, while thousands of others will be enabled to adjust themselves to existing conditions and to take advantage of any permanent facilities for rural credits which it may be found possible to establish. To this end the passage of the proposed amendments to the Bankruptcy Act are indispensable. Some such legislation must precede the application of any permanent plan for providing farm loans, and I would again urge upon the government the need for action at this session of parliament.
There is another point, Mr. Speaker, on which I feel it is my duty to say a few words. I refer to the proposed embargo on pulpwood. I will not go into the details of that question, as many hon. members know more about it than I do and they can treat the subject more adequately. It has been shown, and conclusively shown, I believe, to every member of this House who has given the matter a careful and unbiased study, that only the very small group of manufacturers who are urging an embargo on pulpwood would benefit by it. Its enforcement would spell injustice and hardships to hundreds who would be deprived of a good, and perhaps a near market for their products. In my own constituency of Provencher many settlers depend entirely upon the sale of pulpwood for their living until their farm products give them a sufficient revenue to live on. As they are located near the main Canadian National railway line, or one of its branches, the nearest point where they can sell their pulpwood to good advantage is International Falls, and the proposed embargo would close down the market to them What would happen then? There is no doubt most of them would have to leave the land to go either to the United States or to increase the number of unemployed in our cities. On behailf of those bona fide settlers I appeal to the government not to chase out of their farms those hard workers who constitute one of the best assets of our country, and who should not be made innocent victims of a few selfish and voracious manufacturers. It has been proven that of the yearly destruction of 
our forests 90 per cent is due to fire, winds and inseicts. Of the remaining 10 per cent statistics show that the proportion used in various industries is as follows:	In Canada,
84 per cent; outside of Canada, 16 per cent. Then. 16 per cent of 10 per cent of all the timber cut or destroyed each year in Canada, or in other words, one-half of one per cent only of such timber is exported. Why is it that to 'save such a smali proportion of our timber the proponents of the embargo wiould not hesitate to injure the settlers, the farmers and the woodland owners? It is that they would reap big profits in forcing the sale of that percentage of timber to their own mills at their own prices. Will the government listen to them, or will they listen to the farmers who claim that our first duty is to protect our forests against fire, insects and other controllable causes of destruction? I hope, Mr. Speaker, the government will not hesitate to give fair treatment to our settlers.
I repeat, M,r. Speaker, -the budget is disappointing to the western people, who look upon it as an anti-national and unfairly balanced policy. If there be an election this year, as has been foreshadowed by some newspapers whidh claim to be well informed, I consider it will be my duty t.o tell the electors of my constituency that the present government has utterly failed to keep the pledges of the Liberal platform of 1919 which seems to have been drafted not in a spirit of sincerity, but as a vote-oatcher.
Before taking my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize the fact that notwithstanding the villainous attacks of petty politicians whose aims seem only to be to find fault with others and to sow discord and strife between the different classes of Canada, the Progressive group has constantly worked for the welfare of the whole country and of every individual of all classes. Our main object has been to try to .place all Canadian citizens as nearly as possible on the same level, not by reducing the higher classes but by improving the lot of those who heretofore had to bear the heaviest burdens and by trying to secure for them a fair share of the prosperity and of the happiness which our country 'has in store for its inhabitants. In trying to reach our aim, we raised ourselves above all questions of race and creed, and we worked to promote harmony and unity in basing our actions on the principle of equal rights to all. In the course of his remarks the other day, the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault) recognized the fact and speaking of the "restoration of harmony and unity between the different races, religions and sections of

The Budget-Mr. Evans
this country" he said that "the great task was accomplished with the co-operation of the Progressive party." I would be glad, Mr. Speaker, were I able to return the compliment to the hon. member for Chamlbly and Vercheres, and to declare that his party has stood by the principles embodied in their platform. On May 15, 1923, in a very eloquent speech delivered on behalf of this group, the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) laid down our policy. He said:
I want to say, moreover, that the Progressives are out for the unity of Canada, and I make bold to say that we have the only basis upon which there can be such unity, that is, the basis of justice as between classes in Canada and as between sections in the community. That is the only real basis upon which there can be any unity. We have no traditional spites and no petty feelings of strife behind us. Our sole stock in trade is what we carry with us, just a straightforward economic policy, that is all. It does not matter what you are religiously, socially or provincially, you are equally welcome into this fellowship, because we do not specialize in any of those things that divide one Canadian from another. The basis on which we work is the basis on which all the people can co-operate.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will say without fear of being contradicted that we have always lived up to those principles, and I feel sure that for the good of Canada the Progressive group will always stand by them.

They have reaped an undue profit on what they have sold or they charged their losses to the home consumer; that is on their export trade.
Despite all that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) said in his speech this year-and he did last year give this House and the country the impression that the government had made it their policy to do away with the tariff as far as protection was concerned-they now seek to tighten up on us by increasing protection, and announced boldly in the budget that goods imported are not to be valued for customs purposes at the price at which they are sold to the trade in the country of origin, but instead they are to be valued according to the discretion of the minister, and at the instigation of the manufacturing or distributing concerns affected. However, since then the government has announced that this change has been withdrawn. As far as we are concerned or as far as the country is concerned, the Acting Minister of Finance, need not have withdrawn the alteration as announced in the budget. The budget statement only crystallized what ha3 been the practice of the Department of Customs for a long time past. It all goes to show that the government have no intention of lowering this wall of protection or of decreasing the cost of living; in fact it seems that they seek by every means possible to increase the price by the dark and devious ways of withdrawing the administration of the tariff act from under statutory regulations, and putting the whole thing at the discretion of the minister. I cannot help viewing this as being all designed to better hide from the public the reason that the cost of living is kept up to its present height.
A tariff board is to be appointed and the government is now seeking to place the responsibility for class privilege on a board to be appointed and composed partly of officers of the Customs and Excise service. I look on this, Sir, as an abandonment of Liberalism and the government's own platform. It is a capitulation as complete as the betrayal of 1897 to the demands of the class that has sought and obtained vast privileges for the last forty years. It is an acknowledgment that the trade prevention tax, or tariff imposition, is the natural right of the urban industrialists of this Dominion. The government is abandoning its own principles, it is putting the responsibility for unjust taxation on a body to be further

removed from the people. Some may say that it will depend very largely upon the personnel of this board as to what the results will be-I deny, Sir, the right of any government to appoint a body of men, however learned or expert in taxation matters, to determine the extent to which one class of the people shall be placed in bondage to another.
This is all to be done for the sake of the industrial area situated between Montreal and Windsor. The appointment of a tariff board is an attempt to permanently establish the tariff imposition on the agriculturists of this Dominion, and to further concentrate the wealth of the country in this industrial area. In view of all this, I ask what prospect is there for western provinces, what prospect is there for the Maritime provinces, when by the force of numbers Quebec and Ontario intend to dominate this Dominion? What else is to be expected but a dissolution of confederation if things go on tins way? By the appointment of a tariff board the government may hope to shirk responsibility in this matter-I say, Sir, that parliament is the only body to deal with this question. To appoint a board is a foregone conclusion that there is a class in this country which has a right to lay under tribute the agriculturist and the worker, and that these have no partnership in this commonwealth. The appointment of a tariff board is a natural step to take by a government which believes in special or class privilege. The Liberal party, I believe, when in power has led in ' this feature since the 1897 revision of the tariff. If the government by its action during the last four years had given the country some assurance that it meant to carry out its own principles as laid down in its platform, a tariff board might have been appointed to best carry out that policy, and the country would have accepted it; but under present conditions this is not possible. The dominant idea seems to be to separate as widely as possible the government and the people. By a tariff board it may be hoped to still widen the gulf, but unless the political perceptions of the people can be lulled into a comatose state of stupidity, the government cannot hope to escape the responsibility. This, along with the immigration scheme to replace the intelligent farmer and worker by an ignorant drudge, seems to be the present policy of the government. Our government has again confirmed itself as the head of the great communism of pelf.

The Budget-Mr. Evans
To show some of the methods, Sir, used by the tariff authorities for greater protection than it would seem the law calls for, I would detain the House just a little longer. I wish to show how completely the Customs Tariff is set aside. The public has believed all along that they knew what duty they had to pay by the classifying of merchandise and the rate imposed, as laid down by the Customs Tariff of 1907, brought up to date by various orders in council. But the fact is they do not know. The Customs Act here comes in, which lays down the method of arriving at the value for duty, and also the method to be used by customs appraisers in arriving at the status of the importer, something which no government has a right to take into account. It would be safe to say that for every dollar collected from large importers, two dollars or more are . collected from the consumer on the very same articles imported in the same quantities. To illustrate this point, I will take as an example any common household utensil, particularly kitchen hardware, which seems to lend itself best to this sort of manipulation. I will set out the status, the discount allowed, the rate of duty, the value for duty, the amount of duty, and the sales tax on these articles as paid by the varying classes of importers. The list price to all is $100. To the small dealer there is a 50 per cent discount plus 15 and 5 per cent; the rate of duty 30 per cent; the value for duty then becomes $40.38, the duty $12.11, the sales tax $3.14: the total cost to this importer would be $55.63. To the large dealer there is a discount of 50 per cent plus 15 and 10; the value for duty would be $38.25; the duty itself $11.47; the sales tax $2.98, or a total cost of $52.70. To the departmental store the total price would be, $49.71. To the jobber there is a 50 per cent discount, plus 15 and 20; the value for duty in that case would be $34.01; the duty $10.20; sales tax, $2.65, or a total of $46.86. Now, to the consumer, for customs purposes no trade discount is allowed; it does not matter What quantity or what the class of goods may be; so the value for duty is $100; the duty itself is $30; the sales tax $7.80, or a total of $137.80. You see, the consumer has to pay $137.80 for what the others get at from $46 to $55. These widely divergent values for duty of the same article purchased in varying quantities by dealers and consumers are governed by sections 40 and 41 of the Customs Act, which read as follows:
Section 40. Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof when sold for home consumption in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time the same were exported directly to Canada.
Section 41 reads:
Such market value shall be the fair market value of such goods in the usual and ordinary commercial acceptation of the term and as sold in the ordinary course of trade.
I think this last sentence gives the authority to classify the different citizens. In the first instance the manufacturer is protected all that he asks, namely, 30 per cent as against the large importer, and as against the man who pays the impost, the consumer, about 90 per cent. In the second case the situation is more glaring, as the protection afforded the manufacturer is a shade over 150 per cent. I would alter sections 40 and 41 to read as follows:
Whenever any duty is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof, when sold for home consumption, by the manufacturer thereof in quantities taking the maximum discount allowed by the manufacturer, in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time when the same were exported directly to Canada.
The value for duty of goods, when subject to any ad valorem duty, imported under other conditions than set out in the foregoing section, shall be the fair value of such goods as sold at the first sale in the principal markets of the country exporting same directly to Canada.
Then section 41 would follow, further confining the transaction in terms of Hade. I believe in free trade, Sir, but if we are to have a tariff at all let us by all means get rid of these injustices, such as the classifying of citizens in the application of the law. It is not the right of any government to discriminate between one citizen and another. That is not government; I would call it brigandage. If every citizen-and here comes the chief objection-was on an equality as regards the law, the chain of privilege, of which the politician forms the chief part, would be badly shattered. I have reason to believe that even the members of the cabinet, or many of them, are unaware to-day of the methods used to fleece the workers of this Dominion. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), speaking the other day, almost pitied the misguided members of the Progressive party in their plea for freer trade, but I venture to say that he himself has no idea of the extent to which the privileged class of this Dominion enjoy protection. Many of them, in fact, are protected against importations by consumers to the extent of about 150 per cent. I ask, Sir, is it any wonder that under these conditions our young men and women are going to the United States, a country of protection, it is true, but where callousness is nc^ embodied in legislation as it is in Canada 1
The Budget-Mr. Evans

For the year 1924 the per capita rate of duty in Canada was S14.65; during the same year in the United States it was $4.86. These figures have been taken from the Canada Year Book and also from the report of the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said that the tariff of the United States was about three times as high as that of Canada, but it is quite the other way. In 1924, $135,122,345 was taken in through the customs tariff, but it cost the country two and a half or three times that amount to collect it. This amount was collected on imports valued at $640,000,000, but the consumption of home manufactured goods was over $1,608,000,000, or just about three times as much as was imported. That would mean that the tariff cost the people of Canada last year some $391,000,000, only $135,000,000 of which went into the Dominion treasury. Over $256,000,000 went into the pockets of the privileged class, for which the people got nothing in return.
Sir Richard Cartwright calculated that the first thirteen years of tariff protection after 1879 and up to 1893, when the great Liberal convention was held in this city, took a billion dollars out of the pockets of the people for which they got no return whatsoever. During some of that time Canada Pad less than four millions of people. Industry in Canada does not need to lean as it does on Agriculture; it is quite capable of bearing its own burdens. Yesterday I came across an advertisement of the Brantford Cordage Company which is very illuminating in view of the deathlike howls from the Conservative party in this House. The Brantford Cordage Company claims on its own admission to be the greatest concern of its kind in the British Empire. The advertisement says:
The Brantford Cordage Company is an old-established business which started operations in 1901. The company now owns three mills, occupying seven and one-half acres at Brantford. It put into operation, last January, the third new mill with most modem equipment, increasing its productive capacity fifty per cent. The business has steadily expanded until to-day it is the largest manufacturer of binder twine in the British Empire.
We all know that twine is on the free list; there is free trade in twine. This is an advertisement offering shares to the public at eight per cent. The advertisement is very interesting in view of the fact that most of our manufacturers say they cannot live without some help from other industries. This is an industry standing on its own feet and not only that, it is doing very well, despite the fact that it is burdened with the high cost
of production due to the high cost of living in a protected country.
In conclusion, I wish to say that there is one thing that must be done. When Right Hon. W. S. Fielding brought in the first budget of this parliament, he emphasized the fact that we would seek reciprocity with the United States. I wonder what the government has to say that it has done during this last three years to bring about that measure which would be so beneficial to the whole of this country. We would like to know. The natural market for the cattle of this country is in the United States. They have the means of finishing beeves there that cannot be attained with the same ease and profit in any part of Canada, owing to the climate and the irregular rainfall over much of the agricultural parts of the Dominion. In the middle states, where com is grown to such an extent, there is always a great supply of the feed necessary to the finishing of beeves. They want our store cattle, which can be raised with ease and profit in western Canada on the tremendous surplus of roughage consequent in any grain growing area. I think, Sir, that everything should be done to bring about the freest kind of trade that is possible with our neighbours to the south. It is no use talking the way our friends of the opposition do and place an embargo on the export of everything we have to sell. We have done plenty in years gone by of this nosecutting business. The prosperity of this country lies in the greatest freedom of exchange that is possible to arrange with all countries, and while we would like to have free trade within the empire, the destiny of this country lies very largely with our neighbours to the south.
I think, Sir, one of the means of attaining this end will be to appoint a representative of this government at Washington, and I would urge on the government the necessity of doing this, and that we should not do anything further to create enmity and ill feeling between ourselves and the people of the neighbouring country, which khould prove the best market for our agricultural products.
I would like to remind the government that their own political platform is a contract which they have violated so far. The budget is today a violation of their own principles. I can never understand the attitude of men who believe that any contract when openly and

The Budget-Mr. Milne
honestly entered into can be violated without any excuse or under any set of circumstances with advantage to those who offered it as their pledge.
